docs.title: Warning
docs.text:
Danger

Georgian letters and any symbols other than the underscore _ are not allowed in the names of archives, folders, files, table columns, variables, functions, classes, arrays, tuples, etc. ❌

Only latin_letters_and_underscores; letter case does not matter much.

Tip

Georgian text can be written into table cells following UTF-8 encoding rules, and data written in the Latin alphabet can be converted for display with Georgian fonts.

docs.title: Transliterator
docs.text:
If table columns already contain entries in Georgian letters, you can easily convert them to Latin letters with PyQGIS code, so that they work with a Georgian font.

Python code

transliteration.py
# the header part can be skipped if we use the QGIS console.
# from qgis.core import (
#     QgsProject,
#     QgsVectorLayer,
#     QgsField
# )
# from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

# function for converting Georgian letters to Latin letters
def georgian_to_latin(text):
    transliteration_map = {
        'ა': 'a', 'ბ': 'b', 'გ': 'g', 'დ': 'd', 'ე': 'e', 'ვ': 'v', 'ზ': 'z', 
        'თ': 'T', 'ი': 'i', 'კ': 'k', 'ლ': 'l', 'მ': 'm', 'ნ': 'n', 'ო': 'o', 
        'პ': 'p', 'ჟ': 'J', 'რ': 'r', 'ს': 's', 'ტ': "t", 'უ': 'u', 
        'ფ': "f", 'ქ': "q", 'ღ': 'R', 'ყ': "y", 'შ': 'S', 'ჩ': 'C', 
        'ც': 'c', 'ძ': 'Z', 'წ': "w", 'ჭ': "W", 'ხ': 'x', 'ჯ': 'j', 
        'ჰ': 'h'
    }
    return ''.join(transliteration_map.get(char, char) for char in text)

# parameters
# the database
layer_path = "D:/GIS/werili/Geodatabase/bagdati.gdb"  
# the name of the layer in the database
layer_name = "Layer_name"  
# the column whose values are written in Georgian letters
input_field = "Layer_name"  
# the new column the information is copied into
output_field = "Layer_name"  

# load the vector layer
layer = QgsVectorLayer(f"{layer_path}|layername={layer_name}", layer_name, "ogr")

if not layer.isValid():
    print("Layer failed to load!")
else:
    print("Layer loaded successfully!")

# check whether the new column exists, add it, update
if output_field not in [field.name() for field in layer.fields()]:
    layer.dataProvider().addAttributes([QgsField(output_field, QVariant.String)])
    layer.updateFields()

# fill the column with the new values
with edit(layer):
    for feature in layer.getFeatures():
        georgian_text = feature[input_field]
        if georgian_text:  
            feature[output_field] = georgian_to_latin(georgian_text)
            layer.updateFeature(feature)

print("Transliteration complete.")

To download the data and upload the assignment, you need to sign in to Google Classroom classroom.google.com Stage I: setting up the folder

Connect QGIS to your main folder (from the Browser window, in Favorites).

Stage II: creating the shapefiles
  • Create a new project in QGIS Left Ctrl+N

Additional information

  • Digitizing the Tbilisi municipality is not allowed. Please choose another town or village. After choosing a settlement, if you are right on a zone boundary and it is unclear which zone you belong to:

    If most of the objects you plan to digitize are in zone 37 — choose 37.

    If most of them are in zone 38 — choose 38.

    If the location is in between and the objects are split evenly — choose 38.

    Zone 38 takes priority.

Basic information

  • Give the layers exact names and save them in the right folder. The layer template is below:

    • Point geometry: houses, schools, stations, buildings, stadiums
    • Line geometry: rivers, railways, roads, cable cars
    • Polygon geometry: parcels, houses, buildings, stadiums, forests

  • Each layer must have at least 10 features; there is no upper limit. If a layer does not have enough data, move to another layer and fill it in.

  • The colour or shape of the symbols is up to you — use your own judgement. However, a blue forest or a green river will be considered irrelevant.

  • Choose the correct UTM zone for the data.

  • Save the digitized data in the layers correctly.

  • Arrange the layers in the project in an organized way.

  • Save the compressed project file as: "Digitalization_project.qgz". Save the uncompressed project file as: "Digitalization_project.qgs". Left Ctrl+Left Shift+S

Note

To download the data and upload the assignment, you need to sign in to Google Classroom classroom.google.com Stage I: organizing the folder

  • Inside it, create these subfolders:

  • Geodatabase

  A[FirstName_LastName_GroupNumber_Assignment_Number] --> F{Style};

Connect QGIS to your main folder (from the Browser window).

Step II: adding a geodatabase

  • Open the "Chiatura_Digitalization_project.qgz" file from the folder and save a copy named "Geodatabase_project" Also save another .qgs file, "Chiatura_Geodatabase_project.qgs"

  • Create a new GeoPackage (with the .gpkg extension) in the Geodatabase folder.

  • With the DB Manager, import the layers that are in the project into the database.

  • Change the layers' sources (Change Data Source) from the shapefiles to the geodatabase feature classes.

  • Use formulas to calculate the information

For the ellipsoid * note that the formula is the part inside the brackets ( $x ) ( $y ) ( $length ) ( $area ) ( $perimeter )

For UTM ( length($geometry) ) ( area($geometry) ) ( perimeter($geometry) ) ( x($geometry) ) ( y($geometry) )

  • Fill in additional information in the attribute table:

For roads: - Create a field "name" and enter values such as "E117" or "S22" for highways, or "Shota Rustaveli Street" for streets. - Create a field "length_m" — to calculate each feature's length in meters (UTM zone). - Create a field "length_km" — to calculate the length in kilometers (UTM zone).

For rivers: - Create a field "name" — for example "Mtiuleti Aragvi" or "Gudamakari Aragvi". If a river has no name, enter "unnamed". - Create a field "length_m" — to calculate the length in meters (UTM zone). - Create a field "length_km" — to calculate the length in kilometers (UTM zone).

For bridges: - Create a field "type" — where you enter the type of bridge: "pedestrian", "vehicle", or "mixed".

For parcels: - Create the owner data fields: "name", "surname", "identity", "personal_id" - "name" — first name (String) - "surname" — surname (String) - "identity" — ID card/passport (String) - "personal_id" — personal number (Integer) - "area_sqm" — area in square meters (UTM zone) - "area_sqkm" — area in square kilometers (UTM zone) - "periemter_m" — perimeter in meters (UTM zone) - "perimeter_km" — perimeter in kilometers (UTM zone)

For restaurants, hotels and stadiums: - Create a field "name" — and enter the name of the object.

Additional information

Note: not every object type is described individually. Process each layer according to its geometry type:

  • Point features: Add fields for the X and Y coordinates (in your projected system).

  • Line features: Add fields for calculating the length:

  • "Length_m" — length in meters (UTM zone)

  • "Length_km" — length in kilometers (UTM zone)

  • Polygon features: Add fields for area and perimeter:

  • "Area_sqm" — area in square meters (UTM zone)
  • "Area_ha" — area in hectares

  • "Perimeter_m" — perimeter in meters

  • If some data is not available for a particular object, leave the cell empty.

Stage III: symbology

  • Split each layer into categories by the "name" and "attribute" fields, or by whatever field you have.

  • Add labels to each object, if you have entered the corresponding information.

  • Save each layer's style in the designated Style folder.

  • Compact the geodatabase with Compact Geodatabase.

  • Click the Save button to save the project, and close it.

docs.text: This page lists additional software recommended for the GIS basic course. These tools are not GIS platforms themselves, but they matter for managing and processing data and for running the course effectively.

docs.title: 🗜️ 1. 7-Zip
docs.text: 7-Zip is a free and open-source file archiver known for its high compression ratio.

docs.title: We use:
docs.text:
• GeoServer | version GeoServer 2.25.x

  • GeoServer is open-source server software built to share geographic data on the web. It uses OGC standards (WMS, WFS, WCS) and lets you read, serve and style spatial data from various formats, such as Shapefile, GeoTIFF, PostGIS and others.

GeoServer is actively used on web mapping platforms (e.g. Leaflet, OpenLayers), and it integrates with technologies such as QGIS, GeoNode, MapStore, Django and many more. It is available as a standalone server and is also integrated into many larger systems.

Tip

GeoServer runs in a Java-based environment and can be installed on Windows, Linux and macOS. Java 11 or 17 is recommended.

docs.title: After installation
docs.text:
• Check the Java environment: The JAVA_HOME variable must be set correctly, and a supported version (OpenJDK or Temurin) must be used. Java 17 or Java 21 Adoptium

  • Access the web interface: GeoServer has a built-in web interface that you open in a browser: http://localhost:8080/geoserver

  • Add spatial data: Start from the Data Stores menu – connect a data source (Shapefile, GeoPackage, PostGIS, etc.).

docs.title: 🧭 The history of GeoServer
docs.text: GeoServer is an open-source, Java-based program created for serving geospatial data on the web according to OGC standards.

docs.title: 🕰️ The beginning — code from the community
docs.text:
• 2001 – the GeoServer project started as an initiative of "The Open Planning Project" and became one of the first implementations of an OGC WFS server.
  • The goal was to create a widely available, standards-compliant geoserver.

docs.title: 🚀 Development and growth
docs.text:
• 2006 – GeoServer gains full WMS support and integrates with Google Earth.
  • 2008 – active integration with PostGIS and expansion of services begins.
  • 2010 – GeoServer becomes an official OSGeo project.
  • From 2020 – WPS (Web Processing Service), INSPIRE and REST API capabilities are refined.

docs.title: 🌍 GeoServer today
docs.text:
• ✅ supports the WMS, WFS, WCS and WMTS standards
  • ✅ combines data from many sources: Shapefile, GeoPackage, PostGIS, Oracle Spatial and others
  • ✅ has rich styling capabilities with SLD and CSS styles
  • ✅ runs in Docker, Tomcat and Spring Boot environments too
  • ✅ widely used in the public, research and commercial sectors

docs.title: 🎓 Why GeoServer?
docs.text:
• 💸 Completely free, with no license restrictions
  • 🌐 supports international standards and integrates with all leading GIS tools
  • 🧰 a powerful and flexible REST API
  • 🗺️ provides styling and presentation of data for web maps
  • 📦 available as WAR, Docker and standalone versions

docs.title: 🔗 Official links
docs.text:
• 🌍 Main site: https://geoserver.org
  • 📚 Documentation: https://docs.geoserver.org
  • 💻 GitHub code: https://github.com/geoserver/geoserver
  • 🐳 Docker version: https://hub.docker.com/r/oscarfonts/geoserver
  • 📜 Standards: https://www.ogc.org/standards

📌 GeoServer is a bridge between spatial data and the web — through it we can access, visualize and integrate open data in modern web technologies.

docs.title: We use:
docs.text:
• QGIS (Quantum GIS) | version QGIS 3.40 LTR

  • QGIS is an open-source platform for spatial analysis and map making that gives users a wide range of capabilities for collecting, managing, analysing and visualizing data. It is widely used in urban planning, environmental protection, transport analysis and public policy. QGIS has a strong modular architecture and a wide variety of extensions (plugins), and it can work both on the desktop and on web platforms. Using it supports decision-making, data-driven planning and a spatial view in real time.

Tip

QGIS runs on Windows, Linux and MacOS — without extra virtual machines. You can install it directly from the official website.

docs.title: After installation
docs.text: • Check the system's regional format It is best to have English (United States) active in the operating system

docs.title: 🧭 The history of QGIS
docs.text: QGIS (Quantum GIS) is a free and open-source geographic information system (GIS) that lets users process, explore and visualize geographic data.

docs.title: 🕰️ The beginning — from idea to program
docs.text:
• 2002 – The idea of QGIS came from the Canadian programmer Gary Sherman, who was looking for an open-source GIS tool to use on Linux.
  • His goal was to create a simple, fast, cross-platform GIS program supporting the main spatial formats.

docs.title: 🛠️ The first versions
docs.text:
• July 2002 – the project was started on SourceForge.
  • October 2002 – the first public version (v0.1) was released; it supported only raster layers and GRASS data.
  • The program was written with C++ and the Qt libraries, which made it cross-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS).

docs.title: 🚀 Development and growth
docs.text:
• 2004–2008 – support for vector layers, GRASS integration, a plugin system and a WMS client were added.
  • 2009 – the QGIS Project Steering Committee (PSC) was created to coordinate the project's development.
  • 2013 – the project changed its name from Quantum GIS → QGIS to make it easier to identify.
  • From 2016 – regular releases begin with the LTR (Long Term Release) model.

docs.title: 🌍 QGIS today
docs.text:
• ✅ translated into 50+ languages
  • ✅ has a versatile plugin system
  • ✅ integrates with GRASS GIS, SAGA, PostGIS, GeoServer, Python, R
  • ✅ used by environmental agencies, universities, municipalities and humanitarian organizations.

docs.title: 🎓 Why QGIS?
docs.text:
• 💸 It is free, with no license restrictions
  • 🧩 easily extended with plugins
  • 🛠️ runs on all major operating systems
  • 🌐 an active community and continuous development

docs.title: 🔗 Official links
docs.text:
• 🌍 Main site: https://qgis.org
  • 📦 Plugin repository: https://plugins.qgis.org
  • 🧪 Code and GitHub: https://github.com/qgis/QGIS

📌 QGIS is a symbol of freedom in the world of geographic data — with it you can make maps and carry out many kinds of geographic analysis.

docs.title: The Georgian term: დიგიტალიზაცია vs დიგიტიზაცია
docs.text:
This page is about Georgian terminology. In English the process is called digitization (or digitizing).

✅ Correct in Georgian: დიგიტალიზაცია (digitalizatsia) ❌ Incorrect in Georgian: დიგიტიზაცია (digitizatsia)

docs.title: 🧾 Definition
docs.text:
Digitization means converting physical or analog data into a digital format.

📌 For example:

Scanning a paper document and saving it as a PDF file.

docs.title: 🧠 Why not „დიგიტიზაცია“?
docs.text:
• The word „დიგიტიზაცია“ is terminologically incorrect in Georgian.
  • The correctly adopted Georgian form of the English digitization is დიგიტალიზაცია.
  • This term is established in Georgian technical and academic vocabulary.

docs.title: 📚 Conclusion
docs.text: In Georgian, use only დიგიტალიზაცია ✅ It is the correct, standard form in the Georgian language.

docs.title: 🗺️ Georeferencing a topographic map in QGIS
docs.text: Georeferencing a topographic map means placing it on geographic coordinates, so that it can be overlaid and analysed together with modern maps or in geographic information systems (GIS). The process involves assigning real coordinates to specific points on the map.

docs.title: 1. Getting a topographic map
docs.text: Find a scanned or digital topographic map (JPEG, TIFF or PNG).

docs.title: 2. Required programs and data
docs.text:
• QGIS (version 3.x or newer)
  • a scanned topographic map (a raster image)
  • objects with known coordinates, or a graticule

docs.title: 🛠️ Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
Step I: loading the map in QGIS
  • Open QGIS
  • In the main window, in the Browser Panel, right-click Favorites, choose your working directory and add it.
Step II: starting georeferencing
  1. Go to Layer > Georeferencer...
  2. Open the image (File > Open Raster)
Step III: marking ground control points (GCPs)
  1. Mark matching points on the image and on a base map (OSM, Google Earth or another).
  2. Use at least 4 well-distributed points.
  3. Set the transformation method:
Method When to use Linear (1st Order) little distortion Polynomial 2/3 medium/strong distortion Thin Plate Spline for smooth stretching (rubber sheeting)
  1. Check the RMS error (View GCP Table)
Step IV: running the transformation
  • After choosing: Raster > Georeferencer > Start Georeferencing
  • The map is stretched based on the given points.
Step V: saving the georeferenced image
  • Use File > Save Raster As...
  • Format: GeoTIFF (.tif) or another georeferenced format
  • Make sure the saved file has the correct CRS (e.g. EPSG:32638)

docs.title: ✅ Checking the accuracy
docs.text:
• Compare it with other spatial data (e.g. buildings, roads).
  • If needed, edit or add new GCPs and georeference the map again.

docs.title: 💡 Additional tips
docs.text:
• Use as many GCPs as possible for a better result.
  • Choose easily recognizable objects — road intersections, river confluences, peaks.
  • Make a backup copy before you finish saving.

🗂️ The result is a georeferenced GeoTIFF or an updated raster file, ready for analysis and for use on maps in QGIS.

docs.title: 📍 Types of georeferencing transformations
docs.text: Georeferencing uses different transformation types, which differ in complexity, the number of ground control points (GCPs) needed and where they are used. Below is an overview of the main transformations, with their pros and cons.

docs.title: 🔹 Linear (Affine) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: used for a linear transformation of the map — translation, rotation, scaling and shear.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 3
  • Pros ✅:
  • simple and fast to compute.
  • preserves straight lines and the ratios of angles.
  • ideal when the map is not distorted.
  • Cons ❌:
  • does not account for non-linear distortion.
  • inaccurate results on heavily distorted maps.

docs.title: 🔸 Second Order Polynomial transformation
docs.text:
• Description: uses quadratic terms to model non-linear distortion of the map.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 6
  • Pros ✅:
  • fits non-linear distortion better.
  • can straighten bent parts of the map.
  • Cons ❌:
  • can introduce extra distortion.
  • needs more control points and more precision.
  • sometimes over-transformation damages the geometry.

docs.title: 🔹 Third Order Polynomial transformation
docs.text:
• Description: by including cubic terms it can correct complex distortion.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 10
  • Pros ✅:
  • ideal for heavily distorted historical maps.
  • offers maximum flexibility in correcting distortion.
  • Cons ❌:
  • very sensitive to small errors in the GCPs.
  • often causes unnatural warping at the edges of the map.
  • hard to control, with a risk of extra distortion.

docs.title: 🔸 Spline (Thin Plate Spline) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: a non-linear interpolation method that fits the control points as closely as possible.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 10+ (recommended)
  • Pros ✅:
  • gives high accuracy at the control points.
  • ideal for strong distortion.
  • Cons ❌:
  • unpredictable distortion can occur between control points.
  • does not preserve geometric ratios.
  • the result is hard to predict.

docs.title: 🔹 Projective (Perspective) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: used to correct perspective distortion, e.g. for obliquely taken photos.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 4
  • Pros ✅:
  • works well for aerial photos.
  • can correctly straighten tilted elements.
  • Cons ❌:
  • suitable only for specific situations.
  • not a universal solution.

docs.title: 🔚 Conclusion
docs.text:
Transformation GCPs needed Advantage Limitation Linear (Affine) 3 fast, simple does not handle non-linear distortion 2nd Order Polynomial 6 better fit to distortion very sensitive to errors 3rd Order Polynomial 10 maximum flexibility risk of extra distortion Spline (Thin Plate Spline) 10+ high accuracy at the GCPs unpredictable in other areas Projective (Perspective) 4 ideal for correcting tilt limited range of use

📌 Tip: when choosing a transformation, consider how distorted the map is, how many GCPs are available and the accuracy you want. For example, a Linear transformation is enough for simple maps, while Spline or Third Order Polynomial suits old or heavily distorted maps better.

docs.title: 📐 Datum
docs.text:
A datum is a mathematical model that defines the shape, size and orientation of the Earth's surface. The Earth is not a perfect sphere — it is an oblate ellipsoid, a slightly flattened sphere.

Datums are essential for representing spatial data correctly and are used in geodesy — the science of measuring and modelling the Earth's surface.

docs.title: 📌 Kinds of reference surfaces
docs.text:
• Ellipsoid – a smooth surface that approximates the shape of the Earth.
  • Geoid – an irregular surface that reflects the Earth's gravity field.

docs.title: 🌍 Two main types of datum:
docs.text:
1. Geographic datum Used to define the geometry of the Earth's surface. Usually based on an ellipsoid.

#### Main geographic datums: - WGS84 – the most common; used by GPS. - NAD83 – for North America. - ETRF89 – for European territories.

  1. Projected datum Used to project the Earth's 3D surface into 2D space. Often represented by a cylindrical or flat (planar) system.

#### Main projected systems: - UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) – for large-scale maps. - SPCS (State Plane Coordinate System) – for maps of small areas.

docs.title: 🗺️ Projection
docs.text:
A projection is a method of representing the Earth's three-dimensional surface on a two-dimensional map.

The Earth is a 3D object and a map is 2D. That is why a projection is needed to create an accurate, readable map.

docs.title: 📊 The difference between a datum and a projection
docs.text:
• A datum defines the size, shape and orientation of the Earth's surface.
  • A projection transforms that surface onto a flat 2D map.

docs.title: 📌 Why do we need projections?
docs.text:
• Maps are easier to read than a globe.
  • Maps allow accurate measurements (distance, area, angle).
  • Maps are essential for visualizing and analysing spatial data.

docs.title: 🌐 Mercator Projection
docs.text:
• A cylindrical projection.
  • Preserves direction (True North).
  • Used for navigation.
  • Distorts the size of objects near the poles (e.g. Greenland looks bigger than it really is).

docs.title: 🌐 Lambert Conformal Conic
docs.text:
• Preserves shape and size near the standard parallels.
  • Often used for the USA and Canada.

docs.title: 🌐 Albers Equal Area
docs.text:
• Preserves area.
  • Suitable for comparing the size of regions.
  • Popular on maps of the USA.

docs.title: 🌐 Robinson Projection
docs.text:
• A compromise projection.
  • Balances shape, size and distance.
  • Widely used on world maps — visually appealing.

docs.title: 🔚 Summary
docs.text:
• A datum defines the model of the Earth (ellipsoid or geoid).
  • A projection transforms the 3D surface onto a 2D map.
  • Both are essential for the accuracy and usability of spatial data.
  • The choice depends on the map's purpose and the area it covers.
