docs.title: 🌐 WGS 84 EPSG:4326
docs.text:
One of the most widely used global systems, used by GPS.

The new rectangular system - Ellipsoid: WGS 84 - Projection: UTM - EPSG: 32638 - UTM zone 38N - EPSG: 32637 - UTM zone 37N

docs.title: 🗺️ Web projection (Web Mercator)
docs.text:
Matches Google Maps, OpenStreetMap and other web maps.

  • EPSG: 3857 - Pseudo-Mercator

The old rectangular system - Ellipsoid: Pulkovo 1942 - Projection: Gauss-Kruger - EPSG: 28408 - zone 8 - EPSG: 28468 - zone 8N - EPSG: 28407 - zone 7 - EPSG: 28467 - zone 7N

docs.title: 📐 Vertical coordinate system (heights)
docs.text: EGM96 height - Unit: meter - Static (based on a fixed datum) - Celestial body: Earth - EPSG: 5773

docs.title: 🆔 What does an EPSG code mean?
docs.text: An EPSG code is a unique identifier for a coordinate system. It defines: - the ellipsoid model (e.g. WGS 84) - the datum - the projection method (e.g. UTM) - the units (meter, degree)

docs.title: 🔍 Breaking down an EPSG code with examples
docs.text:
EPSG:4326 - Name: WGS 84 - Type: geographic system - Units: degrees - Use: GPS, global data

EPSG:32638 - Name: WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N - Type: projected system - Projection: UTM - Units: meter - Use: Georgia and neighbouring regions

📚 Why does this matter? Using the right EPSG code ensures: - accurate geographic alignment of data - correct distance and area calculations - compatibility between GIS programs

docs.title: 🏔️ Georgia's national height system
docs.text: 📌 What is this system? A single vertical system for determining heights across the whole country.

docs.title: 🧭 Reference level
docs.text: It is based on the mean level of the Baltic Sea — the "Kronstadt zero". Heights are measured relative to the geoid.

docs.title: 🏗️ Why does it matter?
docs.text:
• Consistency – standardized data
  • Infrastructure – correct heights for projects
  • GIS and maps – DEMs, terrain analysis
  • Hydrology – water flow, risk assessment

docs.title: 📐 How do we use it?
docs.text:
GPS often gives ellipsoidal heights — a geoid model is needed to convert them to the national system.

In GIS (e.g. QGIS): - load a DEM based on the national height system - assign a projected CRS, e.g. EPSG:32638 - make sure the heights are given relative to the Baltic Sea level

docs.title: 📦 Apache Parquet — a columnar data format
docs.text: Apache Parquet is an open, columnar data format optimized for storing and transferring large-scale analytical data efficiently.

docs.title: 🔍 Why Parquet?
docs.text:
• Columnar storage – data is stored by column rather than by row, which speeds up analytical queries.
  • High compression – data compresses better because one column holds data of the same type.
  • Multi-language support – it can be used with Python (pandas, pyarrow), R, Java, Spark and other technologies.
  • Fits the Hadoop ecosystem – compatible with Hive, Impala, Drill, Spark and others.

docs.title: 🧱 Structure
docs.text:
A Parquet file is made of:

  • Row groups – chunks of data that contain rows.
  • Column chunks – the data of each column inside a row group.
  • Pages – a column chunk is divided into pages. Each page contains data or metadata.

docs.title: 📈 Advantages
docs.text: Advantage Description 🚀 Fast reading Especially efficient when only some columns are needed 💾 Space savings Compresses well and reduces storage load 🔁 Scalability Easily adapts to large data streams 🔌 Ecosystem integration Works well with Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto and others

docs.title: 🧪 How to use it in Python?
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

# convert a CSV to Parquet
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
df.to_parquet("data.parquet")

# read a Parquet file
df_parquet = pd.read_parquet("data.parquet")

💡 Note: the pyarrow or fastparquet library is needed.

docs.title: 🆚 Parquet vs CSV
docs.text: Characteristic Parquet CSV Storage type Columnar Row-based File size Small Large Read speed High Low Metadata Yes No

docs.title: 🌐 Areas of use
docs.text:
• data analytics and BI
  • storing large volumes of data (data lakes)
  • ETL processes
  • preprocessing data for machine learning

docs.title: 📚 Resources
docs.text:
• Apache Parquet official website
  • Parquet and PyArrow documentation

docs.title: ✅ Summary
docs.text: Apache Parquet is a modern, efficient and fast file format for analysing large volumes of data. It is especially useful when only some columns need to be read or when data must be stored compactly.

docs.title: 1. 📦 Geospatial databases
docs.text: A geographic database is a system for storing and managing geometric objects (point, line, polygon) and the attribute data linked to them.

docs.title: 📁 Common formats:
docs.text:
• GeoPackage (.gpkg) – modern and flexible, the main QGIS format. Stores several layers (vector, raster), styles and tabular data in one file.
  • File Geodatabase (.gdb) – ESRI's proprietary format, the main ArcGIS database.
  • Personal Geodatabase (.mdb) – outdated, based on Microsoft Access.
  • SpatiaLite (.sqlite) – based on SQLite, with support for geodata. Works well in QGIS.
  • GeoJSON (.geojson) – ideal for web maps, readable as text.
  • XML (.xml) – for transferring metadata and geostructure.

🔎 See also: ESRI Technical Paper – Data Management

docs.title: 📌 Data sources and correction
docs.text:
🧭 Primary sources of GIS data can be: - remote sensing data (e.g. satellites, drones) - physical registry records (the public registry) - field surveys and GPS measurements - cadastral or regulatory plans

🔧 Correcting data: - correcting attributes with the layer's Field Calculator - determining/changing the CRS or projection - the Join and Relate functions for linking elements

docs.title: 🎛️ In QGIS:
docs.text:
• With the Data Source Manager you can add data from various sources: .shp, .gpkg, PostGIS, WFS/WMS.
  • With the Processing Toolbox you can import, export, clean and filter data.

docs.title: 📐 Creating geometry:
docs.text:
• 🟢 points: schools, houses, stops
  • 🔵 lines: roads, rivers, railways
  • 🟣 polygons: forests, parcels, stadiums

docs.title: 🧹 Optimizing data:
docs.text:
• Delete Layer/Table
  • Vacuum / Compact Database (SpatiaLite/SQLite)
  • Repair Layer Paths – when the data source is lost (the Layer is broken problem)

docs.title: 3. 📊 Attribute tables
docs.text:
• Every vector layer has its own attribute table.
  • You can add, change or calculate column values (with the Field Calculator).
  • Column types: text, numeric, date, boolean.

docs.title: 4. 🆔 OBJECTID / Feature ID
docs.text:
• In QGIS it is known as the FID (Feature ID), and in ArcGIS as OBJECTID.
  • It is generated automatically and is unique for each feature.
  • It is different from Shapefile IDs, which are just sequence numbers.

docs.title: 5. 🔣 Working with fields and assigning symbols
docs.text:
• Add new columns (fields): text, integer, decimal.
  • Use short column names (especially with Shapefiles — at most 10 characters).
  • Use symbol categorization: colours, shapes and symbols with Categorized, Graduated, Rule-Based.

🛑 What happens if a category is missing? - Some features appear on the map with the default symbol. - The attribute table cannot reflect the thematic group.

📍 Solution: Layer Properties > Symbology – add or remove the necessary categories.

docs.title: 6. 🎨 Saving and loading layer styles
docs.text:
• Saving a layer style in QGIS: .qml (QGIS Layer Style) or .sld (OGC Standard).
  • You can use styles:
  • in the same project
  • in other projects, or to share with colleagues

docs.title: 7. 📏 Adding geometry properties
docs.text:
Adding geometric characteristics to the attribute table: - X and Y coordinates (Decimal Degrees) - Length - Area - Perimeter

🔧 Use the Field Calculator: 

$area / 10000  -- area in hectares
length($geometry)  -- line length
x($geometry), y($geometry) -- coordinates

docs.title: 8. 🎁 Packaging and sharing maps in QGIS:
docs.text:
Use Project > Save to GeoPackage – all the project's layers in one file

Export > Save As Image/PDF – an image of the map

QGIS Project Package (.qgz) – the whole project file with styles and data

📘 Conclusion

Geographic databases and data management skills are essential for a professional GIS user. QGIS and ArcGIS both offer versatile tools for organizing, cleaning and presenting data. Students should know which format, data source or structure is best for what, and how to act in each case.

docs.title: 🗺️ KML / KMZ — a format for exchanging spatial data
KML (Keyhole Markup Language)
docs.text:
KML stands for Keyhole Markup Language. It was originally created by Keyhole Inc., which Google acquired in 2004.

It is an XML-based file format designed for displaying geographic data in programs such as Google Earth and Google Maps.

KML files can contain: - points (placemarks), - lines and polygons (paths, areas), - images and text — to describe locations or layers.

The file extension is .kml, and the compressed variant is .kmz — it contains one or more KML files and accompanying data in ZIP format.

📌 Common use cases: - planning and visualizing routes - analysing GPS tracks - geo-overlaying photos - creating tours in Google Earth

KML files also support time data, which lets you create animations of changes over time — for example: - traffic movement - climate events

Coordinates in KML are written in this order: - longitude, - latitude, - and altitude.

KML is supported by many platforms: - Google Earth - ArcGIS / QGIS - NASA World Wind - CesiumJS and other web applications

KML can use network links (NetworkLinks), which let you bring in dynamic content from the internet. — ideal for real-time data (live GPS, sensors).

KML is an OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) standard, which means it is officially recognized for exchanging geographic data.

📦 KMZ is a compressed KML file that stores every needed element in one file (including layers, photos, styles and coordinates) — convenient for sharing and for use in Google Earth.

docs.title: Placemark altitude settings
docs.text: A placemark's altitude settings define the reference level from which height is measured on a 3D map (e.g. in Google Earth).

docs.title: Placemark altitude settings as a diagram
docs.text:
graph LR
    Placemark["📍 Placemark altitude settings"] --> ClampedGround["🟫 Clamped to ground<br>📌 on the ground surface <br> ⛔ altitude cannot be set"]
    Placemark --> ClampedSeaFloor["🌊 Clamped to sea floor<br>📌 on the sea floor<br>⛔ altitude cannot be set"]
    Placemark --> RelativeGround["📐 Relative to ground<br>📏 measured from the ground surface<br>✅ altitude can be entered"]
    Placemark --> RelativeSeaFloor["📐 Relative to sea floor<br>📏 measured from the sea floor<br>✅ altitude can be entered"]
    Placemark --> Absolute["📏 Absolute<br>🌍 from sea level<br>✅ altitude can be entered"]

docs.title: 1. Clamped to ground
docs.text:
• 📌 Description: the point sticks directly to the ground surface.
  • ⛔ Entering an altitude by hand is not possible.
  • 🧭 Example: mark a tree on a hill — it appears on the ground, on top of the hill.

docs.title: 2. Clamped to sea floor
docs.text:
• 📌 Description: the point is placed on the sea floor, not on the water surface.
  • ⛔ Entering an altitude is not possible.
  • 🧭 Example: if you want to show where a submarine sank, it appears on the sea floor.

docs.title: 3. Relative to ground
docs.text:
• 📌 Description: the altitude is measured from the ground surface.
  • ✅ You can give a specific number of meters/feet.
  • 🧭 Example: "100 m" means the point appears 100 meters above the surface — for example, a drone or a tower.

docs.title: 4. Relative to sea floor
docs.text:
• 📌 Description: the altitude is measured from the sea floor.
  • ✅ You can say how many meters above the sea floor it is.
  • 🧭 Example: an underwater robot 20 meters above the sea floor.

docs.title: 5. Absolute (from sea level)
docs.text:
• 📌 Description: the altitude is defined from sea level (Mean Sea Level - MSL).
  • ✅ The value in meters is an absolute height, as on the global model of the map.
  • 🧭 Example: "2000 m" means the point is at the same height as Bakhmaro or Gudauri.

📎 Note: In Google Earth these settings are especially important for correctly defining 3D objects, visibility and animations.

docs.title: 📚 What is GeoNetwork? — simply, for students
🧾 In short: what is GeoNetwork?
docs.text:
GeoNetwork is an open-source system for managing spatial metadata. It helps organizations and users search, share and manage metadata.

🎯 Its main goal is:

better organization and discovery of geographic data over the internet.

docs.title: 🔍 What does metadata mean?
docs.text:
Metadata means a description of data. For example, information about a map layer: - who created it? - when was it created? - what does it represent? - what format is it in? - how can it be used?

📌 GeoNetwork is focused on storing and finding exactly this information in a structured way.

docs.title: 🌐 How does GeoNetwork work?
docs.text: Capability Description 🔎 Search Find map layers, data, documents 📋 Description See a layer's author, license, tags, location 📁 Catalogues Organize data by theme 📤 Export / import With the ISO, INSPIRE and Dublin Core standards 🧩 Integration Works with GeoServer, GeoNode, CKAN and other systems

docs.title: 🧪 For students: what can GeoNetwork be used for?
docs.text:
• 📁 finding specific layers or data for a project
  • 📝 describing their own uploaded layers with correct metadata
  • 🧠 learning international standards (ISO 19115)
  • 🌍 using it in SDI (Spatial Data Infrastructure) projects

docs.title: 👨‍💻 The technical side
docs.text: GeoNetwork is built on: - Java and the Spring Framework - XML data processing - a PostgreSQL database - a connection to GeoServer (e.g. for layer metadata)

docs.title: 📚 How is it different from GeoNode?
docs.text:
Characteristic GeoNode GeoNetwork Serving layers ✅ yes ❌ no Metadata ✅ yes, but simpler ✅ detailed, standardized Map visualization ✅ yes 🔸 viewing only Integration with SDI medium ✅ high ISO standards partly ✅ full support

➡️ GeoNode is more of a GIS platform, while GeoNetwork is a metadata catalogue system.

docs.title: 🔗 More links
docs.text:
• GeoNetwork site: https://geonetwork-opensource.org
  • Documentation: https://geonetwork-opensource.org/manuals
  • GitHub project: https://github.com/geonetwork/core-geonetwork

docs.title: 🌍 What is GeoNode, and how can students use it
🧾 Simply: what is GeoNode?
docs.text:
GeoNode is an open-source platform for managing and sharing geographic data.

🎯 Goal: 👉 to make it easy even for non-geographers to create maps and to upload and share data over the internet.

📦 GeoNode combines: - 🗂️ a data store (vector/rasters) - 🗺️ tools for creating web maps - 👥 user management and access control - 🔗 integration with GeoServer, PostGIS and other systems

docs.title: 🚀 What does GeoNode do in practice?
docs.text: Function Description 📤 Uploading data Students can upload SHP, GeoTIFF, CSV 🗺️ Creating maps Easily add layers and create web maps 👥 Sharing Share maps or data with a link 🔐 Access management Users can decide who can or cannot see the data 📊 Metadata The system stores information about layers (author, project, description)

docs.title: 🧪 For students: how to use GeoNode
docs.text:
1. Go to the platform (e.g. https://your-geonode-instance.org)
  2. Register or sign in
  3. Upload a file – use the Upload menu, choose SHP/GeoTIFF/CSV
  4. Add a description and metadata
  5. Create a map – use the Map Composer
  6. Share the map or data with a link or by embedding it (iframe)

docs.title: 🔧 GeoNode runs on these technologies
docs.text:
• GeoServer – serving layers (WMS/WFS)
  • PostGIS – storing data in a spatial database
  • Django – the website framework (in Python)
  • React – the visual map interface
  • MapStore – the map management interface

docs.title: 📚 How will it help students?
docs.text: ✅ easily process, share and present spatial data ✅ work in teams on projects ✅ learn data management, access and metadata ✅ gain experience on a real GIS platform

docs.title: 🔗 More links
docs.text:
• GeoNode official site: https://geonode.org
  • Documentation: https://docs.geonode.org
  • GitHub project: https://github.com/GeoNode/geonode

docs.title: GeoJSON formats from QGIS and ArcGIS
docs.text:
GeoJSON is a format for exchanging spatial data. It is based on the JSON structure and is widely used in web maps and GIS programs.

Coordinate order

GeoJSON always lists coordinates as [longitude, latitude]. The examples below use approximate coordinates of Tbilisi, Kutaisi and Batumi.

docs.title: 📌 1. QGIS – Newline Delimited GeoJSON (.geojsonl or .ndgeojson)
docs.text:
• Description: each line holds one GeoJSON object (feature).
  • Use: useful for streaming large data or for parallel processing.
  • QGIS export: when exporting, choose Newline delimited GeoJSON.
  • Example:
{"type":"Feature","geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[44.8,41.7]},"properties":{"name":"Tbilisi"}}
{"type":"Feature","geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[42.7,42.27]},"properties":{"name":"Kutaisi"}}

docs.title: 📌 2. QGIS – standard GeoJSON
docs.text:
• Description: the whole FeatureCollection is in one JSON structure.
  • Use: for general purposes, for display on web maps.
  • QGIS export: choose GeoJSON.
  • Example:
{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {
      "type": "Feature",
      "geometry": {
        "type": "Point",
        "coordinates": [44.8, 41.7]
      },
      "properties": {
        "name": "Tbilisi"
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "Feature",
      "geometry": {
        "type": "Point",
        "coordinates": [42.7, 42.27]
      },
      "properties": {
        "name": "Kutaisi"
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 📌 3. ArcGIS – Formatted GeoJSON
docs.text:
• Description: a nicely formatted JSON structure, easy for people to read.
  • ArcGIS Pro: when exporting you can save and format the output as JSON.
  • Use: for writing into code, for transferring through an API.
{
  "type": "FeatureCollection",
  "features": [
    {
      "type": "Feature",
      "geometry": {
        "type": "Point",
        "coordinates": [41.64, 41.65]
      },
      "properties": {
        "name": "Batumi"
      }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: 📌 4. ArcGIS – Non-formatted (Minified) GeoJSON
docs.text:
• Description: all the information is on one line — a compact format.
  • Use: when file size or transfer speed matters.
  • Example:
{"type":"FeatureCollection","features":[{"type":"Feature","geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[41.64,41.65]},"properties":{"name":"Batumi"}}]}

docs.title: 🔚 Summary
docs.text: Format Formatted Multi-line Use QGIS – Newline delimited ❌ ✅ Data streaming QGIS – Standard GeoJSON ✅ ✅ Web maps ArcGIS – Formatted ✅ ✅ Reading in code ArcGIS – Minified ❌ ❌ Fast transfer

docs.title: 🌐 Spatial web services: WMS, WFS, WMTS, WCS and others
docs.text: Spatial web services let us exchange, display and analyse geographic data over the internet. They are based on OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) standards.

docs.title: 🗺️ WMS – Web Map Service
docs.text:
• What it does: generates a map image (PNG, JPEG) on the server and sends it to the client.
  • Use: map visualization — but not attribute analysis.
  • Format: only an image; you cannot read the data directly.

Example request: 

https://myserver/geoserver/wms?SERVICE=WMS&REQUEST=GetMap&...

📌 Used in Leaflet, OpenLayers, QGIS and other viewers.

docs.title: 🧾 WFS – Web Feature Service
docs.text:
• What it does: sends geographic features (e.g. buildings, roads) with their attributes.
  • Format: GML, GeoJSON or other data-oriented formats.
  • Benefit: allows querying, filtering and working with editable data.

Example request: 

https://myserver/geoserver/wfs?SERVICE=WFS&REQUEST=GetFeature&...

📌 Used for analysis, data export and filling in forms.

docs.title: 🗺️ WMTS – Web Map Tile Service
docs.text:
• What it does: sends pre-generated map tiles for fixed scales.
  • Speed: faster than WMS, because it sends the client images that are already cut into tiles.
  • Format: PNG, JPEG tiles.

Example URL (RESTful): 

https://myserver/geoserver/gwc/service/wmts?layer=mylayer&...

📌 Ideal for high-performance maps (e.g. basemaps).

docs.title: 🧊 WCS – Web Coverage Service
docs.text:
• What it does: delivers geographic raster data (coverage), for example terrain or satellite images.
  • Format: TIFF, GRID, NetCDF and others.
  • Use: for analysis and raster modelling.

Example request: 

https://myserver/geoserver/wcs?SERVICE=WCS&REQUEST=GetCoverage&...

📌 Used for modelling the environment, climate and land use.

docs.title: 🛰️ CSW – Catalogue Service for the Web
docs.text:
• searching for and delivering metadata.
  • used in spatial data infrastructures (SDI).

docs.title: 📡 SOS – Sensor Observation Service
docs.text:
• access to sensor data (e.g. temperature, pressure).
  • support for internet-connected sensors.

docs.title: 🧪 WPS – Web Processing Service
docs.text:
• running spatial analysis operations over the internet (buffer, clip, intersection).
  • uses complex server-side processing.

docs.title: 📚 Comparison table
docs.text: Service Data type Format Use WMS Image PNG, JPEG Map visualization WFS Features GML, GeoJSON Attribute analysis WMTS Tiles PNG, JPEG Fast tiles WCS Rasters GeoTIFF, GRID Analytical rasters CSW Metadata XML Finding resources SOS Sensors XML, JSON Sensor data WPS Processes XML Spatial analysis

docs.title: 🎯 Conclusion
docs.text: OGC web services are essential for any web GIS system. Each service serves a specific purpose — images, attribute data, rasters or analysis. Choosing the right service depends on what you want — viewing, querying, analysis or filtering.

docs.title: 💻 The Windows environment and configuring GeoServer
🧭 What is the Windows environment?
docs.text:
The Windows environment means the operating system the user works in (e.g. Windows 10, 11), together with its environment variables, programs, libraries and file structure.

Main components: - 📂 the file system (C:\, D:\, etc.) - ⚙️ environment variables - 🧩 installed programs (.exe) - 🔁 processes and services (Services, Startup apps)

  • The Windows environment is the computer's working environment where every program runs, including Java, Python, QGIS and GeoServer.

docs.title: 🌍 GeoServer in the Windows environment
docs.text:
GeoServer is open-source server software that runs on the Java platform. GeoServer needs:

  • ✅ a correctly configured Java environment (JDK or JRE)
  • ✅ server space (folders, libraries)
  • ✅ the ability of Windows to run scripts (BAT)

docs.title: On Windows, GeoServer can be started in two ways:
docs.text:
1. ZIP version – started with the startup.bat file
  2. Windows Installer (EXE) – installed automatically as a service

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuring the Java environment (for GeoServer)
docs.text:
1. Download Temurin OpenJDK: 🔗 https://adoptium.net/en-GB/temurin/releases

  2. Install the JDK (JDK 17 is recommended)

  3. Set the environment variable:

  4. Variable Name: JAVA_HOME

  5. Variable Value: C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-17.x.x

  6. Add this path to the system Path variable: 

    %JAVA_HOME%\bin

  7. Check it in cmd:

java -version

docs.title: Option 1: the ZIP version
docs.text:
1. Download the GeoServer ZIP archive: 🔗 https://geoserver.org/download

  2. Extract it to a folder (e.g. C:\geoserver)

  3. Run the startup.bat file from the bin folder

docs.title: 📌 Example: what happens in the Windows environment
docs.text: Element Description JAVA_HOME An environment variable that points to where Java is startup.bat A Windows script that starts GeoServer %PATH% A system variable that gives access to java.exe C:\geoserver\data_dir GeoServer's data directory localhost:8080/geoserver The address of the GeoServer UI in the browser

docs.title: 🧠 Why does this matter?
docs.text:
• The correct configuration of the Windows environment decides whether GeoServer will work.
  • GeoServer will not start without a Java environment.
  • Students should know how to start server applications and how to work with system variables.

docs.title: 📚 Additional resources
docs.text:
• GeoServer User Guide
  • JAVA_HOME – official explanation
  • Adoptium Temurin

docs.title: Using the XML format in QGIS
docs.text: QGIS (Quantum GIS) uses the XML format in many places, mainly for configuration and for describing data. Below is a list of the main cases.

docs.title: 🔧 1. Project files (.qgs / .qgz)
docs.text:
• .qgs is an XML file that stores the whole project configuration:
  • layer sources
  • styles (symbology)
  • projection (CRS)
  • print layouts

  • labelling and more

  • .qgz is a compressed version that contains the .qgs XML file inside.

Example: 

<qgis projectname="MyProject" version="3.40">
  <layer-tree-group name="Layers">
    <layer-tree-layer id="roads2020" name="Roads" ... />
  </layer-tree-group>
</qgis>

docs.title: 🗺️ 2. SLD (Styled Layer Descriptor)
docs.text:
• SLD is an OGC standard that describes layer styles in XML.
  • It is used to transfer styles to other platforms, e.g. GeoServer.

docs.title: 🖼️ 3. QML files (QGIS Layer Style)
docs.text:
• QML is QGIS's own XML style format.
  • It stores:
  • symbology
  • colour classification
  • labelling settings
  • It is not the same as SLD, but both are XML formats.

docs.title: 🖨️ 4. Print templates (.qpt)
docs.text:
• .qpt files store map print templates in XML.
  • They include elements such as the map, legend, logo, scale, etc.

docs.title: 📦 5. Processing models (.model3)
docs.text:
• .model3 is a model saved in XML, used in the QGIS Processing Toolbox.
  • It describes:
  • the tools
  • the parameters
  • how they connect

Example: 

<model>
  <algorithm id="native:buffer">
    <parameter name="DISTANCE" value="10"/>
  </algorithm>
</model>

docs.title: 🔌 6. Plugin metadata
docs.text:
• QGIS plugins sometimes use a metadata.xml file for detailed information.
  • This XML is used when registering a plugin in the QGIS Plugin Repository.

docs.title: 🧩 7. UI form templates (.ui)
docs.text:
• Forms created with Qt Designer are stored in XML files with the .ui extension.
  • They are used to design QGIS attribute forms.

docs.title: 📝 Summary
docs.text:
Use Extension Format Description Project .qgs, .qgz XML All project settings Layer style (QGIS standard) .qml XML Symbols, labels Layer style (OGC standard) .sld XML Styled Layer Descriptor Print template .qpt XML Map print design Processing Toolbox model .model3 XML A visual analytical model Form design (Qt Designer) .ui XML Attribute form template

If you have more questions, write to me with specific examples or use cases.

docs.title: The Georgian term: დიგიტალიზაცია vs დიგიტიზაცია
docs.text:
This page is about Georgian terminology. In English the process is called digitization (or digitizing).

✅ Correct in Georgian: დიგიტალიზაცია (digitalizatsia) ❌ Incorrect in Georgian: დიგიტიზაცია (digitizatsia)

docs.title: 🧾 Definition
docs.text:
Digitization means converting physical or analog data into a digital format.

📌 For example:

Scanning a paper document and saving it as a PDF file.

docs.title: 🧠 Why not „დიგიტიზაცია“?
docs.text:
• The word „დიგიტიზაცია“ is terminologically incorrect in Georgian.
  • The correctly adopted Georgian form of the English digitization is დიგიტალიზაცია.
  • This term is established in Georgian technical and academic vocabulary.

docs.title: 📚 Conclusion
docs.text: In Georgian, use only დიგიტალიზაცია ✅ It is the correct, standard form in the Georgian language.

docs.title: Map composition
docs.text: Map composition is the correct arrangement of all the elements of a map so that the information is communicated effectively and clearly. A well-designed map improves perception and helps the user interpret the data correctly.

docs.title: 🧩 Main composition elements
docs.text: Element Description Title A short, precise description that shows what the map is about. Legend Explains the symbols and colours. Scale Shows how distances on the map correspond to real space. North Arrow Helps with orientation. Graticule/Grid A coordinate grid or geographic graticule on the map. Data source States where the data comes from. Author and date Gives the map's author and the date it was made.

docs.title: 🎯 The purpose of map composition
docs.text:
• to present data visually in a clear, logical way
  • to make the map easier to read
  • to give the user context, with the elements needed for interpretation
  • to give a professional and aesthetic impression

docs.title: 🛠️ Creating a map composition in QGIS
docs.text:
1. From the menu choose Project → New Print Layout.
  2. Give it a name and confirm.
  3. Use the tools to add elements to the composition:
  4. Add Map – to insert the map
  5. Add Legend, Add Scale Bar, Add North Arrow – for the corresponding elements
  6. Add Label – to add text
  7. Adjust the size, colours, font and layout.
  8. Print it or save it as PDF/PNG.

docs.title: ✅ Rules for a good map composition
docs.text:
• use contrasting colours for readability
  • do not overload the map with unnecessary elements
  • labels should be clear and clean
  • the legend should include only the symbols that are on the map

docs.title: 📌 An example map might include:
docs.text:
• a title: "Population of Tbilisi districts 2024"
  • a scale: "1:50,000"
  • a legend: data classified by colour
  • a north arrow in the upper right corner
  • a source note: "Data: Geostat, 2024"

Map composition combines cartography, design and spatial analysis — it is the final product we share with other people. That is why planning and executing it is just as important as processing the data.

docs.title: QGIS: absolute vs relative paths
docs.text:
When working in QGIS, choosing the right type of file path matters for the project's portability and for opening it correctly on other devices.

QGIS official documentation:

docs.title: 🧾 Terms and descriptions
docs.text: Term Description Absolute Gives the full path of the file in the computer's file system. For example: C:/Users/ezdanapak/Documents/GIS/data/roads.shp. This path only works on a device with exactly the same structure. Relative Gives the file's location relative to the current QGIS project file (.qgz or .qgs). For example: ./data/roads.shp. This path is portable and ideal when moving the project to another computer.

docs.title: 📁 An example project structure
docs.text:
The QGIS project sits in one shared folder together with the data:

Chiatura_project/             ← the project's main folder
├── project.qgz              ← the QGIS project file
├── data/                    ← the data folder
│   ├── roads.shp            ← layer: roads
│   ├── buildings.shp        ← layer: buildings
│   └── rivers.shp           ← layer: rivers

docs.title: 📌 Relative paths
docs.text:
In QGIS, relative to the project.qgz file, the file paths will be:

./data/roads.shp
./data/buildings.shp
./data/rivers.shp

✅ Recommended when the project is kept in one folder and you plan to move or share it.

docs.title: 📌 Absolute paths
docs.text:
The full address of the file on the computer:

C:/Users/ezdanapak/Documents/Chiatura_project/data/roads.shp
C:/Users/ezdanapak/Documents/Chiatura_project/data/buildings.shp
C:/Users/ezdanapak/Documents/Chiatura_project/data/rivers.shp

⚠️ Not portable. It works only on the same device, with the same path structure.

docs.title: ⚙️ How do you change the path type in QGIS?
docs.text:
1. Open the QGIS project.
  2. Go to the menu: Project → Properties → General
  3. Find the Store paths setting.
  4. Choose one:
  5. Relative – for relative paths
  6. Absolute – for absolute paths

docs.title: ✅ Recommended practice
docs.text:
• Keep the QGIS project and all its data in one shared folder.
  • Use relative paths if:
  • you need to share the project with someone.
  • you need to move the project to another computer.
  • you use Git or a ZIP archive.

docs.title: 📝 Summary
docs.text:
Property Absolute path Relative path Portability ❌ no ✅ yes Works only on one computer ✅ yes ❌ no Recommended for team work ❌ no ✅ yes Path example C:/Users/ezdanapak/data/roads.shp ./data/roads.shp

📌 Tip: always use relative paths when you keep the project files together in one folder and know the project may be opened somewhere else.

docs.title: 📁 QGIS project files: .qgs vs .qgz
docs.text: QGIS (Quantum GIS) uses two main formats for saving project files: .qgs and .qgz. The difference between them concerns how the data is stored and archived. Below is a detailed overview of their characteristics and uses.

docs.title: 🔹 .qgs — XML format
docs.text:
• Description: .qgs is a standard XML file that stores the project data as text.
  • Characteristics:
  • Easy to read: the file can be opened and edited with any text editor (e.g. Notepad++, VS Code).
  • Version control: ideal for working with Git or other version control systems, because the XML format makes changes easy to track.
  • A standalone file: often accompanied by other related files/folders (e.g. project.gpkg, possibly other data files).
  • When to use it:
  • active development of the project.
  • editing by hand or tracking changes.

📌 Example: 

my_project.qgs

docs.title: 🔹 .qgz — a compressed project
docs.text:
• Description: .qgz is a ZIP-compressed archive that contains the .qgs file and other data related to the project.
  • Characteristics:
  • Compact: all the needed data is packed into one file, which makes sharing easier.
  • Hidden structure: it is not directly readable, but QGIS handles it automatically.
  • Convenient for sharing: ideal for handing over the project as a single file.
  • When to use it:
  • final distribution of the project.
  • creating a backup.

📌 Example: 

my_project.qgz

docs.title: ⚖️ Comparison
docs.text: Characteristic .qgs .qgz Format Text (XML) Compressed (ZIP) Readability Easy to read Not directly readable Git support ✔️ suitable ❌ less convenient Sharing Related files are needed too Just one file When to use Development, version control Final distribution, backup

docs.title: ✅ Recommendations
docs.text:
Use .qgs if: - you are actively working on the project. - you need to edit the file by hand or use version control (e.g. with Git).

Use .qgz if: - you want to package the project and share it as a single file. - you are making a backup or sending the project to another user.

📌 Tip: in QGIS you can freely switch between the formats with File > Save As, which lets you choose whichever format suits you best!

docs.title: Why is this critically important?
docs.text:
With QGIS, independent processes matter a lot: when working with large vector layers, complex geoprocessing or heavy rasters, one project freezing (for example, a crash while rendering) can take a whole day's work in other windows down with it.

By default, when you open a new window, the operating system often attaches it to the main process that is already running — on both Windows and Linux.

docs.title: Method 1: modifying the shortcut — the most reliable
docs.text:
QGIS has a built-in option --no-version-check that makes the program bypass the Windows registry and start a completely clean, isolated new session.

Step 1 — open the shortcut's properties

On the Desktop or in the Start menu, find the QGIS icon, right-click it and choose Properties.

Step 2 — find the Target field

In the window that opens, make sure you are on the Shortcut tab and find the field named Target:

"C:\Program Files\QGIS 3.xx.x\bin\qgis-bin.exe"

Step 3 — add the argument

Move the cursor to the very end of the text, add one space and type:

"C:\Program Files\QGIS 3.xx.x\bin\qgis-bin.exe" --no-version-check

Step 4 — save the change

Click Apply → OK. If the system asks for administrator permission, confirm.

From now on, every launch will be a completely independent process.

docs.title: Method 2: Project → New Window
docs.text:
If you are already working in QGIS and want to open a second project in parallel:

  1. In the top menu click Project
  2. Choose New Window (not New, which clears the current window)

With this command QGIS automatically creates a new isolated PID (Process ID).

docs.title: Method 3: a .bat file
docs.text:
@echo off
start "" "C:\Program Files\QGIS 3.xx.x\bin\qgis-bin.exe" --no-version-check

The start "" command tells Windows to start the program in a completely new process. The two empty quotes ("") are the title parameter — they cannot be left out.

Save the file with a .bat extension and double-click it — QGIS opens as a new, isolated process.

docs.title: Closing a frozen QGIS on Windows
docs.text:
1. Open Task Manager: Ctrl + Shift + Esc
  2. Go to the Details tab
  3. Find qgis-bin.exe — you will see several identical entries
  4. Use the CPU/Memory columns to identify the frozen process
  5. Right-click only that one process → End task

⚠️ Do not use the Processes tab — clicking "End Task" there can close every open QGIS at once. From the Details tab, only the one selected process is closed.

docs.title: Method 1: modifying the .desktop file — the most reliable
docs.text:
On Linux, application launchers are .desktop files — the equivalent of a Windows shortcut.

Step 1 — create a personal .desktop file

Instead of changing the system file directly, copy it into your personal folder:

cp /usr/share/applications/qgis.desktop ~/.local/share/applications/qgis.desktop

Step 2 — edit the file

nano ~/.local/share/applications/qgis.desktop

Find the Exec= line. It looks roughly like this:

Exec=qgis %F

Change it to:

Exec=qgis --no-version-check %F

Step 3 — activate the change

update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications/

From now on, launching QGIS from its icon always creates a new, isolated process.

docs.title: Method 2: launching from the terminal
docs.text:
The fastest way — directly from the terminal:

qgis --no-version-check &

The & symbol runs the command in the background, so the terminal stays free. Each such launch creates a new, independent PID.

To open several QGIS windows in parallel, simply repeat the command:

qgis --no-version-check &
qgis --no-version-check &

docs.title: Method 3: a .sh script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
qgis --no-version-check &

Usage:

# save the file, e.g.: ~/qgis_isolated.sh
# make it executable
chmod +x ~/qgis_isolated.sh

# run it
~/qgis_isolated.sh

To put it on the Desktop, create a .desktop file:

[Desktop Entry]
Name=QGIS (Isolated)
Exec=/home/USERNAME/qgis_isolated.sh
Icon=qgis
Type=Application
Terminal=false

Save it as ~/Desktop/qgis_isolated.desktop and make it executable:

chmod +x ~/Desktop/qgis_isolated.desktop

docs.title: Closing a frozen QGIS on Fedora
docs.text:
The graphical way — System Monitor:

  1. Open System Monitor (Activities → System Monitor)
  2. Go to the Processes tab
  3. Find qgis — you will see several entries
  4. Use CPU/Memory to identify the frozen process
  5. Right-click → Kill Process

From the terminal — by PID:

# show the PIDs of all QGIS processes
pgrep -a qgis

# close a specific PID (e.g. 12345)
kill 12345

From the terminal — by CPU:

# an interactive list with CPU load
top -p $(pgrep -d',' qgis)

⚠️ Do not use pkill qgis — this command closes every open QGIS process at once. kill <PID> closes only one specific process.

docs.title: Comparing the methods
docs.text: Method Windows Linux (Fedora) Difficulty Modifying the icon Shortcut → Target .desktop → Exec= Low Quick launch — qgis --no-version-check & Easiest From the menu Project → New Window Project → New Window Easiest Script .bat file .sh file Low Closing a frozen one Task Manager → Details kill <PID> / System Monitor Medium

docs.title: 🗺️ QGIS – calculating area, and coordinate systems
$area vs. area($geometry) · CRS vs. SRS
docs.text:
This page combines two important topics for working in QGIS:

  1. Methods for calculating area ($area and area($geometry))
  2. Coordinate reference systems — CRS and SRS

docs.title: 📐 Calculating area in the QGIS Field Calculator
docs.text:
Calculating the area of polygons is one of the most common tasks in GIS. The QGIS Field Calculator offers two main functions for this:

  • $area
  • area($geometry)

Which to choose depends on the scale, the accuracy you need and the project settings.

docs.title: 🔹 $area
docs.text:
calculates the area of the current feature taking the project settings into account

Characteristics:

  • uses the Project CRS
  • if an ellipsoid is set in the project, the area is calculated ellipsoidally
  • without an ellipsoid it works planimetrically
  • the area units are set in Project Properties → Measurements

✔️ recommended for national or regional scale data ✔️ gives high accuracy

docs.title: 🔹 area($geometry)
docs.text:
calculates only the area of the polygon geometry

Characteristics:

  • the calculation is always planimetric
  • it is based directly on the CRS/SRS of the geometry
  • the area units depend on the CRS units (meter, degree, etc.)

  • it does not take into account:

  • the project ellipsoid

  • custom area units

✔️ ideal for analysis at city or local scale ✔️ fast and simple to use

docs.title: 🌐 Ellipsoidal
docs.text:
Country / region

  • takes the Earth's curvature into account
  • essential for large areas
  • more accurate, but a heavier calculation

docs.title: 🗺️ Planimetric
docs.text:
City / town

  • the Earth is treated as a flat plane
  • effective for small areas
  • fast and practical

docs.title: 🧭 CRS and SRS — coordinate systems
docs.text: How accurate an area calculation is depends directly on which coordinate system (CRS/SRS) your data is in.

docs.title: 🔹 CRS — Coordinate Reference System
docs.text:
CRS is the modern, standard term used in QGIS and other GIS programs.

A CRS includes:

  • the coordinate type (geographic or projected)
  • the Earth model (ellipsoid)
  • the projection method
  • the units of measure
  • the origin and orientation of the coordinates

Examples:

  • EPSG:4326 — WGS 84 (degrees)
  • EPSG:32638 — UTM Zone 38N (meters)

✔️ In QGIS, Project CRS and Layer CRS always mean CRS

docs.title: 🔹 SRS — Spatial Reference System
docs.text:
SRS is an older, more general term.

  • it was used in older GIS documentation
  • it often appears in databases (e.g. PostGIS)
  • it is sometimes used as a synonym for CRS
  • it is less precise as a term

docs.title: 🔍 CRS vs. SRS — comparison
docs.text: Aspect CRS SRS Status Modern standard Old / general Precision of the term High Relatively low Use in QGIS ✔️ main ⚠️ rare Use in documentation Modern Legacy

docs.title: ✅ Practical recommendations
docs.text:
• ✔️ always use the term CRS
  • ✔️ for the area of large territories — $area with an ellipsoid
  • ✔️ in local analysis — area($geometry)

  • ⚠️ check:

  • Layer CRS

  • Project CRS
  • Project Properties → Measurements

docs.title: ✨ Summary
docs.text:
The right CRS + the right area method = accurate GIS analysis

These two factors are decisive, especially when the data is used for making decisions.

docs.title: 🎨 The QGIS QML and SLD formats
🧾 What is QML?
docs.text:
QML (QGIS Markup Language) is the file format QGIS uses to store styling settings.

QML files store how a layer should look in QGIS: - the colour scheme - symbols and strokes - label styles - size, transparency, shadows and other visual effects

docs.title: 📁 What does a QML file look like?
docs.text:
QML is a text file in XML format, so it can be read with any text editor (e.g. Notepad, VS Code).

For example: 

<qgis>
  <renderer-v2 type="singleSymbol">
    <symbol alpha="1" type="marker">
      <layer pass="0" class="SimpleMarker" locked="0">
        <prop k="color" v="255,0,0,255"/>
      </layer>
    </symbol>
  </renderer-v2>
</qgis>

docs.title: 🖌️ What does a QML file store?
docs.text: Component Description Renderer Which kind of styling it is (e.g. single symbol, categorized, graduated) Symbol or Rule The specific style rules and settings Labels Label settings Transparency Transparency Geometry Generator Extra visualization of the geometry

docs.title: 📦 Where is QML used?
docs.text:
• ✅ saving a layer style and reusing it
  • ✅ sharing the same design between projects
  • ✅ standardizing lab assignments
  • ✅ quickly applying a style to many layers

docs.title: 🧭 How do you save and load QML?
➕ Saving QML:
docs.text:
1. Right-click the layer
  2. Choose Properties
  3. Go to Symbology
  4. At the bottom choose Style → Save Style → As QML...

docs.title: 📂 Loading QML:
docs.text:
1. Properties → Symbology
  2. Style → Load Style...
  3. Choose the saved .qml file

docs.title: 🧪 Usage examples
docs.text:
• saving the styling of a lab assignment
  • using the same style on different layers
  • agreeing on colour codes in group work
  • colour classes (graduated symbology)

docs.title: 🎓 Tips:
docs.text:
• Always save a QML style as a separate file so that you can reuse it.
  • Use a naming system (e.g. roads_symbology.qml, population_label.qml)
  • You can export and import it on another computer or share it with a friend.

docs.title: 📎 More links:
docs.text:
• QGIS Documentation: Saving and loading styles
  • QGIS Style Sharing

docs.title: 🧾 The QGIS SLD format and how it compares with QML
🌐 What is SLD?
docs.text: SLD (Styled Layer Descriptor) is an open-standard XML file format used to define the styling of geographic layers. It was developed by the OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) so that different GIS systems can share style information.

docs.title: 📁 What does an SLD file look like?
docs.text:
SLD is an XML text file. For example:

<StyledLayerDescriptor version="1.0.0">
  <NamedLayer>
    <Name>MyLayer</Name>
    <UserStyle>
      <Title>Red Points</Title>
      <FeatureTypeStyle>
        <Rule>
          <PointSymbolizer>
            <Graphic>
              <Mark>
                <WellKnownName>circle</WellKnownName>
                <Fill>
                  <CssParameter name="fill">#FF0000</CssParameter>
                </Fill>
              </Mark>
              <Size>6</Size>
            </Graphic>
          </PointSymbolizer>
        </Rule>
      </FeatureTypeStyle>
    </UserStyle>
  </NamedLayer>
</StyledLayerDescriptor>

docs.title: 📦 Where SLD is used
docs.text:
Styled Layer Descriptor (SLD) is an OGC standard used in GIS systems to style maps. The main areas of use:

  • 🌍 GeoServer, MapServer, Web Map Services (WMS): SLD is the standard on these platforms.
  • 🔄 Transferring styles: sharing styles between QGIS and other GIS servers.
  • 🌐 Styling internet maps: the visual design of web maps.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
1. Go to: Properties → Symbology → Style → Save Style...
  2. Choose the .sld format.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
1. Go to: Properties → Symbology → Style → Load Style...
  2. Choose the .sld file.

docs.title: 🔄 QML vs SLD: comparison
docs.text: Characteristic QML SLD Format XML (QGIS's internal style) XML (OGC standard) Support QGIS only QGIS, GeoServer, MapServer Use Local projects Web maps, GIS servers Functionality Broad, flexible Standardized, sometimes limited Area of use Labs, fieldwork Web maps, GeoServer publishing

docs.title: 🎓 Recommendations
docs.text: Situation Use QML Use SLD Working on local projects ✅ ❌ Sharing a style from QGIS to QGIS ✅ ❌ Working with GeoServer ❌ ✅ Styling WMS maps ❌ ✅ Full control over the style ✅ ❌

docs.title: 📎 Additional resources
docs.text:
• 📖 QGIS Documentation: SLD Support
  • 📜 OGC Styled Layer Descriptor Specification

docs.title: 📁 QGIS – Save Vector Layer As: format options
docs.text: In the QGIS Save Vector Layer As... window you can save layers in various formats — each of them suits different needs and environments.

docs.title: 🗂️ Vector formats available in QGIS
docs.text: Format name Extension(s) Description GeoPackage .gpkg 💡 A modern, recommended format. Stores many layers, attributes and styles in one file and supports UTF-8. ESRI Shapefile .shp 📦 A legacy format, widely supported. One layer only, limited fields, and many companion files (.dbf, .shx, .prj). GeoJSON .geojson, .json 🌐 Text-based, compatible with the web and with Leaflet. KML .kml 🌍 An XML format intended for Google Earth. DXF .dxf 🏗️ For integration with CAD systems. Stores geometry and some attributes. CSV .csv 📊 Tabular data. If it contains coordinates, it can be used as a point layer. GML .gml 📁 An XML-based OGC standard, good for exchanging data. MapInfo File .tab, .mif 🧭 Formats used by MapInfo GIS. SpatiaLite .sqlite 🧱 Built on an SQLite database, a compatible format — similar to GeoPackage. Memory (no file) 🧠 A temporary layer in memory. Not saved to a file. PostgreSQL Database 🛢️ Saving directly to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database. MySQL / MSSQL Database 🔗 Database formats — need connection settings. WFS-T Service 🌐 Web Feature Service (Transactional) – sends the data to a server. DXF Export (QCAD/AutoCAD) .dxf 👷 A CAD file for geometry. JSON/TopoJSON .json, .topojson 📡 For WebGIS use. FlatGeobuf .fgb ⚡ A fast, streaming-oriented alternative to GPKG.

docs.title: ✅ Tips
docs.text:
• GeoPackage (.gpkg) — 🥇 the recommended modern format, replacing Shapefile.
  • GeoJSON / TopoJSON — works best with Leaflet and web maps.
  • Shapefile (.shp) — needed only if you require backward compatibility with older systems.
  • DXF / DWG — use it when working with CAD.
  • PostgreSQL/PostGIS — use it if your organization uses spatial databases.

🔄 Format support depends on the GDAL version and how QGIS was built.

📌 See more information:

The QGIS Save Vector Layer As... function lets you save spatial data in many formats — each with its own advantages and areas of use.

docs.title: 🔹 GeoPackage (.gpkg)
docs.text:
• ✅ stores many layers in one file (points, lines, polygons, rasters)
  • ✅ UTF-8 support for correct text encoding
  • ✅ saved styles and metadata
  • 🟢 recommended as a modern, stable, cross-platform file format

docs.title: 🔸 Shapefile (.shp)
docs.text:
• 📦 a classic format, very widely supported
  • ❗ only one layer per file
  • ❗ field names are limited to 10 characters
  • ❗ extra files are required (.shx, .dbf, .prj)

docs.title: 🌐 GeoJSON / KML
docs.text:
• 🌍 ideal for web maps and for sharing with Google Earth
  • ✅ text-based, human-readable
  • ✅ easy to embed in JavaScript libraries (Leaflet, Mapbox)

docs.title: 🏗️ DXF (.dxf)
docs.text:
• 💼 a format for exchanging CAD data
  • 🎯 precise geometry for integration with AutoCAD and other CAD programs

docs.title: 🖼️ GeoTIFF (.tif)
docs.text:
• 🛰️ the standard for satellite imagery, DEMs and indices (NDVI, hillshade)
  • ✅ supports multiband data and metadata
  • ✅ widely supported across platforms

docs.title: 🧾 IMG / ASCII
docs.text:
• 🕰️ legacy and modelling formats
  • 💡 useful for environmental simulations or specialized GIS modules

docs.title: 📄 CSV / Excel (.csv / .xlsx)
docs.text:
• 🔗 a simple way to import attribute tables and join data to layers
  • 🧭 if you have coordinates, you can turn them straight into a point map

docs.title: ✅ Key takeaways
docs.text:
• 🎯 Choosing the right format ensures:
  • data integrity
  • cross-platform compatibility (ArcGIS, GRASS, FME)
  • easier collaboration on projects
  • 🏙️ Whether it is urban planning, infrastructure design or cadastral databases — the format matters.

ℹ️ Tip: If you are starting a new project, start with the .gpkg format — it is simple, stable and flexible!

docs.title: 📘 What is RAM, and the QGIS temporary layer
💡 What is RAM?
docs.text:
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the computer's short-term memory. It temporarily stores the data of the programs and files that are currently running.

  • Like a work desk — the bigger it is, the more things can be spread out at once.
  • Programs such as QGIS use RAM to process data and store temporary results.
  • When the computer or program shuts down, the contents of RAM are erased.

📌 Example: when you create a new project in QGIS and load a map into it, the map is held in RAM temporarily until you save the file to disk.

docs.title: 📍 Why is RAM important for QGIS?
docs.text:
• QGIS works with spatial data, which can be quite large.
  • Sometimes you need a temporary layer that is not saved on your computer, only in RAM.
  • Such a layer is the Temporary Scratch Layer.

docs.title: 🧪 The Temporary Scratch Layer in QGIS
docs.text:
A Temporary Scratch Layer is a temporary layer that: - is stored only in the computer's RAM - disappears when you close the project (if you have not saved it) - is used for quick testing, drawing, or even for temporarily storing the results of calculations

🧠 Analogy: a temporary layer is like a note on a scrap of paper that gets thrown away when you leave the room — unless you copy it into a permanent notebook.

docs.title: ✅ When should you use a scratch layer?
docs.text:
• when you want to quickly draw a new object (e.g. a point or polygon) to try something
  • when you need the data only for this session
  • when you are doing spatial analysis and the result is temporary

docs.title: ❗ Remember:
docs.text:
• A temporary layer is not saved automatically — you have to save it yourself (Export → Save Features As…) if you want to keep it as a file.
  • If you close QGIS, the layer is deleted.

docs.title: 🔁 How RAM and the scratch layer relate
docs.text: Component Function RAM Storing temporary data in the computer Scratch Layer A temporary spatial layer stored in RAM while QGIS is running

docs.title: 📷 A visual example:
docs.text:
graph LR
A[QGIS program] --> B[Temporary Layer]
B --> C((RAM))
C -->|temporary storage| D[Results and visualization]

docs.title: 📎 Additional resources:
docs.text:
• GeeksForGeeks: What is RAM?
  • QGIS Documentation: Temporary Layers

docs.title: 🗺️ Georeferencing a topographic map in QGIS
docs.text: Georeferencing a topographic map means placing it on geographic coordinates, so that it can be overlaid and analysed together with modern maps or in geographic information systems (GIS). The process involves assigning real coordinates to specific points on the map.

docs.title: 1. Getting a topographic map
docs.text: Find a scanned or digital topographic map (JPEG, TIFF or PNG).

docs.title: 2. Required programs and data
docs.text:
• QGIS (version 3.x or newer)
  • a scanned topographic map (a raster image)
  • objects with known coordinates, or a graticule

docs.title: 🛠️ Step-by-step instructions
docs.text:
Step I: loading the map in QGIS
  • Open QGIS
  • From the main window, go to the Browser Panel and load the topographic image (raster layer)
Step II: starting georeferencing
  1. Go to Raster > Georeferencer > Georeferencer...
  2. Open the image (File > Open Raster)
  3. Set the coordinate system (Settings > Transformation Settings)
Step III: marking ground control points (GCPs)
  1. Mark matching points on the image and on a known map (OSM, Google Earth or another).
  2. Use at least 4 well-distributed points.
  3. Set the transformation method:
Method When to use Linear (1st Order) little distortion Polynomial 2/3 medium/strong distortion Thin Plate Spline for smooth stretching (rubber sheeting)
  1. Check the RMS error (View GCP Table)
Step IV: running the transformation
  • After choosing: Raster > Georeferencer > Start Georeferencing
  • The map is stretched based on the given points.
Step V: saving the georeferenced image
  • Use File > Save Raster As...
  • Format: GeoTIFF (.tif) or another georeferenced format
  • Make sure the saved file has the correct CRS (e.g. EPSG:32638)

docs.title: ✅ Checking the accuracy
docs.text:
• Compare it with other spatial data (e.g. buildings, roads).
  • If needed, edit or add new GCPs and georeference the map again.

docs.title: 💡 Additional tips
docs.text:
• Use as many GCPs as possible for a better result.
  • Choose easily recognizable objects — road intersections, river confluences, peaks.
  • Make a backup copy before you finish saving.

🗂️ The result is a georeferenced GeoTIFF or an updated raster file, ready for analysis and for use on maps in QGIS.

docs.title: 📍 Types of georeferencing transformations
docs.text: Georeferencing uses different transformation types, which differ in complexity, the number of ground control points (GCPs) needed and where they are used. Below is an overview of the main transformations, with their pros and cons.

docs.title: 🔹 Linear (Affine) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: used for a linear transformation of the map — translation, rotation, scaling and shear.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 3
  • Pros ✅:
  • simple and fast to compute.
  • preserves straight lines and the ratios of angles.
  • ideal when the map is not distorted.
  • Cons ❌:
  • does not account for non-linear distortion.
  • inaccurate results on heavily distorted maps.

docs.title: 🔸 Second Order Polynomial transformation
docs.text:
• Description: uses quadratic terms to model non-linear distortion of the map.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 6
  • Pros ✅:
  • fits non-linear distortion better.
  • can straighten bent parts of the map.
  • Cons ❌:
  • can introduce extra distortion.
  • needs more control points and more precision.
  • sometimes over-transformation damages the geometry.

docs.title: 🔹 Third Order Polynomial transformation
docs.text:
• Description: by including cubic terms it can correct complex distortion.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 10
  • Pros ✅:
  • ideal for heavily distorted historical maps.
  • offers maximum flexibility in correcting distortion.
  • Cons ❌:
  • very sensitive to small errors in the GCPs.
  • often causes unnatural warping at the edges of the map.
  • hard to control, with a risk of extra distortion.

docs.title: 🔸 Spline (Thin Plate Spline) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: a non-linear interpolation method that fits the control points as closely as possible.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 10+ (recommended)
  • Pros ✅:
  • gives high accuracy at the control points.
  • ideal for strong distortion.
  • Cons ❌:
  • unpredictable distortion can occur between control points.
  • does not preserve geometric ratios.
  • the result is hard to predict.

docs.title: 🔹 Projective (Perspective) transformation
docs.text:
• Description: used to correct perspective distortion, e.g. for obliquely taken photos.
  • Minimum GCPs needed: 4
  • Pros ✅:
  • works well for aerial photos.
  • can correctly straighten tilted elements.
  • Cons ❌:
  • suitable only for specific situations.
  • not a universal solution.

docs.title: 🔚 Conclusion
docs.text:
Transformation GCPs needed Advantage Limitation Linear (Affine) 3 fast, simple does not handle non-linear distortion 2nd Order Polynomial 6 better fit to distortion very sensitive to errors 3rd Order Polynomial 10 maximum flexibility risk of extra distortion Spline (Thin Plate Spline) 10+ high accuracy at the GCPs unpredictable in other areas Projective (Perspective) 4 ideal for correcting tilt limited range of use

📌 Tip: when choosing a transformation, consider how distorted the map is, how many GCPs are available and the accuracy you want. For example, a Linear transformation is enough for simple maps, while Spline or Third Order Polynomial suits old or heavily distorted maps better.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
Band combinations for landsat 8

Remote sensing indices

Remote sensing indices

Raster data is spatial information based on a grid structure. Each element of this grid — a pixel — carries a specific value that represents some attribute or layer (e.g. elevation, temperature, colour).

docs.title: 📌 Main characteristics
docs.text:
• made of a grid of pixels (grid cells)
  • each pixel has:
  • a location (its place in the grid)
  • a resolution (the geographic size of each pixel)
  • a value (e.g. a colour code, elevation, temperature)
  • the data is stored as a matrix (rows and columns)

docs.title: 🖼️ Types of raster data
docs.text: Type Description Examples 📷 Colour image (True Color) A visual image with red, green and blue bands Satellite photos, Google Earth 🌡️ Thematic raster Each pixel represents an attribute or category Land use maps, soil types ⛰️ Digital elevation model (DEM) A matrix of elevation data Terrain analysis, slope calculation 🌫️ Hyperspectral/multispectral images Many spectral bands, with highly precise information Environmental monitoring, agriculture

docs.title: 📏 Geographic resolution
docs.text:
• Spatial (geographic) resolution: the physical size one pixel covers in the real world (e.g. 10 m × 10 m).
  • The smaller the pixel size, the more detailed the image.

docs.title: 🗂️ Raster vs Vector
docs.text: Parameter Raster Vector Data type Grid Point, line, polygon Data volume Large Relatively small Processing Fast for analysis Complex analysis Areas of use Terrain, temperature, satellite images Roads, buildings, boundaries

docs.title: 🛠️ Software for working with rasters
docs.text:
• QGIS – open-source GIS software (Georeferencer, Raster Calculator)
  • ArcGIS – a professional platform with broad functionality
  • GDAL – a library for raster and vector data

docs.title: 🎓 Areas of use
docs.text:
• environmental monitoring and climate analysis
  • interpreting satellite images
  • urban planning and land use
  • natural resource management

docs.title: 📊 Types of resolution in remote sensing
docs.text:
Category Spatial resolution Spectral resolution Temporal resolution Radiometric resolution 📌 Definition The size of the ground area represented by a pixel The ability to distinguish wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum How often images of the same location are acquired The sensor's sensitivity to small differences in energy 📏 How it is measured Pixel size (e.g. 10 m, 30 m, 0.5 m) The number, width and placement of spectral bands The interval between images (e.g. 1 day, 5 days) Bits per pixel (e.g. 8-bit = 256 levels) 📈 High resolution Small pixels; more spatial detail More, narrower spectral bands More frequent data acquisition Higher precision for detecting small differences 🎯 Areas of use Urban maps, precision agriculture, habitat delineation Crop classification, mineral detection, vegetation indices Change detection, phenology, emergencies Crop stress, water turbidity, thermal variation 📷 Examples WorldView-3 (0.31 m), Sentinel-2 (10 m), Landsat 8 (30 m) AVIRIS (224 bands), Hyperion (220), Sentinel-2 (13) MODIS (1-2 days), Sentinel-2 (5 days), Landsat 8 (16 days) Landsat 8 (12-bit), Sentinel-2, MODIS (12–16 bit) 💾 Effect on file size Higher resolution = more pixels = a larger file More bands = a wider spectrum = a larger file Frequent acquisitions = more volume over time More bits per pixel = more data and processing time ⚖️ Trade-offs High detail reduces the area covered and increases volume Narrow bands increase noise and reduce signal quality High frequency often comes with less spatial detail High bit depth increases data volume ⚙️ What it depends on Sensor design and altitude, orbit Filters and wavelength limits The satellite's orbit (sun-synchronous, geostationary), swath width Sensor electronics, the precision of analog-to-digital conversion 🔗 Related concepts GSD (Ground Sampling Distance), Pixel Footprint Bandwidth, Hyperspectral vs. Multispectral Temporal frequency, Repeat cycle, Temporal aliasing Digital Number (DN), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)

📝 Note: understanding these characteristics correctly helps you choose for tasks such as land cover change, disaster mapping, environmental monitoring and precision agriculture.

docs.title: ✅ Summary
docs.text: Raster data is ideal for representing continuous, surface-type data. Use it when you need a detailed image or attributes that vary continuously (for example, elevation, temperature, illumination, etc.).

docs.title: 🌍 Terrain data and processing it in QGIS
🔍 What terrain data is
docs.text:
Terrain is the combination of the heights, slopes and shapes of the Earth's surface. Analysing it is essential for:

  • geomorphological research
  • hazard assessment (landslides, floods, etc.)
  • infrastructure planning
  • landscape modelling and visualization

docs.title: 🛰️ The main sources of terrain data
1. SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission)
docs.text:
• Extension: .tif (GeoTIFF)
  • Global coverage at 30 m and 90 m resolution
  • Source: https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/

docs.title: 2. ASTER GDEM
docs.text:
• Extension: .tif
  • Global coverage at ~30 m resolution
  • Source: https://asterweb.jpl.nasa.gov/gdem.asp

docs.title: 3. Copernicus DEM
docs.text:
• Extension: .tif
  • High-accuracy terrain (30 m and 10 m)
  • Source: https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/

docs.title: 4. ALOS PALSAR
docs.text:
• Extension: .tif
  • Detailed terrain data (12.5 m)
  • Source: https://asf.alaska.edu/

docs.title: 5. GeoPortal.ge (NAPR)
docs.text:
• Georgia's national data
  • Source: https://www.geoportal.ge/

  3. Slope – a slope map

docs.title: 📁 CAD and GIS: DXF/DWG files in geographic information systems
🔹 Introduction
docs.text:
CAD (Computer-Aided Design) is a family of systems used in engineering, architecture, surveying and construction for precise modelling of spatial objects. Its main formats are:

  • DWG (Drawing): a proprietary format developed by AutoDesk.
  • DXF (Drawing Exchange Format): an open text format created to make sharing DWG with other systems easy.

docs.title: 🔹 The main differences between CAD and GIS
docs.text: Parameter CAD GIS Purpose A precise technical drawing Spatial analysis and a database Coordinates Often local, without a projection Georeferenced, global File format DWG, DXF Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, DB Type of information Lines, points, text Geometry + attribute data

docs.title: 🔹 DXF/DWG files in GIS
docs.text: GIS systems (e.g. QGIS, ArcGIS) often need to import CAD files, especially when survey drawings must be combined with other spatial data.

docs.title: 🔸 Importing DWG/DXF in QGIS
docs.text:
• QGIS support:
  • QGIS can load DXF files directly as vector layers (point, line, polygon).

  • DWG files need GDAL/OGR support or conversion to DXF.

  • Process:

  • Open QGIS → Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer
  • Choose the DXF file
  • Several layers appear: entities, points, lines, polygons, annotations.

docs.title: 🔸 In ArcGIS
docs.text:
ArcGIS can import CAD files directly if they are correctly georeferenced.

  • The CAD file opens automatically as a CAD Dataset.
  • It can be converted to a Feature Class.
  • The CAD to Geodatabase or Feature Class to Feature Class tools are used.

docs.title: 🔹 Georeferencing a CAD file
docs.text:
A CAD file does not always contain a geographic system. You need:

  • to assign the correct coordinate system in GIS
  • or to georeference it using reference points — known points

docs.title: 🔹 Usage examples in GIS
docs.text:
1. Integrating architectural drawings with urban GIS data
  2. Adding existing infrastructure to urban planning maps
  3. Visualizing utility networks (water, electricity, gas)
  4. Analysing survey data together with other spatial layers

docs.title: 🔹 Converting CAD → GIS
docs.text: Tool Description ogr2ogr Converting DXF → Shapefile or GeoJSON QGIS Processing DXF layers → Shapefile ArcGIS Toolboxes CAD to GDB/Feature Class

docs.title: 🔹 Good practice
docs.text:
• Use only the DXF (R2007 or lower) format for QGIS.
  • Make sure the CAD drawing is built with accurate coordinates.
  • Use a layer structure (layer names), so that they are easy to classify in GIS.

docs.title: 🔤 Attribute field types — Shapefile and GeoPackage
docs.text:
Like a spreadsheet, a vector layer's attribute table is made of fields (columns) and records (rows). Each field has a data type that determines what kind of value can be stored in it — an integer, a decimal, text, a date, etc.

Important

The field type and its limits depend on the file format. The same data is stored differently in a Shapefile and in a GeoPackage. Choosing the right format and type avoids losing or distorting data (e.g. dropping the time from a date, truncating text, cutting a field name short).

docs.title: 📊 Basic data types (theory)
docs.text:
Type Description Example Integer / int A whole number (no decimals) 42, -7, 2025 Integer64 / bigint A large whole number (64-bit) 9000000000 Real / Double / Float A decimal (floating-point) number 3.14, -0.5, 1250.75 String / Text A text value "road", "Tbilisi" Date A date (year-month-day) 2025-07-10 DateTime Date + time 2025-07-10 14:30:00 Boolean A logical value True / False

Integer vs Double

  • Integer — a whole number; it does not store decimals (5, not 5.0).
  • Double / Float — stores the decimal part (5.75). Double (64-bit) is more precise than Float (32-bit).
  • If you store area or length — use Double; if you store a count of objects or an ID — Integer.

docs.title: 🗂️ Shapefile field types (.dbf)
docs.text: In a Shapefile, attributes are stored in a .dbf (dBASE) file. This is an old format, and it has strict limits.

docs.title: Supported types
docs.text: dBASE code QGIS name Description Limit C Text (string) Text max. 254 characters N Integer (32 bit) Whole number width ≤ 10 digits (int32) N Integer64 (64 bit) Large whole number width ≤ 18–20; not stored reliably N/F Real / Double Decimal number width + precision (max. ~15 significant digits) D Date Date format YYYYMMDD, date only L Boolean Logical (T/F) 1 character

docs.title: ❗ The main limits of Shapefile
docs.text:
• 🏷️ Field name — at most 10 characters. A longer name is cut automatically (temperature → temperatur), which can cause duplicates.
  • ✂️ Text — at most 254 characters. Longer text is truncated.
  • ⏰ There is no DateTime or Time type. Only Date. The time part is lost.
  • 🔢 Integer64 is not fully supported — very large numbers can be damaged or turned into Real.
  • 🈳 Weak support for NULL (empty) values — an empty field is often stored as 0 or as empty text.
  • 🌍 Encoding problems — Georgian/Unicode text needs a correct .cpg file (UTF-8), otherwise the text gets garbled.
  • 📐 One geometry type per file (Point / Line / Polygon — separately).

A typical mistake

If you store a date and time (2025-07-10 14:30) in a Shapefile field, the time is lost — only 2025-07-10 is stored. In this case, use GeoPackage.

docs.title: 📦 GeoPackage field types (.gpkg)
docs.text: GeoPackage (.gpkg) is a modern, open (OGC) format built on an SQLite database. Its type system is much richer and more flexible than Shapefile's.

docs.title: Supported types
docs.text: GeoPackage type Range / description QGIS equivalent BOOLEAN 0 / 1 (true/false) Boolean TINYINT 8-bit integer (−128…127) Integer SMALLINT 16-bit integer Integer MEDIUMINT 32-bit integer Integer (32 bit) INTEGER / INT 64-bit integer Integer64 (64 bit) FLOAT 32-bit decimal Real (float) DOUBLE / REAL 64-bit decimal Real (double) TEXT / TEXT(n) Text (no limit, or max. n) Text DATE Date YYYY-MM-DD Date DATETIME Date + time (ISO 8601, with time zone) DateTime BLOB Binary data (e.g. an image) Binary

docs.title: ✅ Advantages of GeoPackage over Shapefile
docs.text:
• 🏷️ No 10-character limit on field names.
  • 📝 Text is practically unlimited (the 254-character limit no longer applies).
  • ⏱️ Full DateTime support — date, time and time zone are stored.
  • 🔢 Real 64-bit Integer64 support.
  • 🈳 Full NULL support (empty ≠ zero).
  • 🌍 UTF-8 encoding is built in — Georgian text is stored without problems.
  • 🗃️ Many layers in one file (and many geometry types) — unlike Shapefile.
  • 📁 One file instead of .shp/.shx/.dbf/.prj/.cpg.

docs.title: ⚖️ Shapefile vs GeoPackage — comparing fields
docs.text:
Characteristic 🗂️ Shapefile (.dbf) 📦 GeoPackage (.gpkg) Field name length ≤ 10 characters Practically unlimited Text length ≤ 254 characters Unlimited / TEXT(n) Integer (32 bit) ✅ ✅ (MEDIUMINT) Integer64 (64 bit) ⚠️ unreliable ✅ (INTEGER) Real / Double ✅ ✅ (DOUBLE) Date ✅ ✅ DateTime (date+time) ❌ ✅ Boolean ✅ (L) ✅ (BOOLEAN) Binary / BLOB ❌ ✅ NULL value ⚠️ weak ✅ full UTF-8 (Georgian) ⚠️ depends on .cpg ✅ built in Number of files min. 3 (.shp/.shx/.dbf) 1 (.gpkg)

Recommendation

For new projects use GeoPackage — it does not have Shapefile's limits (field name, text length, date+time). Keep Shapefile only for compatibility (e.g. when exchanging with older programs).

docs.text:

  • GDAL — GeoPackage vector driver

docs.title: 🗺️ Shapefile — one of the most common GIS formats
docs.text:
A Shapefile (.shp format) is one of the most common and historically important vector data formats, used to store and share geographic data. It consists of several related files that together make up a complete geodata layer.

📎 Official description: Shapefile – Wikipedia

docs.title: 📐 Geometry types in a shapefile
docs.text:
A shapefile layer can have only one type of geometry: - 📍 Point - ➖ Line - 🔷 Polygon

💡 Each shapefile contains only one geometry type — for example, one file for points and another for polygons.

docs.title: 🔤 Encoding and projection
docs.text: 📌 Important: choose the right text encoding (e.g. UTF-8, CP1251) and the correct coordinate reference system (CRS). 📍 For example, EPSG:32638 (UTM zone 38N, WGS 84) is common in Georgia.

docs.title: 📂 The structure of a shapefile
docs.text:
Technically, a shapefile consists of at least 3 main files:

Extension Contents .shp Geometry (points, lines, polygons) .shx Index (offset information) .dbf Attribute data (similar to .xls)

📎 Additional files: .prj (projection), .cpg (encoding), .qml (QGIS style) and others.

docs.title: ❗ What happens if a component is missing?
docs.text:
➡️ If the .shx or .dbf file is deleted: - the layer will not load correctly in QGIS. - you may see only the geometry or only the attributes, but not both together.

📌 Always keep all the components of a shapefile in one folder.

docs.title: 🌐 Assigning and changing the projection
docs.text:
• 📥 Assigning: if the file has no .prj, use the "Assign Projection" function.
  • 🔄 Changing: use "Reproject Layer" in QGIS, or "Save As…" in another CRS.

docs.title: 🗃️ Absolute vs relative paths
docs.text:
Term Description Absolute Gives the full path of the file (e.g. C:/Users/data/roads.shp) Relative Gives the file's location relative to the project file (e.g. ./data/roads.shp)

✅ Relative paths are recommended, especially for projects you share.

docs.title: 📌 Conclusion
docs.text: The Shapefile remains a standard vector format in many GIS systems. Knowing how to use it correctly and understanding its structure is an essential step for both beginners and professional map makers.

docs.title: Linux for geographers
docs.text:
This is not just another Linux tutorial. The internet has thousands of those, and many of them are excellent. This is something else: Linux through the lens of a geographer's tasks.

A simple example shows the difference. A typical tutorial teaches find like this:

find /path -name "*.txt"

Here, it is taught like this:

# out of 1,200 orthophotos, find the ones taken in 2024
# and move them into one folder — you won't drag 1,200 files by hand
find /data/ortho -name "*_2024*.tif" -exec mv {} /data/ortho_2024/ \;

It is the same command. You will remember the second one, because it solves a pain you have actually had.

docs.title: Why a geographer needs Linux
docs.text:
\"QGIS runs on Windows too — so what?\"

True. You don't need Linux for QGIS. But:

  • Servers run Linux. GeoServer, PostGIS, MapProxy, GeoNode — if you ever want your map to go on the web instead of staying on your laptop, you will be dealing with a server.
  • GDAL is built on the command line. QGIS's buttons are a shell around GDAL commands. When you need to process 300 rasters, you won't click a button 300 times.
  • Remote sensing and ML tools — almost all of them come out on Linux first.
  • It is free and transparent. That is as much a value as QGIS being open source.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
For geographers, GIS specialists and students who have never touched Linux. No prior knowledge is needed — we start from what a terminal is.

It helps if you already know QGIS — then the GIS examples will be more useful to you. If not, GIS Basic is a good place to start.

docs.title: How to learn
docs.text:
The only rule

You cannot learn Linux by reading. Type every command by hand. Not by copying — type it. The mistakes you make while typing are exactly the places where your knowledge gets stuck.

You need a practice system. Do not use your work computer. The options are in the 00 — Setup chapter: a virtual machine (recommended), dual-boot, or WSL.

The chapters are written in order — from 01 to 12. Each one builds on the previous one.

docs.title: The certification path
docs.text:
This documentation covers the objectives of three exams:

Exam Type What it gives you LPIC-1 101 Test (multiple choice) Linux fundamentals, distribution-independent LPIC-1 102 Test (multiple choice) Scripting, networking, security, administration RHCSA (EX200) Practical — a live system, a timer Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 administration

The chapters are organized by topic, not by exam — LPI's numbering is exam logistics, not a learning order. At the bottom of each page it says which objective it corresponds to.

Full matrix of certification objectives

In that matrix you also mark your progress — which objectives you have covered and which remain.

RHCSA is a different genre

LPIC-1 is a test — reading notes and memorizing works. In RHCSA you are given a system and you do the tasks. For that you need labs, not notes.

docs.title: Certification objectives
docs.text:
This page does two things:

  1. Coverage map — which official objective is explained in which chapter.
  2. Progress tracker — tick a box when you finish a topic. Your whole preparation is visible on one page.

How to tick a box

The boxes are written in the text. To tick one, change - [ ] to - [x] in the file and push the change. That way your progress is also recorded in the Git history.

Weight = how many questions to expect in the exam. Each LPIC-1 exam has a total weight of 60. Spend more time on high-weight topics.

LPIC-1 · 101LPIC-1 · 102RHCSA · EX200

Exam: 101-500 · test, 60 questions, 90 minutes · total weight 60

Exam: 102-500 · test, 60 questions, 90 minutes · total weight 60

Exam: EX200 (RHEL 9) · practical — a live system, ~2.5 hours · weights are not published

This is not a test

You do the tasks on a real system and the result is checked automatically. "I know how it's done" is not enough — you have to do it by hand, fast. Every item needs a lab.
