docs.title: Finding files — find
docs.text:
Goal

You will learn to find what you need among thousands of files — by name, size, date — and to run a command directly on what you find.

Prerequisite: 01 — The command line · Time: ~40 minutes

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
You have a folder with 1,200 orthophotos. You need only the 2024 ones, in another folder. In Windows Explorer you start a search, wait, then hold Ctrl and select 300 files by hand — and one wrong click undoes everything.

On Linux this is one line. And most importantly, you can save that line and run it again tomorrow on the 2025 data.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
find is not a "search box". It is a pipeline for processing files. Its logic has three parts, always in this order:

find  [where to look]  [by what criteria]  [what to do with the results]

find /data/ortho -name "*.tif" -exec gdalinfo {} \;
Part Role /data/ortho Where to look -name "*.tif" By what criteria -exec gdalinfo {} \; What to do with the results

The most common beginner mistake

find is recursive by default — it goes into every subfolder. find / scans the whole system and takes minutes. Always start from a specific folder, not from /.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
find .              # the current folder and all subfolders
find /data/ortho    # a specific path
find . -maxdepth 1  # only the current folder, don't go into subfolders

docs.title: Criteria
docs.text:
Criterion Meaning Example -name Name (case-sensitive) -name "*.shp" -iname Name (case-insensitive) -iname "*.TIF" -type f Files only -type d Folders only -size +100M Larger than 100 MB + more, - less -mtime -7 Changed in the last 7 days -empty Empty

Quotes are required

find . -name *.tif will not work correctly. The shell expands the asterisk before handing it to find. Always write -name "*.tif" — in quotes.

docs.title: Combining criteria
docs.text:
# TIF files larger than 100 MB — both conditions at once (AND is the default)
find /data -name "*.tif" -size +100M

# TIF or TIFF (OR)
find /data \( -name "*.tif" -o -name "*.tiff" \)

# everything except TIF
find /data ! -name "*.tif"

docs.title: What to do with the results
docs.text:
find . -name "*.tif" -print            # print the path (the default)
find . -name "*.tif" -delete           # delete  ⚠️
find . -name "*.tif" -exec ls -lh {} \;   # run a command on each one

In -exec, {} is "the path of the found file", and \; marks the end of the command.

Look first, then act

-delete and -exec are irreversible. Always look at the list with a plain find first:

find /data/ortho -name "*_2024*.tif"        # 1. see what it finds
find /data/ortho -name "*_2024*.tif" -delete # 2. only then act

docs.title: GIS example
docs.text:
Separating the 2024 photos out of 1,200 orthophotos

# 1. first, see how many there are
find /data/ortho -name "*_2024*.tif" | wc -l
# 312

# 2. create the target folder
mkdir -p /data/ortho_2024

# 3. move them
find /data/ortho -name "*_2024*.tif" -exec mv {} /data/ortho_2024/ \;

The disk is full — what is eating the space?

# files larger than 500 MB, sorted by size
find /data -type f -size +500M -exec du -h {} + | sort -rh | head -20

A geographer's disk is usually filled by two things: uncompressed GeoTIFFs and QGIS temporary files. This command finds both.

Batch reprojection with GDAL

# every shapefile from WGS84 → UTM 38N
find /data/vector -name "*.shp" -exec ogr2ogr -t_srs EPSG:32638 \
    /data/vector_utm/{} {} \;

This is exactly where the difference shows. In QGIS this would take an hour of clicking for 40 files. Here — one command, which you can save and repeat.

Finding the leftover companion files of a .shp

A shapefile is really 4–7 files. Often the .shp has been deleted, but the .dbf and .shx remain:

find /data/vector -name "*.dbf" | while read f; do
    [ -f "${f%.dbf}.shp" ] || echo "orphan: $f"
done

This is already a preview of 09 — Scripting.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Practice data

Create a test structure:

mkdir -p ~/lab/ortho/{2023,2024,2025}
cd ~/lab/ortho
touch 2023/tbilisi_2023_01.tif 2023/tbilisi_2023_02.tif
touch 2024/tbilisi_2024_01.tif 2024/rustavi_2024_01.tif 2024/rustavi_2024_02.TIF
touch 2025/batumi_2025_01.tif
touch 2024/notes.txt 2024/tbilisi_2024_01.tfw

2. Find

  • all .tif files (files only, not folders)
  • all .tif and .TIF — with one command
  • only the files whose name contains rustavi
  • everything that is not .tif
  • only folders

3. Act

Move all the 2024 files (case-insensitive!) into a new folder ~/lab/ortho_2024/. Check with -print first, then -exec.

Answers 
# 2
find . -name "*.tif" -type f
find . \( -iname "*.tif" \)                  # -iname catches both
find . -name "*rustavi*"
find . -type f ! -name "*.tif"
find . -type d

# 3
mkdir -p ~/lab/ortho_2024
find . -iname "*_2024_*" -type f -print                        # look first
find . -iname "*_2024_*" -type f -exec mv {} ~/lab/ortho_2024/ \;

Did you notice?

In task 2, -iname "*.tif" is simpler than \( -name "*.tif" -o -name "*.TIF" \). On Linux there is almost always a shorter way — but you should still know -o, because when combining different criteria there is no other way.

docs.title: To remember
docs.text:
find [where] [criterion] [action]
  • quotes on -name — always
  • first -print, then -delete / -exec
  • searching from / is slow — start from a specific folder
  • -iname ignores case, -name does not

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
RHCSA is a practical exam — you are given a live system and complete tasks against a timer. Reading notes is not enough for that. This section collects scenarios you have to do by hand.

How to work on a lab

  1. Take a clean virtual machine (a snapshot is a must).
  2. Start a timer.
  3. Try the solution without help first — man and --help are allowed, the internet is not (the same as in the exam).
  4. Only after that, look at the answer.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: (in preparation)

docs.title: Lab 02 — Files and folders
docs.text:
Task

A colleague left you a mess — 2 years of field data in one folder. Sort it, clean it up and archive it. Don't drag a single file by hand.

Time Difficulty Chapters Exam 25 minutes Beginner 02 · 03 LPIC-1 103.3 · RHCSA

Rules

  • Start the timer before you begin
  • man and --help — allowed (they are allowed in the exam too)
  • The internet, ChatGPT, the answers on this page — not allowed
  • If you don't finish in 25 minutes, stop and look at the answer. Then do it again from scratch against the timer.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run this block to create the practice environment:

rm -rf ~/lab02 && mkdir -p ~/lab02/field_data && cd ~/lab02/field_data

# field points
for y in 2024 2025; do
  for m in 03 06 09; do
    for i in 1 2 3; do
      touch "points_${y}_${m}_0${i}.shp" "points_${y}_${m}_0${i}.dbf" \
            "points_${y}_${m}_0${i}.shx" "points_${y}_${m}_0${i}.prj"
    done
  done
done

# orthophotos — a few large ones
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  head -c 12M /dev/urandom > "ortho_2024_0${i}.tif"
done
head -c 40M /dev/urandom > ortho_2025_huge.TIF

# junk
touch temp1.tmp temp2.tmp '~qgis_backup.qgz~' thumbs.db
mkdir -p empty_folder1 empty_folder2
echo "CRS: EPSG:32638, surveyor: T. Beridze" > readme.txt
echo "CRS: EPSG:32637, surveyor: N. Kapanadze" > readme_rustavi.txt

ls -la ~/lab02/field_data | head

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1 — Inventory (3 min)

Count and answer:

  1. How many files are in field_data in total?
  2. How many .shp files are there?
  3. Which file is the largest?
  4. How much space does the whole folder take?

2 — Sorting by year (6 min)

Create ~/lab02/sorted/2024/ and ~/lab02/sorted/2025/.

Move every file into the right folder based on its name.

⚠️ ortho_2025_huge.TIF is in upper case — it must also end up in 2025.

3 — Cleaning up the junk (4 min)

Delete from field_data:

  • all .tmp files
  • thumbs.db
  • all empty folders
  • all files whose name starts or ends with a tilde (~)

⚠️ Look at the list first, then delete. readme.txt must not be deleted.

4 — Metadata (4 min)

Both readme files contain a CRS. Find with one command which file contains EPSG:32638 — without opening the files.

5 — Archive (5 min)

  1. Archive the whole ~/lab02/sorted/ folder as ~/lab02/field_2024_2025.tar.gz.
  2. Check the archive's size.
  3. List its contents — without extracting the archive.

6 — Symbolic link (3 min)

Create a link ~/current_project that points to ~/lab02/sorted/2025/. Check with ls -l that it is a link and not a copy.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
# run at the end of the lab
cd ~/lab02
echo "--- 2024:"; ls sorted/2024 | wc -l      # should be 41
echo "--- 2025:"; ls sorted/2025 | wc -l      # should be 37
echo "--- junk:"; find field_data -name "*.tmp" -o -name "thumbs.db" | wc -l  # 0
echo "--- empty:"; find field_data -type d -empty | wc -l   # 0
echo "--- archive:"; ls -lh field_2024_2025.tar.gz
echo "--- link:"; ls -l ~/current_project
Answers — try it yourself first

1 — Inventory

ls -1 | wc -l                      # number of files
find . -name "*.shp" | wc -l       # 18
ls -lhS | head -3                  # sorted by size, largest at the top
du -sh .                           # total size of the folder

2 — Sorting

mkdir -p ~/lab02/sorted/{2024,2025}
cd ~/lab02/field_data
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f -iname "*2024*" -exec mv {} ~/lab02/sorted/2024/ \;
find . -maxdepth 1 -type f -iname "*2025*" -exec mv {} ~/lab02/sorted/2025/ \;

-iname is a must — -name "*2025*" would also catch the upper-case .TIF, but make it a habit: you can't trust the case of file names.

And -maxdepth 1 is there so it doesn't go into the newly created subfolders.

3 — Cleaning up

find . -name "*.tmp" -o -name "thumbs.db" -o -name "~*" -o -name "*~"   # look first
find . \( -name "*.tmp" -o -name "thumbs.db" -o -name "~*" -o -name "*~" \) -delete
find . -type d -empty -delete

The brackets are critical

Adding -delete without brackets would act only on the last condition — that is how find reads -o. Without brackets this command would delete something other than you think. This is exactly where people lose data with find.

4 — Metadata

grep -l "EPSG:32638" *.txt
# readme.txt

-l (list) shows only the file name, not its contents.

5 — Archive

cd ~/lab02
tar -czf field_2024_2025.tar.gz sorted/
ls -lh field_2024_2025.tar.gz
tar -tzf field_2024_2025.tar.gz | head
Flag Meaning -c create -z gzip compression -f file — the next argument is the file name -t list — just the list, without extracting -x extract

Did you notice the archive barely got smaller?

Files created with /dev/urandom are random bytes and cannot be compressed. Real GeoTIFFs are often like this too — if a raster is already compressed (LZW, DEFLATE, JPEG), tar -z spends extra time with no result. In that case tar -cf (without compression) is faster.

6 — Link

ln -s ~/lab02/sorted/2025 ~/current_project
ls -l ~/current_project
# lrwxrwxrwx ... current_project -> /home/user/lab02/sorted/2025

The first letter l means link. Without -s you would get a hard link, which does not work on folders at all.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• batch processing with find criteria and -exec
  • why brackets are needed with -o — a matter of data safety
  • the four tar flags that cover 95% of cases
  • symbolic links — for keeping a stable project path in GIS

docs.title: 📝 PyQGIS — Practical assignments
docs.text:
This section collects practical assignments for students. Every operation must be done with PyQGIS (in the QGIS Python console).

# Assignment Topics 1 Assignment 1 Creating a layer, deleting fields, XY, area/perimeter (UTM), duplicates 2 Assignment 2 Attribute and spatial selection, deleting, clipping, DMS → decimal, lengths (ellipsoid/UTM) 3 Assignment 3 Coming soon 4 Assignment 4 Filter, geometry conversion, creating a layer, coordinate conversion 5 Assignment 5 Raster statistics, reclassification, histogram, contour lines

docs.title: 📋 General rules
docs.text:
• Name your folder with your first and last name, e.g. Giorgi_Kapanadze_task1.
  • Use only Latin letters and underscores in the names of archives, folders, files, table columns, variables, functions and classes. Georgian letters and other symbols are not allowed.
  • Where the assignment does not specify them, choose the names of layers, columns and output folders yourself, following GIS file organization principles.
  • Take full-screen screenshots (Snipping Tool). Upload only the screenshots to the class.
  • On university computers, work in the C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Users\Public\Documents folder.
  • Write every operation in PyQGIS and save screenshots of the code in a screenshot folder.

docs.title: 📦 Data
docs.text:
The data for the assignments is in the folder sample_data/practice. Each assignment page lists the files it needs.

The elevation model srtm_45_04.tif (24 MB) is downloaded separately from a GitHub Release. The other files are in the osm/ and task_04/ folders.

The OpenStreetMap layers (Georgia, 8 shapefiles) are in one archive: OSM_shp_PyQGIS.zip (8 MB; including gis_osm_roads_free_Batumi). Data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

docs.title: 💡 Solutions
docs.text:
Under each problem there is a collapsed "Solution" block. Try it on your own first and open the block only afterwards. Paths and column names in the solutions are illustrative; adapt them to your data.

General helper code (used in all assignments) 
from qgis.core import *
import processing

base = r'C:/Users/Public/Documents/practice'   # your working folder

def save_shp(layer, path):
    """Saves a layer as a Shapefile (UTF-8)."""
    opts = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
    opts.driverName = 'ESRI Shapefile'
    opts.fileEncoding = 'UTF-8'
    res = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
        layer, path, QgsProject.instance().transformContext(), opts)
    return res[0] == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError

docs.title: 📝 Assignment 1
docs.text:
Required topics: Creating layers, Deleting, Attribute calculations, Vector geoprocessing

Data: sample_data/practice/osm/ (gis_osm_places_free_1, gis_osm_protected_areas_a_free_1; OpenStreetMap, EPSG:4326). All OSM layers in one archive: OSM_shp_PyQGIS.zip (8 layers, 8 MB)

Here and in the following solutions the general helper code is used.

Required: work on a copy

Deleting fields, calculating values and deleting features all happen directly in the file. Before you start, copy both layers (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, .cpg) into your shp folder and work only on the copy.

docs.title: Part 1 (folder: part_1)
docs.text:
1. Create a line layer regline_layer with CRS EPSG:32637 and save it in the shp folder.
  2. Load gis_osm_places_free_1 and delete the columns osm_id, code, fclass.
  3. Calculate XY coordinates on the same layer.
  4. Find duplicate points and delete them from the same layer.
Solution 1.1 
layer = QgsVectorLayer('LineString?crs=EPSG:32637', 'regline_layer', 'memory')
save_shp(layer, base + '/shp/regline_layer.shp')
Solution 1.2 
places = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/gis_osm_places_free_1.shp', 'places', 'ogr')
idx = [places.fields().lookupField(n) for n in ('osm_id', 'code', 'fclass')]
places.dataProvider().deleteAttributes([i for i in idx if i != -1])
places.updateFields()
print(places.fields().names())   # ['population', 'name']
Solution 1.3 
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant
places.dataProvider().addAttributes([QgsField('x', QVariant.Double),
                                     QgsField('y', QVariant.Double)])
places.updateFields()
ix = places.fields().lookupField('x')
iy = places.fields().lookupField('y')

places.startEditing()
for f in places.getFeatures():
    p = f.geometry().asPoint()
    places.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), ix, p.x())
    places.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), iy, p.y())
places.commitChanges()

The coordinates are in the layer's CRS (EPSG:4326: x is longitude, y is latitude, in degrees).

Solution 1.4 
seen, dup_ids = set(), []
for f in places.getFeatures():
    key = f.geometry().asWkt()
    if key in seen:
        dup_ids.append(f.id())
    else:
        seen.add(key)

places.startEditing()
places.deleteFeatures(dup_ids)
places.commitChanges()
print(len(dup_ids), 'deleted,', places.featureCount(), 'left')

processing.run('native:deleteduplicategeometries', ...) creates a new layer, so a loop that deletes features from the same layer is used here.

Expected result: 159 of the 5263 points are deleted (5104 remain). All duplicates also have identical attributes.

docs.title: Part 2 (folder: part_2)
docs.text:
1. Create a polygon layer polygon_layer with CRS EPSG:4326 and save it in the shp folder.
    1. Load gis_osm_protected_areas_a_free_1 and delete the columns osm_id, code.
  2. Calculate area and perimeter in the same layer using the appropriate UTM zone.
  3. Find fully duplicated features (same geometry and same attributes) and delete them from the same layer.
Solution 2.1 
layer = QgsVectorLayer('Polygon?crs=EPSG:4326', 'polygon_layer', 'memory')
save_shp(layer, base + '/shp/polygon_layer.shp')

pa = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/gis_osm_protected_areas_a_free_1.shp', 'protected', 'ogr')
idx = [pa.fields().lookupField(n) for n in ('osm_id', 'code')]
pa.dataProvider().deleteAttributes([i for i in idx if i != -1])
pa.updateFields()
Solution 2.2 
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant
pa.dataProvider().addAttributes([QgsField('area_km2', QVariant.Double),
                                 QgsField('perim_km', QVariant.Double)])
pa.updateFields()
ia = pa.fields().lookupField('area_km2')
ip = pa.fields().lookupField('perim_km')

ctx = QgsProject.instance().transformContext()
transforms = {}                       # zone -> transform

pa.startEditing()
for f in pa.getFeatures():
    g = QgsGeometry(f.geometry())     # a copy, so the original is not changed
    lon = g.centroid().asPoint().x()
    zone = int((lon + 180) // 6) + 1
    if zone not in transforms:
        transforms[zone] = QgsCoordinateTransform(
            pa.crs(), QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem(f'EPSG:326{zone}'), ctx)
    g.transform(transforms[zone])
    pa.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), ia, g.area() / 1e6)
    pa.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), ip, g.length() / 1e3)
pa.commitChanges()

On a polygon, g.length() returns the perimeter. In 4326, g.area() would give square degrees, so we first transform the geometry into a projected CRS.

The data spans two UTM zones (37N and 38N), so the zone is determined separately for each feature.

Check: the first feature (national_park) ≈ 168.27 km², perimeter ≈ 96.94 km. The total of all 120 features ≈ 13,366 km² (zone 38: 104 features, zone 37: 16).

Solution 2.3 

seen, dup_ids = set(), []
for f in pa.getFeatures():
    key = (f.geometry().asWkt(), f['fclass'])
    if key in seen:
        dup_ids.append(f.id())
    else:
        seen.add(key)

pa.startEditing()
pa.deleteFeatures(dup_ids)
pa.commitChanges()
print(len(dup_ids), 'deleted,', pa.featureCount(), 'left')
Expected result: 7 of the 120 features are deleted (113 remain).

The same geometry often has two records (national_park and nature_reserve). Comparing by geometry alone (f.geometry().asWkt()) would delete 53 features and lose the second record's fclass, so fclass is part of the key. osm_id and code are already deleted, so they take no part in the comparison.

docs.title: 📝 Assignment 2
docs.text:
Required topics: Attribute selection, Spatial selection, Deleting, Coordinate conversion, Vector geoprocessing

Data: sample_data/practice/osm/ (gis_osm_places_free_1, gis_osm_adminareas_a_free_1, gis_osm_roads_free_Batumi; OpenStreetMap, EPSG:4326). All OSM layers in one archive: OSM_shp_PyQGIS.zip

Here and in the following solutions the general helper code is used.

Required: work on a copy

Deleting features and adding fields happen directly in the file. Before you start, copy the layers (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, .cpg) into your shp folder and work only on the copy.

docs.title: Part 1 (folder: part_1)
docs.text:
1. In gis_osm_places_free_1, select the feature whose population is 1331 and export it to shp.
  2. Delete from the same layer gis_osm_places_free_1 the features whose osm_id is greater than 1014750524 and less than 10926200653.
  3. Load gis_osm_adminareas_a_free_1 and select the municipality "ჭიათურის მუნიციპალიტეტი" (Chiatura Municipality; by the name column, fclass = admin_level6). In gis_osm_places_free_1, select the features that fall inside this municipality, clip them and save the result as gis_osm_places_free_1_Chiatura in the shp folder.
Solution 1.1 
places = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/gis_osm_places_free_1.shp', 'places', 'ogr')
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(places)

places.selectByExpression('"population" = 1331')
print(places.selectedFeatureCount())          # 1
processing.run('native:saveselectedfeatures',
    {'INPUT': places, 'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/places_pop_1331.shp'})
places.removeSelection()
Solution 1.2 
places.selectByExpression(
    'to_int("osm_id") > 1014750524 AND to_int("osm_id") < 10926200653')
print(places.selectedFeatureCount(), 'to delete')

places.startEditing()
places.deleteSelectedFeatures()
places.commitChanges()
print(places.featureCount(), 'left')

osm_id is a text (String) field. The expression "osm_id" > 1014750524 would compare it as text and give a wrong result, so to_int("osm_id") is needed.

Expected result: 1190 of the 5263 features are deleted (4073 remain).

Solution 1.3 
adm = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/gis_osm_adminareas_a_free_1.shp', 'adminareas', 'ogr')
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(adm)
adm.selectByExpression(
    '"fclass" = \'admin_level6\' AND "name" = \'ჭიათურის მუნიციპალიტეტი\'')
print(adm.selectedFeatureCount())                 # 1

# features of places that fall inside the selected municipality
processing.run('native:selectbylocation', {
    'INPUT': places, 'PREDICATE': [0],           # 0 = intersects
    'INTERSECT': QgsProcessingFeatureSourceDefinition(adm.id(), True),
    'METHOD': 0})
print(places.selectedFeatureCount())              # 106

# clip: only the selected features, by the selected municipality
processing.run('native:clip', {
    'INPUT': QgsProcessingFeatureSourceDefinition(places.id(), True),
    'OVERLAY': QgsProcessingFeatureSourceDefinition(adm.id(), True),
    'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/gis_osm_places_free_1_Chiatura.shp'})

QgsProcessingFeatureSourceDefinition(layer.id(), True) means "selected features only". If you pass the layer directly, the algorithm uses all features. That is why the layers must first be added to the project (addMapLayer).

"name" = 'ჭიათურა' alone would pick the town polygon (admin_level8), not the municipality, so fclass is required too.

Expected result: gis_osm_places_free_1_Chiatura has 106 points (Chiatura, Khunevi, Rgani and others).

docs.title: Part 2 (folder: part_2)
docs.text:
1. Create a point layer points with CRS EPSG:4326 and save it in the shp folder.

  2. Write the coordinates into a txt file. Read them with a script, convert them to decimal degrees and print them in the console:

    • 42°17'2.95"N, 43°16'55.79"E
    • 42°17'26.48"N, 43°16'46.89"E

    For this particular task you may use AI in addition to the template script.

  3. In the gis_osm_roads_free_Batumi layer (roads of Batumi), calculate the length in two separate columns: WGS_Length (ellipsoidal) and UTM_Length (in the UTM zone projection). Look at the data: do you need to change the coordinate reference system?

Solution 2.1 
layer = QgsVectorLayer('Point?crs=EPSG:4326', 'points', 'memory')
save_shp(layer, base + '/shp/points.shp')
Solution 2.2

coords.txt (one point per line: latitude, longitude): 

42°17'2.95"N, 43°16'55.79"E
42°17'26.48"N, 43°16'46.89"E

import re

def dms(text):
    d, m, s, hemi = re.match(r'(\d+)°(\d+)\'([\d.]+)"([NSEW])', text.strip()).groups()
    value = int(d) + int(m) / 60 + float(s) / 3600
    return -value if hemi in 'SW' else value

with open(base + '/coords.txt', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
    for line in fh:
        lat, lon = [dms(part) for part in line.split(',')]
        print(round(lat, 6), round(lon, 6))
Expected result: 
42.284153 43.282164
42.290689 43.279692

The ° symbol is not ASCII, so save the file as UTF-8 and pass encoding='utf-8'. Latitude (N/S) comes first and longitude (E/W) second; to create a point use QgsPointXY(lon, lat), longitude first.

Solution 2.3

The layer's CRS is EPSG:4326 (degrees), so geometry().length() would return degrees. For length we need either an ellipsoidal measurement or a transformation into a projected CRS. 

from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant
roads = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/gis_osm_roads_free_Batumi.shp', 'roads', 'ogr')
print(roads.crs().authid())                       # EPSG:4326

roads.dataProvider().addAttributes([QgsField('WGS_Length', QVariant.Double),
                                    QgsField('UTM_Length', QVariant.Double)])
roads.updateFields()
iw = roads.fields().lookupField('WGS_Length')
iu = roads.fields().lookupField('UTM_Length')

ctx = QgsProject.instance().transformContext()
d = QgsDistanceArea()                             # ellipsoidal length
d.setSourceCrs(roads.crs(), ctx)
d.setEllipsoid('WGS84')

# Batumi ~41.6°E -> UTM zone 37N -> EPSG:32637
to_utm = QgsCoordinateTransform(roads.crs(), QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32637'), ctx)

roads.startEditing()
for f in roads.getFeatures():
    g = QgsGeometry(f.geometry())                 # a copy
    wgs = d.measureLength(g) / 1000               # km
    g.transform(to_utm)
    utm = g.length() / 1000                       # km
    roads.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), iw, wgs)
    roads.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), iu, utm)
roads.commitChanges()

Batumi lies entirely in one UTM zone. To compute the zone: int((lon + 180) // 6) + 1 (41.6°E → 37).

Check: the total of all 11,738 lines: WGS_Length ≈ 1202.6 km, UTM_Length ≈ 1202.8 km. The difference is small and comes from the scale distortion of UTM.

The gis_osm_roads_free_Batumi layer was made from the all-Georgia gis_osm_roads_free_1 (332,755 lines) by clipping it with the Batumi municipality. The table has no "city" field, so the spatial operation native:clip was used.

docs.title: 📝 Assignment 4
docs.text:
Required topics: Attribute selection, Geometry conversions, Creating layers, Coordinate conversion

Data: sample_data/practice/task_04/ (points, sdstas, koordinatebi.txt)

docs.title: Part 1 (folder: part_1)
docs.text:
1. Load points and filter the features where real = 1. Save them as my_shp1.shp.
  2. Load points, delete the geometrically duplicated features and save the result as my_shp_without_geo_duplicates.
  3. Load my_shp_without_geo_duplicates, delete the column ORIG_FID and save the result as my_shp_without_ORIG_FID.
Solution 
pts = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/points.shp', 'points', 'ogr')

# 1
processing.run('native:extractbyexpression', {
    'INPUT': pts, 'EXPRESSION': '"real" = 1',
    'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/my_shp1.shp'})

# 2
processing.run('native:deleteduplicategeometries', {
    'INPUT': pts, 'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/my_shp_without_geo_duplicates.shp'})

# 3
nodup = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/my_shp_without_geo_duplicates.shp', 'nodup', 'ogr')
processing.run('native:deletecolumn', {
    'INPUT': nodup, 'COLUMN': ['ORIG_FID'],
    'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/my_shp_without_ORIG_FID.shp'})

docs.title: Part 2 (folder: part_2)
docs.text:
1. Load sdstas and convert its geometry to lines. Save the result as sdstas_line.
  2. Create a point layer test1.shp with the fields ID (int), Name (string), Person_ID (double); CRS EPSG:4326.
  3. Create a point layer test_1.shp with the fields ID (int), saxelwodeba (string), tipi (string); CRS EPSG:32638. Add one record at the coordinates 4683402.40, 358412.16 (the start point): ID = 1, first text field "saxeli", second "ucnobia".
  4. The folder contains koordinatebi.txt. Use PyQGIS to convert both coordinates to decimal degrees.
Solution 2.1 
sd = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/sdstas.shp', 'sdstas', 'ogr')
# polygons -> lines (for points, use native:pointstopath)
processing.run('native:polygonstolines', {
    'INPUT': sd, 'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/sdstas_line.shp'})
Solution 2.2 – 2.3 
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField('Name', QVariant.String))
fields.append(QgsField('Person_ID', QVariant.Double))
w = QgsVectorFileWriter(base + '/shp/test1.shp', 'UTF-8', fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:4326'), 'ESRI Shapefile')
del w   # close the file

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField('saxelwodeba', QVariant.String))
fields.append(QgsField('tipi', QVariant.String))
w = QgsVectorFileWriter(base + '/shp/test_1.shp', 'UTF-8', fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'), 'ESRI Shapefile')
f = QgsFeature(fields)
# 358412.16 = X (easting), 4683402.40 = Y (northing)
f.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(358412.16, 4683402.40)))
f.setAttributes([1, 'saxeli', 'ucnobia'])
w.addFeature(f)
del w

The assignment writes the coordinates Y first (4683402.40), then X (358412.16). In UTM the X value (easting) has 6 digits, so you have to swap their order in QgsPointXY.

Solution 2.4 
tr = QgsCoordinateTransform(QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
                            QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:4326'),
                            QgsProject.instance())
with open(base + '/koordinatebi.txt', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
    for line in fh:
        parts = line.replace(',', ' ').split()
        if len(parts) < 2:
            continue
        x, y = float(parts[0]), float(parts[1])   # check the file format
        p = tr.transform(QgsPointXY(x, y))
        print(round(p.y(), 6), round(p.x(), 6))    # lat, lon

docs.title: 📝 Assignment 5
docs.text:
Required topics: Raster statistics, Terrain

Data: sample_data/practice/task_05/ (Raster/srtm_45_04.tif, shp/geo_regions.shp)

docs.title: Part 1
docs.text:
1. Load the raster srtm_45_04 and use PyQGIS to print minimumValue, maximumValue, mean, sumOfSquares in the console.

  2. Reclassify the raster into three classes:

    • class 1: -5 … 0
    • class 2: 0 … 2000
    • class 3: 2000 … 3500

    Result: srtm_45_04_reclassified.tif. 3. Build a histogram of the same raster with PyQGIS.

Solution 1.1 
dem = base + '/Raster/srtm_45_04.tif'
rl = iface.addRasterLayer(dem, 'srtm_45_04')
st = rl.dataProvider().bandStatistics(1, QgsRasterBandStats.All)
print('minimumValue:', st.minimumValue)
print('maximumValue:', st.maximumValue)
print('mean:', st.mean)
print('sumOfSquares:', st.sumOfSquares)
Solution 1.2 
processing.run('native:reclassifybytable', {
    'INPUT_RASTER': rl, 'RASTER_BAND': 1,
    'TABLE': [-5, 0, 1,
               0, 2000, 2,
               2000, 3500, 3],
    'NO_DATA': -9999, 'RANGE_BOUNDARIES': 0, 'NODATA_FOR_MISSING': True,
    'DATA_TYPE': 5,
    'OUTPUT': base + '/Raster/srtm_45_04_reclassified.tif'})
Solution 1.3 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
bins = 50
h = rl.dataProvider().histogram(1, bins, st.minimumValue, st.maximumValue)
step = (st.maximumValue - st.minimumValue) / bins
xs = [st.minimumValue + i * step for i in range(bins)]
plt.bar(xs, h.histogramVector, width=step, align='edge')
plt.xlabel('Elevation (m)'); plt.ylabel('Pixels')
plt.savefig(base + '/Raster/histogram.png')
plt.show()

docs.title: Part 2
docs.text:
1. Use PyQGIS to extract contour lines from srtm_45_04 at a 200 m interval.
  2. Load geo_regions.shp from the \shp folder. Clip the raster with the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region, build a histogram of the clipped raster and name the result Samegrelo_z_s.tif.
  3. Print the number of rows and columns of Samegrelo_z_s.tif in the console.
Solution 2.1 
processing.run('gdal:contour', {
    'INPUT': dem, 'BAND': 1, 'INTERVAL': 200, 'FIELD_NAME': 'ELEV',
    'OUTPUT': base + '/shp/contours_200.shp'})
Solution 2.2 – 2.3 

regions = QgsVectorLayer(base + '/shp/geo_regions.shp', 'geo_regions', 'ogr')
mask = processing.run('native:extractbyexpression', {
    'INPUT': regions,
    'EXPRESSION': '"name_en" = \'Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti\'',  # check in the table
    'OUTPUT': 'memory:'})['OUTPUT']

out = base + '/Raster/Samegrelo_z_s.tif'
processing.run('gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer', {
    'INPUT': dem, 'MASK': mask, 'CROP_TO_CUTLINE': True,
    'NODATA': -9999, 'OUTPUT': out})

clip = QgsRasterLayer(out, 'Samegrelo_z_s')
print('rows:', clip.height(), 'columns:', clip.width())
For the histogram, use the same code as in Solution 1.3, with clip instead of rl.

docs.title: QgsProject.instance() in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsProject.instance() is the global object of the current QGIS project. It is the single access point to the project's data, layers, CRS and settings.

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
In QGIS one project is always open (it may be empty). QgsProject.instance() returns exactly that project — the Singleton pattern:

QGIS application
    │
    └── QgsProject  (only one instance)
            │
            ├── Layers
            ├── CRS (coordinate reference system)
            ├── Variables
            ├── Path (.qgz file)
            └── Settings

💡 Singleton is a design pattern where a class can have only one instance. instance() always returns the same object.

docs.title: 📦 Import
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject

# Singleton — every call returns the same object
project = QgsProject.instance()

print(type(project))
# → <class 'qgis._core.QgsProject'>

# two calls — one and the same object
a = QgsProject.instance()
b = QgsProject.instance()
print(a is b)  # → True

docs.title: Adding a layer
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsProject

layer = QgsVectorLayer(
    r'C:\GIS\shapefile\regions.shp',
    'Regions',
    'ogr'
)

if layer.isValid():
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)
    print("✅ Layer added to the project")

docs.title: Listing all layers
docs.text:
project = QgsProject.instance()

# dictionary — {layer_id: QgsMapLayer}
all_layers = project.mapLayers()

for layer_id, layer in all_layers.items():
    print(f"ID: {layer_id[:8]}...  name: {layer.name()}")

docs.title: Finding a layer by name
docs.text:
# by name (a list — several may match)
layers = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('Roads')

if layers:
    layer = layers[0]
    print(f"✅ Found: {layer.name()} — {layer.featureCount()} features")
else:
    print("❌ Layer not found")

docs.title: Finding a layer by ID
docs.text:
layer_id = "roads_abc123_20250101"

layer = QgsProject.instance().mapLayer(layer_id)

if layer:
    print(f"✅ {layer.name()}")
else:
    print("❌ ID not found")

docs.title: Removing a layer
docs.text:
layer = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('TempLayer')[0]

# remove by ID
QgsProject.instance().removeMapLayer(layer.id())

# or directly by object
QgsProject.instance().removeMapLayer(layer)

print("🗑️ Layer removed from the project")

docs.title: 🌐 CRS — coordinate reference system
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem

project = QgsProject.instance()

# the project's current CRS
crs = project.crs()
print(crs.authid())       # → "EPSG:32638"
print(crs.description())  # → "WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N"

# change the project CRS
new_crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:4326')
project.setCrs(new_crs)
print("✅ CRS changed:", project.crs().authid())

docs.title: 📁 The project file
docs.text:
project = QgsProject.instance()

# full path of the project file
print(project.fileName())
# → "C:/GIS/Projects/my_project.qgz"  or "" if not saved

# project title
print(project.title())
# → "GGTC Pipeline Map"

# change the title
project.setTitle("GGTC Pipeline Map 2025")

# save the project
project.write()
print("💾 Project saved")

# save to a new path
project.write(r'C:\GIS\Projects\backup.qgz')

docs.title: 🔧 Transform context
docs.text:
transformContext() is the coordinate transformation context, which is required in the modern PyQGIS API (QgsVectorFileWriter.create(), writeAsVectorFormatV3()):

from qgis.core import QgsProject, QgsVectorFileWriter

transform_context = QgsProject.instance().transformContext()

options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
options.driverName   = "ESRI Shapefile"
options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(
    r'C:\GIS\output.shp',
    fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point,
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
    transform_context,          # ← QgsProject.instance().transformContext()
    options
)
del writer

docs.title: 🧩 Variables
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsExpressionContextUtils, QgsProject

project = QgsProject.instance()

# set a variable
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setProjectVariable(project, 'company',  'GGTC')
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setProjectVariable(project, 'map_year', 2025)

# read a variable
scope = QgsExpressionContextUtils.projectScope(project)
print(scope.variable('company'))   # → "GGTC"
print(scope.variable('map_year'))  # → 2025

# used in QGIS expressions as: @company, @map_year

docs.title: 🧹 Clearing the project
docs.text:
# remove all layers
QgsProject.instance().removeAllMapLayers()
print("🗑️ All layers removed")

# clear the project completely (layers + settings)
QgsProject.instance().clear()
print("🔄 Project cleared")

⚠️ clear() is irreversible. All of the project's data, variables and settings are removed.

docs.title: 📡 Signals
docs.text:
QgsProject emits PyQt signals, so you can listen to events:

project = QgsProject.instance()

# when layers are added
project.layersAdded.connect(
    lambda layers: print(f"➕ Added: {[l.name() for l in layers]}")
)

# when layers are removed
project.layersRemoved.connect(
    lambda ids: print(f"🗑️ Removed: {ids}")
)

# when the project is saved
project.projectSaved.connect(
    lambda: print(f"💾 Saved: {project.fileName()}")
)

# when the CRS changes
project.crsChanged.connect(
    lambda: print(f"🌐 CRS changed: {project.crs().authid()}")
)

docs.text: Method Purpose Return type instance() The project's Singleton object QgsProject addMapLayer(layer) Add a layer QgsMapLayer removeMapLayer(id) Remove a layer by ID — mapLayers() Dictionary of all layers dict mapLayersByName(name) Find layers by name list mapLayer(id) Find a layer by ID QgsMapLayer crs() The project CRS QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem setCrs(crs) Change the CRS — fileName() Path of the .qgz file str title() Project title str write() Save bool clear() Clear everything — transformContext() Coordinate transformation context QgsCoordinateTransformContext removeAllMapLayers() Remove all layers —

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsProject.instance() is a Singleton: always one and the same object
  • The project's layers, CRS, variables and path are all available from here
  • transformContext() is required in QgsVectorFileWriter.create() and writeAsVectorFormatV3()
  • Signals: adding/removing layers, CRS changes and saving are all events you can listen to
  • clear(): be careful, it is an irreversible full reset

👉 QgsProject.instance() is the central hub of PyQGIS. Any interaction with the project starts from this object.

docs.title: isValid() in PyQGIS
docs.text: isValid() is PyQGIS's "health check". It tells you whether an object loaded successfully and is ready to work with.

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
When you create a layer in QGIS, it is always created in memory, even if the file does not exist or the path is wrong. That is exactly why we need isValid():

QgsVectorLayer("wrong/path.shp", "layer", "ogr")
        │
        ▼
  object created ✅   ←── always
        │
        ├── isValid() → True   ✅  data found
        └── isValid() → False  ❌  data not found

docs.title: 📦 Where does it come from?
docs.text:
isValid() is defined in the QgsMapLayer class, the common parent class of all PyQGIS layers:

QgsMapLayer          ← isValid() is defined here
    ├── QgsVectorLayer
    └── QgsRasterLayer

📌 So you can use isValid() on any layer, vector or raster.

docs.title: ▶️ Simple use
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer

layer = QgsVectorLayer(
    r'C:\GIS\shapefile\lake.shp',
    'Lake Layer',
    'ogr'
)

if not layer.isValid():
    print("❌ The layer did not load — check the file path")
else:
    print("✅ The layer is valid — you can work with it")

⚠️ Tip: always call isValid() after loading a layer. Without it, later operations can crash QGIS.

docs.title: 🛠 Where else is isValid() found?
docs.text:
isValid() is not only in layers; other important PyQGIS classes have it too:

Class What isValid() checks QgsVectorLayer The data source (file/database) was found and opened QgsRasterLayer The raster file loaded successfully QgsGeometry The geometry meets the OGC standards (it is not "broken") QgsPointXY The point is initialized with valid coordinates QgsRectangle The rectangle is initialized with valid coordinates QgsMessageBar The visual element for showing messages is ready

docs.title: 🔍 QgsVectorLayer — a detailed example
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsProject

# ✅ correct path
layer = QgsVectorLayer(
    r'C:\GIS\shapefile\roads.shp',
    'Roads',
    'ogr'
)

if layer.isValid():
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)
    print(f"✅ Loaded — {layer.featureCount()} features")
    print(f"   CRS: {layer.crs().authid()}")
    print(f"   Type: {layer.geometryType()}")
else:
    print("❌ The layer did not load")

# ❌ wrong path — the object is still created!
layer = QgsVectorLayer(
    r'C:\GIS\missing_file.shp',
    'Test',
    'ogr'
)

print(layer)           # → <QgsVectorLayer: ...>   ← the object exists
print(layer.isValid()) # → False                   ← but it is not valid

docs.title: 🔷 QgsGeometry — geometry validation
docs.text:
QgsGeometry.isValid() checks the OGC standards, i.e. geometric correctness:

from qgis.core import QgsGeometry

# ✅ a valid geometry
geom_ok = QgsGeometry.fromWkt("POLYGON ((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 1, 0 0))")
print(geom_ok.isValid())   # → True

# ❌ a "broken" geometry — the polygon intersects itself (butterfly)
geom_bad = QgsGeometry.fromWkt("POLYGON ((0 0, 1 1, 1 0, 0 1, 0 0))")
print(geom_bad.isValid())  # → False

# the reason for the error
if not geom_bad.isValid():
    print(geom_bad.lastError())
    # → "Ring self-intersection" or similar

💡 To fix a geometry automatically: geom.makeValid() (QGIS 3.x+)

docs.title: 🔗 Together with processing.run()
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject

result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']

# check isValid() on the processing result too
if not temp_layer or not temp_layer.isValid():
    print("❌ The processing result is invalid")
elif temp_layer.featureCount() == 0:
    print("⚠️ The layer is empty")
else:
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(temp_layer)
    print(f"✅ {temp_layer.featureCount()} features added")

docs.title: ⚡ try / except + isValid() — best practice
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsProject

def load_layer(path: str, name: str) -> QgsVectorLayer | None:
    """
    Loads a layer and validates it.
    Returns a QgsVectorLayer on success, otherwise None.
    """
    try:
        layer = QgsVectorLayer(path, name, 'ogr')

        if not layer.isValid():
            print(f"❌ [{name}] — failed to load: {path}")
            return None

        QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)
        print(f"✅ [{name}] — {layer.featureCount()} features | {layer.crs().authid()}")
        return layer

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ Exception: {e}")
        return None


# usage
layer = load_layer(r'C:\GIS\shapefile\regions.shp', 'Regions')

if layer:
    # we only work with a valid layer
    for feat in layer.getFeatures():
        print(feat['name'])

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• isValid() is the object's "health check": is it ready to work with or not
  • It is defined in QgsMapLayer, so it works on vector and raster layers
  • The object is always created; isValid() → False does not mean the object does not exist
  • QgsGeometry.isValid() checks geometric correctness (self-intersection, ring validity)
  • Skipping isValid() before later operations is a potential cause of crashes

👉 Rule: after loading any layer, the first step is always isValid().

docs.title: lookupField() in PyQGIS
docs.text: lookupField() finds the index of a column (field) in a vector layer's (QgsVectorLayer) attribute table by its name.

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
When working with a field, most QGIS functions ask not for its name (e.g. "population") but for its position number (e.g. 0, 1, 2...). lookupField() is the "bridge" from name to index:

layer.lookupField("population")
        │
        ▼
    "population" ──►  2   ✅  found
    "wrong"      ──► -1   ❌  not found

docs.title: ⚙️ Main characteristics
docs.text: Characteristic Description What it returns An integer (int) — the field index If the field is not found Returns -1 Letter case Not sensitive (case-insensitive) Where it is defined In the QgsVectorLayer and QgsFields classes

docs.title: ▶️ Simple use
docs.text:
Suppose we have a layer and want to know the index of the column named "population", so that we can then change data in that column.

# assume layer is your active vector layer
layer = iface.activeLayer()

# look up the field index by name
field_name = "population"
field_index = layer.lookupField(field_name)

if field_index != -1:
    print(f"The index of field '{field_name}' is: {field_index}")

    # for example, read this value of the first feature:
    feature = next(layer.getFeatures())
    print(f"Value: {feature[field_index]}")
else:
    print(f"❌ No field named '{field_name}' was found!")

docs.title: 💡 Why use it?
docs.text:
If you write feature[2] directly, your code breaks as soon as someone adds or deletes a column in the table. lookupField() always gives you the correct index, no matter where that column is in the list.

❌ unreliable                          ✅ reliable
──────────────                         ──────────────
value = feature[2]                     idx = layer.lookupField("population")
     │                                 value = feature[idx]
     ▼                                      │
a bug when the column                       ▼
order changes                         always correct, regardless
                                      of schema changes

📌 Rule: always use lookupField(); never hardcode an index.

docs.title: 🛠 A practical example — together with changeAttributeValues
docs.text:
lookupField() is especially useful for bulk updates of attributes:

from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer

layer = iface.activeLayer()

# get the index by name
pop_idx = layer.lookupField("population")

if pop_idx == -1:
    print("❌ Field 'population' not found")
else:
    # edit mode
    layer.startEditing()

    # bulk update with changeAttributeValues
    updates = {}
    for feat in layer.getFeatures():
        # double the population of every feature
        updates[feat.id()] = {pop_idx: feat[pop_idx] * 2}

    layer.dataProvider().changeAttributeValues(updates)
    layer.commitChanges()

    print(f"✅ {len(updates)} features updated")

docs.title: 🔍 Defensive pattern
docs.text:
def get_field_index(layer, field_name):
    """Safely returns the field index, or raises an error."""
    idx = layer.lookupField(field_name)
    if idx == -1:
        available = [f.name() for f in layer.fields()]
        raise ValueError(
            f"Field '{field_name}' not found. "
            f"Available fields: {available}"
        )
    return idx


# usage
try:
    idx = get_field_index(layer, "population")
    print(f"✅ Index: {idx}")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"❌ {e}")

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• lookupField(field_name) returns the field index by name
  • It returns -1 if the field is not found, so always check!
  • It makes code reliable: it does not break when the attribute schema changes
  • It is used together with changeAttributeValues(), updateFeature() and other index-based operations
  • Best practice: never use a hardcoded index; always convert from the name

👉 Rule: before you touch an attribute by index, the first step is always lookupField().

docs.title: 🗺️ PyQGIS scripts for geospatial calculations
docs.text:
This page contains Python scripts for geospatial calculations in QGIS, including:

  • calculating the length of a line layer
  • calculating the area and perimeter of a polygon layer
  • calculating population density in the table
  • creating new fields and writing constant values

All scripts use the QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) and assume the relevant layers exist in the QGIS project.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Calculating the length of a line layer
docs.text: This script calculates the length of the features of a line layer (e.g. Rivers) and stores the result in a new field Len_M.

docs.title: 📜 Code
docs.text:
# get the layer named 'Rivers'
layers = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('Rivers')
layer = layers[0]

# access the data provider
pv = layer.dataProvider()

# add a new field 'Len_M' for the length (double type)
pv.addAttributes([QgsField('Len_M', QVariant.Double)])
layer.updateFields()

# define the calculation expression
expr1 = QgsExpression('length($geometry)')

# create the expression context
cntx = QgsExpressionContext()
cntx.appendScopes(QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer))

# edit the layer and calculate the length
with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        cntx.setFeature(i)
        i['Len_M'] = expr1.evaluate(cntx)
        layer.updateFeature(i)

docs.title: 💡 Explanation
docs.text:
• Choosing the layer: gets the layer named 'Rivers' from the QGIS project.
  • Field: creates a new field Len_M to store each feature's length.
  • Expression: length($geometry) is used to calculate the length of each feature's geometry.
  • Update: the expression is evaluated for each feature and the Len_M field is updated.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Calculating the area and perimeter of a polygon layer
docs.text: This script calculates the area and perimeter of the features of a polygon layer (e.g. nakveti, land parcels) and stores the results in new fields Area_sq_m and Perimeter.

docs.title: 📜 Code
docs.text:
# get the layer named 'nakveti'
layers = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('nakveti')
layer = layers[0]

# access the data provider
pv = layer.dataProvider()

# add new fields for area and perimeter
pv.addAttributes([QgsField('Area_sq_m', QVariant.Double)])
pv.addAttributes([QgsField('Perimeter', QVariant.Double)])
layer.updateFields()

# define the calculation expressions
expr1 = QgsExpression('area($geometry)')
expr2 = QgsExpression('perimeter($geometry)')

# create the expression context
cntx = QgsExpressionContext()
cntx.appendScopes(QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer))

# edit the layer and calculate area and perimeter
with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        cntx.setFeature(i)
        i['Area_sq_m'] = expr1.evaluate(cntx)
        i['Perimeter'] = expr2.evaluate(cntx)
        layer.updateFeature(i)

docs.title: 💡 Explanation
docs.text:
• Choosing the layer: gets the layer named 'nakveti'.
  • Fields: creates two new fields: Area_sq_m for area and Perimeter for perimeter.
  • Expressions:
  • area($geometry) — calculates the area
  • perimeter($geometry) — calculates the perimeter
  • Update: both expressions are evaluated for each feature and the fields are updated.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Calculating population density in the table
docs.text:
This script calculates population density in a layer (e.g. Municipalitys) with the formula:

[ D = \frac{P}{A} ]

where:

  • D — population density
  • P — population (the Mosaxl_200 field)
  • A — area (in square meters or square kilometers)

docs.title: 📜 Code
docs.text:
# get the layer named 'Municipalitys'
layers = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('Municipalitys')
layer = layers[0]

# access the data provider
pv = layer.dataProvider()

# add new fields for area, area in km² and density
pv.addAttributes([
    QgsField('area', QVariant.Double),
    QgsField('area_km', QVariant.Double),
    QgsField('simwidrove', QVariant.Double)
])
layer.updateFields()

# define the calculation expressions
expr1 = QgsExpression('$area')                 # area in square meters
expr2 = QgsExpression('"area"/1000000')        # area in square kilometers
expr3 = QgsExpression('"Mosaxl_200"/area_km')  # population density

# create the expression context
cntx = QgsExpressionContext()
cntx.appendScopes(QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer))

# calculate the area
with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        cntx.setFeature(i)
        i['area'] = expr1.evaluate(cntx)
        layer.updateFeature(i)

# convert the area to square kilometers
with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        cntx.setFeature(i)
        i['area_km'] = expr2.evaluate(cntx)
        layer.updateFeature(i)

# calculate the population density
with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        cntx.setFeature(i)
        i['simwidrove'] = expr3.evaluate(cntx)
        layer.updateFeature(i)

docs.title: 💡 Explanation
docs.text:
• Choosing the layer: gets the layer named 'Municipalitys'.
  • Fields: creates three new fields — area (m²), area_km (km²), simwidrove (density).
  • Expressions:
  • expr1: $area — calculates the area in square meters
  • expr2: "area"/1000000 — converts the area to square kilometers
  • expr3: "Mosaxl_200"/area_km — calculates the population density
  • Update: the calculations run in three separate loops so the dependencies are built correctly (area → area_km → simwidrove).

docs.title: 4️⃣ Creating new fields and writing constant values
docs.text: If we don't need an expression and every feature should get the same text/number, we add the field and write the value directly.

docs.title: 📜 Code
docs.text:
layers = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('Rivers')
layer = layers[0]

pv = layer.dataProvider()
pv.addAttributes([
    QgsField('Type', QVariant.String),
    QgsField('Type_Eng', QVariant.String)
])
layer.updateFields()

# if we use QVariant.Int instead of QVariant.String,
# the value must be a number and the quotes are no longer needed

with edit(layer):
    for i in layer.getFeatures():
        i['Type'] = 'mdinare'
        i['Type_Eng'] = 'River'
        layer.updateFeature(i)

docs.title: 💡 Explanation
docs.text:
• with edit(layer) opens edit mode and saves the changes at the end of the block.
  • QgsExpressionContext is not needed here, because we are not evaluating an expression. It is only required when QgsExpression.evaluate() is used (see items 1–3).

docs.title: ⚙️ Notes
docs.text:
• Prerequisites: make sure the layers (Rivers, nakveti, Municipalitys) exist in the QGIS project and contain the required fields (e.g. Mosaxl_200 for population).
  • Running: the scripts should be run in the QGIS Python console or inside a QGIS plugin.
  • Error handling: checking that the layer exists and the fields are available is recommended.
  • Efficiency: for large datasets, consider optimization (e.g. a single editing session).

📘 Autogenerated educational resource for QGIS scripting with PyQGIS.

docs.title: Creating a layer (ESRI Shapefile)
docs.text:
Official documentation Class: QgsWkbTypes GDAL OGR To choose a coordinate system: Coordinate Systems Worldwide

For details on QgsField, QgsFields(), QVariant, QgsFeature(), iface, etc. see the Explanations section < < <

docs.title: Point layer
docs.text:
Some definitions

  • The geometry is specified here because the writer needs to take it into account; instead of QgsWkbTypes.Point you can use Line, Polygon, Unknown, Null.

docs.title: ✅ The main geometry types in PyQGIS:
docs.text:
Type Layer type (as a string) Example in code Point "Point" QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(x, y)) MultiPoint "MultiPoint" QgsGeometry.fromMultiPointXY([QgsPointXY(x1, y1), QgsPointXY(x2, y2)]) Line "LineString" QgsGeometry.fromPolylineXY([QgsPointXY(x1, y1), QgsPointXY(x2, y2)]) MultiLine "MultiLineString" QgsGeometry.fromMultiPolylineXY([[QgsPointXY(x1, y1), QgsPointXY(x2, y2)], [QgsPointXY(x3, y3), QgsPointXY(x4, y4)]]) Polygon "Polygon" QgsGeometry.fromPolygonXY([[QgsPointXY(x1, y1), QgsPointXY(x2, y2), QgsPointXY(x3, y3), QgsPointXY(x1, y1)]]) MultiPolygon "MultiPolygon" QgsGeometry.fromMultiPolygonXY([[[QgsPointXY(x1, y1), QgsPointXY(x2, y2), QgsPointXY(x3, y3), QgsPointXY(x1, y1)]]])
  • shapefile_home is a variable and goes through the script under a meaningful name
  • QgsFields() creates the columns of the attribute table
  • File Handling - "r" - Read - Default value. Opens a file for reading, error if the file does not exist
  • the writer collects the information, the encoding, the columns, the geometry and the coordinate system, and combines them into a container.
  • the new layer is created and saved with the 'ESRI Shapefile' driver.
  • the encoding, projection, driver, etc. must be passed as arguments
  • the function returns an object, defined as writer in the code, that can add and write new features to the layer.

Test the code directly in the QGIS Python console, which you can open with the shortcut

Left Ctrl+Left Alt+P

new_shapefile_point.py
shapefile_home = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\saxli.shp'

layerfield = QgsFields() 

layerfield.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int)) # column 1

layerfield.append(QgsField('Field_1', QVariant.String)) # column 2

layerfield.append(QgsField('Field_2', QVariant.Double, len=10, prec=2)) # column 3

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(shapefile_home, 'UTF-8', layerfield, QgsWkbTypes.Point, \

               QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'), 'ESRI Shapefile')


del(writer)

This shortcut helps you comment code out or back in Left Ctrl+Left Shift+:

We can also write data to the layer right here

new_shapefile_point_with_data.py
# this part of the code goes in after the writer is created

fc = QgsFeature() # creates a spatial feature

# creates the geometry at a predefined coordinate
fc.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56))) 

# puts information into the attribute table, following
# the columns we defined when creating the layer
fc.setAttributes([1, 'text', 25])  # (ID, 'text for this cell', number)

writer.addFeature(fc) # add the feature to the layer

Where del(writer) goes

The code that adds features must come after the writer is created and before del(writer). del(writer) closes the file and writes the data to disk, so writer.addFeature(fc) no longer works after it.

The full sequence in one script:

new_shapefile_point_full.py
shapefile_home = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\saxli.shp'

layerfield = QgsFields()
layerfield.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int))
layerfield.append(QgsField('Field_1', QVariant.String))
layerfield.append(QgsField('Field_2', QVariant.Double, len=10, prec=2))

# 1. the writer is created
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(shapefile_home, 'UTF-8', layerfield, QgsWkbTypes.Point, \
               QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'), 'ESRI Shapefile')

# 2. a feature is added to the writer
fc = QgsFeature()
fc.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56)))
fc.setAttributes([1, 'text', 25])
writer.addFeature(fc)

# 3. finally the writer is closed
del(writer)

# 4. the layer is added to the QGIS project
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(shapefile_home, '', 'ogr')

docs.title: Adding the layer to the QGIS project
docs.text:
shapefile_point.py
# shapefile_home: the file name - '': the layer name - ogr: vector file

# iface.addVectorLayer decides which layer is added to the QGIS Layers panel.
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(shapefile_home, '', 'ogr')

Creating a new point vector layer from coordinate pairs and adding it to the QGIS project.

create_shapefile_with_tuples.py
fn = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\new_shapefile_point_tuples.shp'



layerfield = QgsFields()

layerfield.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int))

layerfield.append(QgsField('Category', QVariant.String))



writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(fn, 'UTF-8', layerfield, QgsWkbTypes.Point, \

              QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'), 'ESRI Shapefile')



XY = [(356671.0049, 4679923.0988),

(356672.2015, 4679929.5719),

(356672.9728, 4679933.1198),

(356674.5925, 4679935.2022),

(356676.0579, 4679936.8219),

(356676.9835, 4679938.1332),

(356645.632, 4679901.1075),

(356654.4244, 4679905.3495),

(356659.9775, 4679909.2829),

(356664.2194, 4679912.7536),

(356668.055, 4679916.8107)]  


for i in XY:

    fc = QgsFeature()

    fc.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(i[0], i[1])))

    fc.setAttributes([XY.index(i), 'lake'])

    writer.addFeature(fc)



del(writer)



layer = iface.addVectorLayer(fn, '', 'ogr')

XY.index(i) or enumerate?

In the loop above, XY.index(i) gives us the ID. It searches the list for the element and returns its position. This works, but if the list contains two identical points, both get the same ID, and it also searches the list from the start every time. A simple alternative is enumerate, which gives us the number and the element itself:

for n, (x, y) in enumerate(XY, start=1):
    fc = QgsFeature()
    fc.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(x, y)))
    fc.setAttributes([n, 'lake'])   # n = 1, 2, 3 ...
    writer.addFeature(fc)

start=1 means counting starts at 1 (by default it starts at 0).

docs.title: Creating a layer with a function (improved version)
docs.text:
The scripts above make us rewrite the geometry, the fields and the path by hand every time. The function below:

  • works with any geometry (Point, LineString, Polygon, Multi...)
  • works with both Shapefile and GeoPackage (it picks the driver from the extension)
  • checks whether the file and folder exist, and gives a clear message on error
  • takes the fields from a simple list and adds all features at once
  • finally adds the layer to the project
create_layer_function.py
import os
from qgis.core import (
    QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsFields, QgsField, QgsFeature, QgsGeometry,
    QgsPointXY, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem, QgsProject, QgsVectorLayer, QgsWkbTypes
)
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant

# field types as strings, so we don't need QVariant every time
FIELD_TYPES = {
    'int': QVariant.Int,
    'str': QVariant.String,
    'float': QVariant.Double,
    'date': QVariant.Date,
}

# extension -> OGR driver
DRIVERS = {'.shp': 'ESRI Shapefile', '.gpkg': 'GPKG', '.geojson': 'GeoJSON'}


def create_layer(path, geom_type, epsg, fields, features=None,
                 overwrite=False, add_to_project=True):
    """
    path        - full file path (.shp / .gpkg / .geojson)
    geom_type   - QgsWkbTypes.Point, QgsWkbTypes.LineString, QgsWkbTypes.Polygon ...
    epsg        - e.g. 32638
    fields      - [('ID', 'int'), ('Name', 'str'), ('Area', 'float')]
    features    - [(geometry, [attributes]), ...]  (optional)
    overwrite   - whether to overwrite the file if it already exists
    """
    folder, ext = os.path.dirname(path), os.path.splitext(path)[1].lower()

    if ext not in DRIVERS:
        raise ValueError(f'Unsupported format: {ext}')
    if not os.path.isdir(folder):
        os.makedirs(folder)          # create the folder if it does not exist
    if os.path.exists(path) and not overwrite:
        raise FileExistsError(f'The file already exists: {path}')

    crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem(f'EPSG:{epsg}')
    if not crs.isValid():
        raise ValueError(f'Invalid EPSG code: {epsg}')

    qfields = QgsFields()
    for name, ftype in fields:
        qfields.append(QgsField(name, FIELD_TYPES[ftype]))

    options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
    options.driverName = DRIVERS[ext]
    options.fileEncoding = 'UTF-8'
    options.actionOnExistingFile = QgsVectorFileWriter.CreateOrOverwriteFile

    writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(
        path, qfields, geom_type, crs,
        QgsProject.instance().transformContext(), options
    )
    if writer.hasError() != QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
        raise RuntimeError(writer.errorMessage())

    for geom, attrs in (features or []):
        fc = QgsFeature(qfields)
        fc.setGeometry(geom)
        fc.setAttributes(attrs)
        writer.addFeature(fc)

    del writer   # the file is closed and the data is written to disk

    layer = QgsVectorLayer(path, os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(path))[0], 'ogr')
    if add_to_project and layer.isValid():
        QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)
    return layer

docs.title: Usage examples
docs.text:
A point layer with data

example_points.py
pts = [(356671.0049, 4679923.0988), (356672.2015, 4679929.5719)]

features = [
    (QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(x, y)), [i, 'lake'])
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(pts, start=1)
]

layer = create_layer(
    r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\lakes.shp',
    QgsWkbTypes.Point, 32638,
    fields=[('ID', 'int'), ('Category', 'str')],
    features=features,
    overwrite=True
)

An empty polygon layer in a GeoPackage (we will draw the data by hand later)

example_polygon_gpkg.py
layer = create_layer(
    r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\parcels.gpkg',
    QgsWkbTypes.Polygon, 32638,
    fields=[('ID', 'int'), ('Owner', 'str'), ('Area_m2', 'float')],
    overwrite=True
)

Why GeoPackage?

Shapefile has limits: a field name is at most 10 characters, text up to 254 characters, and one layer is made of 3–7 files. .gpkg has none of these problems, so it is the better choice for new projects.

About QVariant

Since QGIS 3.38, QVariant.Int and similar types have been replaced by QMetaType.Type.Int. The old form still works, but it may show a warning.

docs.title: Creating a point layer from a CSV file
docs.text:
Coordinates are often in a table (e.g. points collected with GPS). The script below reads a CSV and uses the create_layer() function described above to create the layer.

An example CSV file (points.csv, the first line is the header):

ID,Name,X,Y
1,Lake 1,356671.0049,4679923.0988
2,Lake 2,356672.2015,4679929.5719
3,Spring,356676.9835,4679938.1332
create_layer_from_csv.py
import csv

csv_path = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\points.csv'
out_path = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points.gpkg'

features = []

# utf-8-sig also opens UTF-8 files saved by Excel (with a BOM)
with open(csv_path, newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig') as f:
    for n, row in enumerate(csv.DictReader(f), start=2):  # line 1 is the header
        try:
            x = float(row['X'].replace(',', '.'))
            y = float(row['Y'].replace(',', '.'))
            attrs = [int(row['ID']), row['Name']]
        except (KeyError, ValueError) as e:
            print(f'Line {n} skipped: {e}')   # a bad line does not stop us
            continue

        features.append((QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(x, y)), attrs))

layer = create_layer(
    out_path,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point, 32638,
    fields=[('ID', 'int'), ('Name', 'str')],
    features=features,
    overwrite=True
)

print(f'Added {len(features)} features')

Things to watch out for

  • The coordinate column names (X, Y) and the EPSG code (32638) must match your data. For geographic coordinates (longitude/latitude) use 4326.
  • If the CSV is separated by semicolons (;), add delimiter=';' to DictReader.
  • The create_layer() function must already have been run in the same console.

A quick alternative

If we don't need to save the layer to a file, QGIS can open the CSV directly as points: 

uri = 'file:///C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/points.csv?delimiter=,&xField=X&yField=Y&crs=EPSG:32638'
layer = QgsVectorLayer(uri, 'points', 'delimitedtext')
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)

docs.title: Adding fields to an existing layer
docs.text: For adding new columns to an existing layer and calculating them, see the page attribute table calculations.

docs.title: ℹ️ Explanations – PyQGIS components
docs.text:
This section gives short explanations of frequently used objects and classes that you need when writing PyQGIS scripts.

❗ These components often come up when creating layers or working with attributes or geometry.

docs.title: 🔹 QgsField
docs.text:
Used to define a layer field (an attribute column). It holds the field's name and type.

Example:

QgsField("name", QVariant.String)
# creates a text field named "name"

docs.title: 🔹 QgsFields
docs.text:
Represents a collection of fields (i.e. several QgsFields together). It is needed when you have to pass all fields at once, for example when creating a layer.

Example:

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField("name", QVariant.String))

docs.title: 🔹 QVariant
docs.text:
A Qt data type class that QGIS uses to define the types of attribute values (e.g. String, Int, Double, etc.).

Examples:

  • QVariant.String – a text field
  • QVariant.Int – an integer
  • QVariant.Double – a decimal number

docs.title: 🔹 QgsFeature
docs.text:
Represents one object (a point, line or polygon) with its geometry and attributes.

Example:

feature = QgsFeature()
feature.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(44.8, 41.7)))
feature.setAttributes(["Tbilisi"])

docs.title: 🔹 iface
docs.text:
iface (Interface) is the main QGIS object used to interact with the QGIS interface (Layers Panel, Map Canvas, etc.).

Example:

iface.addVectorLayer("/path/to/file.shp", "My Layer", "ogr")
# adds the layer directly to the QGIS project

⚠️ iface is only available in the QGIS Python Console. It does not work in a standard Python script.

docs.title: 🔹 Other useful classes
docs.text: Class Description QgsGeometry A geometry object (point, line, polygon, etc.) QgsPointXY A 2D point object – with x and y coordinates QgsVectorLayer A vector layer object QgsProject The QGIS project – lets you add and manage layers QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem Defines a coordinate system by EPSG code

docs.title: Geometry conversions
docs.text:
Official documentation Converting a point layer to a line — Point to Line Conversion Points to path: Converting a line layer to a polygon — Lines to polygon Lines to polygons: Converting a polygon layer to lines — Polygon to Lines Conversion Polygons to lines: Getting points from a line layer — Points along geometry Points along geometry:

Geometry Conversions — changing the geometry type of vector layers using processing.run().

docs.title: Some definitions
docs.text:
• processing.run means the QGIS Processing Toolbox. [method/function]
  • The word native means a QGIS tool, and pointstopath is its name.
  • The code inside it follows the dictionary principle {}: the argument holds key:value pairs.

Warning

Pay attention to 'ORDER_EXPRESSION': '"ID"' in the tool, because not every layer has this ID column in its table, and it must be replaced with the right one. Otherwise the program crashes completely.

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
In PyQGIS you can convert the geometry of a vector layer into another type, by calling QGIS Processing Toolbox tools directly from code.

Point  ──→  Line  ──→  Polygon
  ↑                       │
  └───── Points along ←───┘
Conversion Tool Processing ID Point → line Points to Path native:pointstopath Line → polygon Lines to Polygons qgis:linestopolygons Polygon → line Polygons to Lines native:polygonstolines Line → points Points along Geometry native:pointsalonglines

docs.title: 🧩 processing.run() — how does it work?
docs.text:
processing.run("provider:toolname", { parameters })
  • processing.run — calling the QGIS Processing Toolbox from code
  • native — a built-in QGIS tool
  • qgis — the QGIS algorithm library
  • { ... } — parameters as a key: value dictionary

docs.title: 🟢 Point → line
docs.text:
Points to Path — converting a point layer to a line

📎 Official documentation: Points to Path

fn     = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points_to_line.shp'

processing.run("native:pointstopath", {
    'INPUT'            : fn,
    'CLOSE_PATH'       : True,    # True = the line is closed (a loop)
    'ORDER_EXPRESSION' : '"ID"',  # ⚠️ column name — see the warning
    'NATURAL_SORT'     : False,
    'GROUP_EXPRESSION' : '',
    'OUTPUT'           : output
})

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, 'Points to Line', 'ogr')

⚠️ ORDER_EXPRESSION: this parameter defines in what order the points are joined into a line. Not every layer has an "ID" column — check your layer's attributes and replace it with the right column name. Without the column, or with a wrong name, the program gives an ERROR.

📌 The result is a line in which the points are joined in sequence according to ORDER_EXPRESSION.

docs.title: 🔵 Line → polygon
docs.text:
Lines to Polygons — converting a line layer to a polygon

📎 Official documentation: Lines to Polygons

fn     = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\line_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\polygon_from_line.shp'

processing.run("qgis:linestopolygons", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': output
})

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, 'Line to Polygon', 'ogr')

📌 The first and last point of the line are joined automatically, forming a closed geometry (a polygon).

💡 The line should be closed or nearly so; otherwise the result may be unexpected.

docs.title: 🟠 Polygon → line
docs.text:
Polygons to Lines — converting a polygon layer to lines

📎 Official documentation: Polygons to Lines

fn     = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\polygon_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\line_from_polygon.shp'

processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': output
})

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, 'Polygon to Line', 'ogr')

📌 The polygon's outline becomes a line — useful for buffers, edge analysis and visualization.

docs.title: 🟣 Line → points (Points along geometry)
docs.text:
Points along Geometry — placing points along a line at equal distances

📎 Official documentation: Points along Geometry

fn     = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\line_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points_on_line.shp'

processing.run("native:pointsalonglines", {
    'INPUT'       : fn,
    'DISTANCE'    : 5,    # ← distance between points (in CRS units)
    'START_OFFSET': 0,    # ← skip from the start of the line
    'END_OFFSET'  : 0,    # ← skip from the end of the line
    'OUTPUT'      : output
})

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, 'Points along Line', 'ogr')

📌 DISTANCE is in CRS units: if the layer is in metric coordinates (e.g. EPSG:32638), 5 means 5 meters.

💡 In geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326) DISTANCE is in degrees — in that case change the projection to a metric one (EPSG:32638) for a correct result.

docs.title: 🗂️ Keeping results temporarily (memory layer)
docs.text:
Use 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT' or 'memory:' for OUTPUT if you don't want a file:

result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'   # ← in memory only
})

# the temporary layer
temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(temp_layer)

💡 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT' is deleted automatically when the session ends. If you need to keep a file, use a full path.

docs.title: ⚡ Error handling
docs.text:
import processing
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer

fn     = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points_to_line.shp'

try:
    result = processing.run("native:pointstopath", {
        'INPUT'            : fn,
        'CLOSE_PATH'       : True,
        'ORDER_EXPRESSION' : '"ID"',
        'NATURAL_SORT'     : False,
        'GROUP_EXPRESSION' : '',
        'OUTPUT'           : output
    })

    layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, 'Points to Line', 'ogr')

    if not layer or not layer.isValid():
        print("❌ The layer did not load")
    else:
        print(f"✅ Layer loaded — {layer.featureCount()} features")

except Exception as e:
    print(f"❌ Processing error: {e}")

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
In this topic we covered:

Conversion Processing ID Result 🟢 Point → line native:pointstopath Points are joined in sequence 🔵 Line → polygon qgis:linestopolygons The line closes and forms an area 🟠 Polygon → line native:polygonstolines The outline becomes a line 🟣 Line → points native:pointsalonglines Evenly spaced points on the line

👉 Every conversion uses processing.run() — the power of the QGIS Processing Toolbox directly from code.

docs.title: 🟢 Converting a point layer to a line (Point to Line Conversion)
docs.text:
Points_to_line.py
fn = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\points_to_line.shp'

processing.run("native:pointstopath", {
    'INPUT': fn,
    'CLOSE_PATH': True,
    'ORDER_EXPRESSION': '"ID"',
    'NATURAL_SORT': False,
    'GROUP_EXPRESSION': '',
    'OUTPUT': output
})

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, '', 'ogr')

📌 The result is a line that follows the order of the points.

docs.title: 🟢 Converting a line layer to a polygon (Line to Polygon)
docs.text:
Line_to_polygon.py
fn = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\line_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\Polygon_layer_from_line.shp'

processing.run("qgis:linestopolygons", {'INPUT':fn, 'OUTPUT':output})
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, '', 'ogr')

📌 The lines are joined and a polygon geometry is formed.

docs.title: 🟢 Converting a polygon layer to lines (Polygon to Lines Conversion)
docs.text:
Polygon_to_Line_Conversion.py
fn = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\Polygon_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\Line_layer_from_polygon.shp'

processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {'INPUT':fn,'OUTPUT':output})
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, '', 'ogr')

📌 The elements of the polygon layer become lines, following their outline/shape.

docs.title: 🟢 Getting points from a line layer (Points along geometry)
docs.text:
Points_along_geometry.py
fn = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\Line_layer.shp'
output = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GK\PyQGIS\shp\Points_placed_on_line.shp'

processing.run("native:pointsalonglines", {'INPUT':fn,'DISTANCE':5,'START_OFFSET':0,'END_OFFSET':0,'OUTPUT':output})
layer = iface.addVectorLayer(output, '', 'ogr')

📌 Places points at a given spacing on every element of a line layer.
