docs.title: Quick decision table (2025–2026)
docs.text: Situation Recommendation Is del required? A simple one-off writer create() + del writer ✅ by hand Exporting a layer writeAsVectorFormatV3() ❌ no Writing many files in a loop try / finally + del writer ✅ by hand Clean, modular code contextmanager wrapper ✅ automatic OOP / a reusable class ShapefileWriter (__exit__) ✅ automatic Maximum stability any with approach ✅ guaranteed

docs.title: 💎 The key message
docs.text:
PyQGIS  =  Python  +  C++
GC      ≠  enough
  • del writer: always use it with writers you create by hand
  • try / finally: guaranteed cleanup in any scenario
  • contextmanager: a clean with style with minimal code
  • The ShapefileWriter class: an OOP approach, reusable across the project
  • writeAsVectorFormatV3: the cleanest way to export layers

API used: QGIS 3.22–3.44+ | PyQGIS | SIP wrapper | C++ destructor pattern

docs.title: The C++ destructor in the PyQGIS context
docs.text:
C++ | Python | SIP Wrapper | PyQGIS | memory management

A destructor is a special method of a C++ class that is called automatically when an object is destroyed. It releases resources: closes files, frees memory, closes connections.

docs.title: 📋 Contents (destructor)
docs.text:
1. What is a destructor?
  2. C++ vs Python — lifecycle
  3. SIP wrapper — two-layer architecture
  4. The problem in PyQGIS
  5. del — calling the C++ destructor by hand
  6. QgsVectorFileWriter — full lifecycle
  7. Cleanup patterns
  8. Other PyQGIS classes that need cleanup

docs.title: 🔧 What is a destructor?
docs.text:
In C++ every class can have a constructor and a destructor:

class QgsVectorFileWriter {
public:
    // constructor — the object is created
    QgsVectorFileWriter(const QString& path, ...) {
        // ✅ the file is opened
        // ✅ a buffer is allocated
        // ✅ a lock is taken
    }

    // destructor — the object is destroyed
    ~QgsVectorFileWriter() {
        // ✅ the buffer is written to disk (flush)
        // ✅ the file is closed
        // ✅ the lock is released
        // ✅ the memory is freed
    }
};

docs.title: Properties of a destructor
docs.text:
✅ automatic      — C++ calls it itself when the object leaves its scope
✅ only one       — a class can have only one destructor
✅ no parameters  — ~ClassName() — takes no arguments
✅ guaranteed     — in C++ it is always called for stack objects

docs.title: Automatic call in C++
docs.text:
void someFunction() {
    QgsVectorFileWriter writer("output.shp", ...);  // constructor

    writer.addFeature(feat1);
    writer.addFeature(feat2);

}   // ← the function ends → ~QgsVectorFileWriter() automatically!
    //   the file is closed, the buffer is written

docs.title: ⚖️ C++ vs Python — lifecycle
docs.text: C++ and Python manage object lifetimes completely differently:

docs.title: C++ — deterministic destruction
docs.text:
// C++ — we know exactly where the object is destroyed
{
    Writer w("file.shp");   // constructor — exactly here
    w.addFeature(f);
}                           // destructor — exactly here, at the end of the scope
                            // "deterministic" — predictable in advance

docs.title: Python — non-deterministic GC
docs.text:
# Python — we cannot know exactly where it is cleaned up
writer = SomePythonObject()
writer.do_something()
writer = None    # the reference is gone... but when will the GC clean up?
                 # maybe now, maybe later — "non-deterministic"

docs.title: How the SIP wrapper behaves
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(...)
# ↑ this creates:
#   1. a Python wrapper object (small, on Python's heap)
#   2. a C++ QgsVectorFileWriter object (with the file resources)
#   The Python wrapper "owns" the C++ object — it stores a pointer

del writer
# ↑ this:
#   1. drops the Python wrapper
#   2. SIP notices: the Python side is gone → call the C++ destructor!
#   3. ~QgsVectorFileWriter() → flush + close + unlock

docs.title: ⚠️ The problem in PyQGIS
docs.text: Python's GC does not call the C++ destructor at an exact moment. This leads to:

docs.title: Problem 1 — the file stays locked
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter("output.shp", ...)
writer.addFeature(feat)

# writer = None ← the reference is gone, but the GC has not run yet

# the next code cannot touch this file:
os.remove("output.shp")   # ❌ PermissionError: file is in use!
shutil.move("output.shp", "backup/")  # ❌ WinError 32

docs.title: Problem 2 — the data is not written
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter("output.shp", ...)

for feat in features:
    writer.addFeature(feat)
    # ↑ the features are in the buffer, not on disk yet!

# the GC has not cleaned up yet → ~QgsVectorFileWriter() not called yet
# → flush() has not happened → the last features are lost!

layer = QgsVectorLayer("output.shp", "Layer", "ogr")
# the .shp file may be:
# → empty (0 features)
# → incomplete (the last batch is lost)
# → corrupted (header ≠ content)

docs.title: Problem 3 — a memory leak in a loop
docs.text:
for i in range(10000):
    writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(f"layer_{i}.shp", ...)
    writer.addFeature(feat)
    # del writer ← this line is missing!
    # the GC cannot keep up → C++ objects pile up → RAM fills up
    # → QGIS freezes / slows down / crashes

docs.title: 🗑️ del — calling the C++ destructor by hand
docs.text:
Python's del removes a reference. When the last reference is removed, Python frees the object right away → it calls the SIP destructor:

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter("output.shp", ...)

writer.addFeature(feat1)
writer.addFeature(feat2)

del writer
# ↑ exactly on this line:
#   Python: reference_count(writer) → 0
#   SIP:    "Python no longer needs it" → C++ destructor!
#   C++:    ~QgsVectorFileWriter()
#             → buffer → disk (flush)
#             → file.close()
#             → release the OS lock
#             → C++ object memory → free()

docs.title: del vs = None
docs.text:
# ✅ both work — the reference count drops to 0
del writer       # ← the most explicit, clear in the code
writer = None    # ← the same effect, less readable

# ⚠️ this does not work — a reference still exists!
backup = writer  # another variable holds a reference
del writer       # ← Python: reference_count = 1 (backup still exists!)
                 # → the C++ destructor is not called yet!

docs.title: Visualizing the reference count
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(...)
  → Python object: ref_count = 1

backup = writer
  → Python object: ref_count = 2

del writer
  → Python object: ref_count = 1  ← still alive!

del backup
  → Python object: ref_count = 0  ← now: C++ destructor!

docs.title: 🔄 QgsVectorFileWriter — full lifecycle
docs.text:
QgsVectorFileWriter(path, encoding, fields, geomType, crs, driver)
         │
         │  constructor
         ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  the C++ object is "alive"   │
│  ✅ output.shp is open       │
│  ✅ OS lock taken            │
│  ✅ buffer ready             │
└──────────────────────────────┘
         │
         │  addFeature(feat) — into the buffer
         ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  features are in the buffer  │
│  ⚠️ not on disk yet          │
│  ⚠️ the file is not complete │
└──────────────────────────────┘
         │
         │  del writer  ←── this line!
         ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  ~QgsVectorFileWriter()      │  C++ destructor
│  ✅ flush() — buffer → disk  │
│  ✅ file.close()             │
│  ✅ OS lock released         │
│  ✅ memory freed             │
└──────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
   output.shp — complete and readable ✅

docs.title: Pattern 1 — del (minimal)
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(
    shapefile_path, 'UTF-8', fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point, crs, 'ESRI Shapefile'
)

writer.addFeature(feat)

del writer   # C++ destructor → flush + close

⚠️ Weak point: if an exception occurs, the code stops before del and del does not run.

docs.title: Pattern 2 — try / finally (guaranteed)
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(
    shapefile_path, fields, QgsWkbTypes.Point, crs,
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(), options
)

try:
    for feat in features:
        writer.addFeature(feat)
    print(f"✅ {len(features)} features written")

except Exception as e:
    print(f"❌ Error: {e}")

finally:
    del writer          # ← always runs — even on an exception!
    print("🔒 C++ destructor called — file closed")

✅ finally is Python's guarantee: it always runs, regardless of exceptions.

docs.title: Pattern 3 — contextmanager (with style)
docs.text:
from contextlib import contextmanager
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsProject

@contextmanager
def vector_writer(path, fields, geom_type, crs):
    options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
    options.driverName   = "ESRI Shapefile"
    options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"

    writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(
        path, fields, geom_type, crs,
        QgsProject.instance().transformContext(), options
    )

    if writer.hasError() != QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
        raise RuntimeError(writer.errorMessage())
    try:
        yield writer                    # hands the writer to Python
    finally:
        del writer                      # C++ destructor — guaranteed!

# usage:
with vector_writer(path, fields, QgsWkbTypes.Point, crs) as writer:
    for feat in features:
        writer.addFeature(feat)
# ← the with block ended → del automatically

docs.title: Pattern 4 — writeAsVectorFormatV3 (no del needed)
docs.text:
# here the writer lives in the internal scope of a C++ function
# → C++'s automatic destructor does the work → we don't need del

error, _, _, _ = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
    layer, path,
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(),
    options
)

if error == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("✅ Export — del was not needed")

docs.title: Comparing the patterns
docs.text:
┌──────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ Pattern          │ Cleanup       │ Code clarity │ Who calls it     │
├──────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ del writer       │ ❌ without try│ ✅ simple    │ by hand          │
│ try / finally    │ ✅ guaranteed │ 🔶 medium    │ by hand, finally │
│ contextmanager   │ ✅ guaranteed │ ✅ clean     │ automatic        │
│ writeAsVectorV3  │ ✅ C++ auto   │ ✅ clean     │ C++ automatic    │
└──────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────┘

docs.title: 🔍 Other PyQGIS classes that need cleanup
docs.text: QgsVectorFileWriter is not the only class where releasing C++ resources by hand matters:

docs.title: QgsDataProvider — the data source
docs.text:
# ✅ removing a QgsVectorLayer also closes its provider
layer = QgsVectorLayer(path, "Layer", "ogr")
QgsProject.instance().removeMapLayer(layer.id())
# ← C++ QgsOgrProvider destructor → the OGR file handle is closed

docs.title: QgsFeatureIterator — closing the iterator
docs.text:
# ⚠️ on large layers the iterator keeps a C++ connection open
it = layer.getFeatures()

for feat in it:
    if feat['ID'] == target_id:
        break       # ← the iterator stopped, but the C++ connection is still open!

# ✅ close it by hand
it.close()          # ← C++ destructor → DB cursor / file handle closed

docs.title: QgsRasterLayer — a raster file
docs.text:
raster = QgsRasterLayer(tiff_path, "DEM", "gdal")

# the GDAL dataset is open at the C++ level
# removing it from QgsProject → C++ GDAL destructor
QgsProject.instance().removeMapLayer(raster.id())

docs.title: QgsTransaction — a database transaction
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsTransaction

transaction = QgsTransaction.create(layer)
transaction.begin()

try:
    layer.startEditing()
    # ... changes ...
    transaction.commit()
except:
    transaction.rollback()   # ← release the C++ connection
finally:
    del transaction          # ← C++ destructor → DB connection cleanup

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
C++ destructor
      │
      ├── automatic in C++ — at the end of the scope
      │
      └── in PyQGIS — not automatic because of the SIP wrapper
                │
                ├── del writer    → Python ref=0 → SIP → C++ destructor
                ├── try/finally   → guaranteed even on exceptions
                ├── contextmanager → with block → automatic del
                └── writeAsVectorFormatV3 → C++ scope → automatic
Python statement C++ effect writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(...) QgsVectorFileWriter() constructor — the file is opened writer.addFeature(feat) Written to the buffer — not on disk yet del writer ~QgsVectorFileWriter() — flush + close + unlock
  • C++ destructor = the class's cleanup method, with the ~ClassName() syntax
  • SIP wrapper = Python's "shell" around a C++ object — a two-layer world
  • del = removes the Python reference → SIP → the C++ destructor is called
  • try/finally = guaranteed cleanup, even on errors
  • Python GC ≠ C++ destructor: the GC is non-deterministic, the destructor is deterministic

docs.title: native: and qgis: — the difference in PyQGIS
docs.text:
In processing.run() the first argument always looks like this:

processing.run("native:pointstopath", {...})
processing.run("qgis:selectbyattribute", {...})
#               ↑
#          provider:toolname
#          ─────────────────
#          prefix : tool name

The prefix tells QGIS where to look for the tool.

docs.title: 🔑 The main difference
docs.text: native: qgis: Written in C++ Python Speed ⚡ fast 🐢 relatively slow Maintained in The QGIS Core library QGIS Python Plugins Stability ✅ high 🔶 may change between versions Thread-safe ✅ 🔶 not always Location qgis/src/analysis/ python/plugins/processing/

docs.title: 🔧 native: — C++ tools
docs.text: native: tools are built into the C++ core of QGIS. They are the fastest and most stable.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# point → line
processing.run("native:pointstopath", {
    'INPUT'            : layer,
    'ORDER_EXPRESSION' : '"ID"',
    'CLOSE_PATH'       : False,
    'OUTPUT'           : 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# buffer
processing.run("native:buffer", {
    'INPUT'    : layer,
    'DISTANCE' : 100,
    'SEGMENTS' : 5,
    'OUTPUT'   : 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# polygon → line
processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : layer,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# points along a line
processing.run("native:pointsalonglines", {
    'INPUT'   : layer,
    'DISTANCE': 50,
    'OUTPUT'  : 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# Dissolve
processing.run("native:dissolve", {
    'INPUT' : layer,
    'FIELD' : ['Region'],
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# delete duplicate geometries
processing.run("native:deleteduplicategeometries", {
    'INPUT' : layer,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

docs.title: Where does the code live?
docs.text:
QGIS Source Code:
  qgis/src/analysis/processing/
    ├── qgsalgorithmbuffer.cpp          ← native:buffer
    ├── qgsalgorithmpointstopath.cpp    ← native:pointstopath
    ├── qgsalgorithmpolygonstolines.cpp ← native:polygonstolines
    └── ...

docs.title: 🐍 qgis: — Python tools
docs.text: qgis: tools are written in Python and are part of the QGIS Processing Framework.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# select by attribute ('კახეთი' = Kakheti, as stored in the data)
processing.run("qgis:selectbyattribute", {
    'INPUT'    : layer,
    'FIELD'    : 'Region',
    'OPERATOR' : 0,        # 0 = equals (=)
    'VALUE'    : 'კახეთი',
    'METHOD'   : 0         # 0 = new selection
})

# line → polygon
processing.run("qgis:linestopolygons", {
    'INPUT' : layer,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# field calculation
processing.run("qgis:fieldcalculator", {
    'INPUT'         : layer,
    'FIELD_NAME'    : 'area_ha',
    'FIELD_TYPE'    : 0,       # 0 = Float
    'FIELD_LENGTH'  : 10,
    'FIELD_PRECISION': 2,
    'FORMULA'       : '$area / 10000',
    'OUTPUT'        : 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# random selection
processing.run("qgis:randomselection", {
    'INPUT' : layer,
    'METHOD': 0,     # 0 = Number of selected features
    'NUMBER': 10
})

docs.title: Where does the code live?
docs.text:
QGIS Source Code:
  python/plugins/processing/algs/qgis/
    ├── SelectByAttribute.py      ← qgis:selectbyattribute
    ├── LinesToPolygons.py        ← qgis:linestopolygons
    ├── FieldCalculator.py        ← qgis:fieldcalculator
    └── ...

docs.title: ⚡ Why the difference in speed?
docs.text:
native:buffer (C++)                    qgis:selectbyattribute (Python)
─────────────────────────────────      ─────────────────────────────────
compiled binary code                   interpreted Python code
         │                                        │
         ▼                                        ▼
executed directly by the CPU           Python interpreter → bytecode → CPU
         │                                        │
         ▼                                        ▼
    ~10x faster                          overhead on every operation

The practical difference:

import time

# a layer with 100,000 features

start = time.time()
processing.run("native:buffer", {'INPUT': large_layer, 'DISTANCE': 100, 'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'})
print(f"native: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")   # → native:  1.2s

start = time.time()
processing.run("qgis:buffer", {'INPUT': large_layer, 'DISTANCE': 100, 'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'})
print(f"qgis:   {time.time() - start:.2f}s")   # → qgis:   11.8s  (existed in older versions)

💡 That is exactly why many qgis: tools were rewritten as native: during the QGIS 3.x cycle.

docs.title: 🔄 qgis: → native: — migration
docs.text:
As QGIS 3.x developed, many qgis: tools were rewritten in C++ and became native:. The old qgis: name is often kept as an alias, so old code still works.

# in QGIS 3.x these two are often the same:
processing.run("qgis:dissolve", {...})    # ← alias
processing.run("native:dissolve", {...}) # ← the real implementation

# the QGIS toolbox responds with:
# "qgis:dissolve is deprecated, use native:dissolve"

docs.title: By version
docs.text: Tool Old New (3.x) Dissolve qgis:dissolve native:dissolve Buffer qgis:fixeddistancebuffer native:buffer Polygon to Lines qgis:polygonstolines native:polygonstolines Points along Geometry qgis:pointsalonglines native:pointsalonglines Centroid qgis:centroids native:centroids

docs.title: 🌐 Other prefixes
docs.text:
Besides native: and qgis: there are other prefixes:

# gdal: — the GDAL library (raster, vector)
processing.run("gdal:translate", {...})
processing.run("gdal:warpreproject", {...})
processing.run("gdal:rasterize", {...})

# grass7: — GRASS GIS tools
processing.run("grass7:v.buffer", {...})
processing.run("grass7:r.slope.aspect", {...})

# saga: — SAGA GIS tools
processing.run("saga:slopeaspectcurvature", {...})

# 3d: — QGIS 3D tools
processing.run("3d:tessellate", {...})

docs.title: Comparing the prefixes
docs.text: Prefix Language Specialization native: C++ Vector, general geoprocessing qgis: Python General, selection, fields gdal: C++ Raster, format conversion grass7: C Hydrology, analysis, raster saga: C++ Modelling, terrain analysis 3d: C++ 3D geometry

docs.text:
# all tools
for alg in QgsApplication.processingRegistry().algorithms():
    print(alg.id())
# → native:buffer
# → native:pointstopath
# → qgis:selectbyattribute
# → gdal:translate
# → ...

# by a search word
for alg in QgsApplication.processingRegistry().algorithms():
    if 'point' in alg.id().lower():
        print(alg.id(), '→', alg.displayName())

# → native:pointsalonglines → Points along Geometry
# → native:randompointsinextent → Random points in extent

docs.title: Finding out a tool's parameters
docs.text:
# full description of a tool
import processing
processing.algorithmHelp("native:pointstopath")
# prints:
# Points to Path (native:pointstopath)
# Parameters
# INPUT: Input layer [vector: point]
# ORDER_EXPRESSION: Order expression [expression]

docs.title: Visually, in the Processing Toolbox
docs.text:
QGIS → Processing → Toolbox (Ctrl+Alt+T)
     → right-click on a tool
     → "Copy as Python Command"
     → gives you the code directly, with processing.run()

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
processing.run("native:pointstopath", {...})
               ↑
               └── native: = C++ = fast, stable ✅

processing.run("qgis:selectbyattribute", {...})
               ↑
               └── qgis: = Python = flexible, editable 🔶
  • native:: written in C++, fast, the first choice if it exists
  • qgis:: written in Python, slower, sometimes an alias of native:
  • In new code, always use native: where possible
  • gdal:, grass7:, saga:: specialized libraries
  • processing.algorithmHelp("native:toolname"): find out a tool's parameters

👉 In the QGIS Processing Toolbox you can always see a tool's name with its native: or qgis: prefix.

docs.title: TEMPORARY_OUTPUT in PyQGIS
docs.text: TEMPORARY_OUTPUT is a special value of processing.run() that does not save the result to a file; instead it creates a temporary layer in memory (RAM).

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
In processing.run() the 'OUTPUT' parameter is usually given a file path:

# the usual way — a file on disk
processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': r'C:\GIS\output.shp'   # ← file on disk
})

With TEMPORARY_OUTPUT the result is not written to a file:

# TEMPORARY_OUTPUT — in memory only
processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'     # ← in RAM, no file is created
})

docs.title: 🧱 Structure — what happens inside?
docs.text:
processing.run(...)
       │
       ▼
  result → QgsVectorLayer (memory provider)
       │
       ├── type:     "memory:"
       ├── file:     does not exist on disk
       ├── lifetime: the QGIS session
       └── access:   via the result['OUTPUT'] object

docs.title: ▶️ Correct use
docs.text:
processing.run() always returns a dictionary. With TEMPORARY_OUTPUT, result['OUTPUT'] holds a QgsVectorLayer object (not a string):

result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# result['OUTPUT'] → a QgsVectorLayer object
temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']

print(type(temp_layer))
# → <class 'qgis._core.QgsVectorLayer'>

print(temp_layer.name())
# → "Polygons to lines"

print(temp_layer.featureCount())
# → 42  (number of features)

docs.title: 🗺️ Showing it in QGIS — addMapLayer()
docs.text:
The layer does not appear in the QGIS Layers panel automatically; you have to add it yourself:

from qgis.core import QgsProject

result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']

# add it to the QGIS Layers panel
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(temp_layer)

💡 Without addMapLayer() the layer exists in memory, but it is not visible.

docs.title: 🔗 Chaining — output as input
docs.text:
The most powerful use of TEMPORARY_OUTPUT is feeding one tool's result into another:

fn = r'C:\GIS\shapefile\polygon_layer.shp'

# step 1: polygon → line
step1 = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# step 2: line → points (step1's result goes straight in as input)
step2 = processing.run("native:pointsalonglines", {
    'INPUT'   : step1['OUTPUT'],   # ← the QgsVectorLayer directly
    'DISTANCE': 10,
    'OUTPUT'  : 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

# step 3: add the final result to the map
final_layer = step2['OUTPUT']
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(final_layer)

print(f"✅ {final_layer.featureCount()} points placed")

📌 No intermediate paths or files — everything stays in memory.

docs.title: 💾 Saving a temporary layer to a file
docs.text:
If you have done the analysis and need a file at the end:

from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsProject

result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
    'INPUT' : fn,
    'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
})

temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']

# option A — writeAsVectorFormatV3
options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
options.driverName   = "ESRI Shapefile"
options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"

save_path = r'C:\GIS\output_final.shp'

error, _, _, _ = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
    temp_layer,
    save_path,
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(),
    options
)

if error == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("✅ File saved:", save_path)
else:
    print("❌ Error:", error)

# option B — processing.run savefeatures
processing.run("native:savefeatures", {
    'INPUT' : temp_layer,
    'OUTPUT': r'C:\GIS\output_final.shp'
})

docs.title: 🔄 TEMPORARY_OUTPUT vs a file path
docs.text: TEMPORARY_OUTPUT File path Stored in RAM (memory) Disk Speed ⚡ fast 🐢 relatively slow Lifetime Until the end of the QGIS session Permanent Shown automatically ❌ addMapLayer() needed ❌ addVectorLayer() needed Type of result['OUTPUT'] QgsVectorLayer str (path) Chaining ✅ directly ❌ the path has to be passed again Disk space ✅ not needed ❌ needed

docs.title: ⚡ Error handling
docs.text:
try:
    result = processing.run("native:polygonstolines", {
        'INPUT' : fn,
        'OUTPUT': 'TEMPORARY_OUTPUT'
    })

    temp_layer = result['OUTPUT']

    if not temp_layer or not temp_layer.isValid():
        print("❌ The layer is invalid")
    elif temp_layer.featureCount() == 0:
        print("⚠️ The layer is empty — no features found")
    else:
        QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(temp_layer)
        print(f"✅ {temp_layer.featureCount()} features added to the map")

except Exception as e:
    print(f"❌ Processing error: {e}")

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• TEMPORARY_OUTPUT: a result without a file, in RAM only
  • result['OUTPUT'] → a QgsVectorLayer object (not a string)
  • QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(): you have to add it to the panel yourself
  • Chaining: one result is passed directly as the next tool's 'INPUT'
  • When the session ends, every TEMPORARY_OUTPUT is deleted automatically

👉 Use TEMPORARY_OUTPUT for intermediate steps, for testing, or when you don't need a file in the end.

docs.title: WKT and WKB — a full explanation
docs.text:
OGC standard | geometry encoding | GIS | PostGIS | PyQGIS

WKT and WKB are two standards for geometry serialization. Both are formats defined by the OGC (Open Geospatial Consortium) that represent geometric shapes (point, line, polygon...) uniformly, regardless of language or platform.

docs.title: 📋 Contents
docs.text:
1. Basic definition
  2. WKT — Well-Known Text
  3. WKB — Well-Known Binary
  4. Similarities and differences
  5. Geometry types
  6. 3D and M variants
  7. EWKT and EWKB — the PostGIS extension
  8. Use in PostGIS
  9. Use in PyQGIS
  10. Use in other technologies
  11. The OGC standard
  12. Comparison table

docs.title: 🔑 Basic definition
docs.text:
geometry (in memory)
         │
         ├──→  WKT  →  "POINT (41.69 44.83)"          ← read by people
         │
         └──→  WKB  →  0101000000...3D0A57404048F340   ← read by computers
WKT WKB Full name Well-Known Text Well-Known Binary Format Text (ASCII / UTF-8) Binary (bytes) Readability ✅ for people ❌ for people Size Large Small (≈ 2-3x) Speed Slow (parsing) Fast (direct read) Standard OGC SFA OGC SFA

docs.title: 📝 WKT — Well-Known Text
docs.text: WKT is a text format for expressing geometry. It is human-readable, and ideal for debugging and documentation.

docs.title: WKT syntax
docs.text: GEOMETRY_TYPE (coordinates)

docs.title: Simple examples
docs.text:
POINT (44.8015 41.6938)

LINESTRING (44.80 41.69, 44.81 41.70, 44.82 41.68)

POLYGON ((44.79 41.69, 44.82 41.69, 44.82 41.71, 44.79 41.71, 44.79 41.69))

💡 Coordinate order: in WKT the coordinates are in X Y order — in geographic systems X=lon, Y=lat.

docs.title: 💾 WKB — Well-Known Binary
docs.text: WKB is a binary format: the same geometry, but as bytes. A computer reads it directly, no parsing needed.

docs.title: Byte order (endianness)
docs.text:
01 → Little-Endian (LE) — Intel/AMD x86 — the most common
00 → Big-Endian (BE)    — network byte order, SPARC

docs.title: WKB in hexadecimal form (HEX-WKB)
docs.text:
WKB is often used in databases and APIs as a hexadecimal string:

Point (44.8015, 41.6938) WKB Hex:
0101000000713D0A57404046403D0A573D0A4846 40

Parts:
01         → byte order (Little-Endian)
01000000   → geometry type (Point = 1)
713D0A5740404640 → X = 44.8015 (IEEE 754 double)
3D0A573D0A484640 → Y = 41.6938 (IEEE 754 double)

docs.title: WKB geometry type codes
docs.text:
1  → Point
2  → LineString
3  → Polygon
4  → MultiPoint
5  → MultiLineString
6  → MultiPolygon
7  → GeometryCollection

1001 → PointZ
1002 → LineStringZ
1003 → PolygonZ
2001 → PointM
3001 → PointZM

docs.title: Similarities
docs.text:
✅ both are OGC SFA (Simple Features Access) standards
✅ both represent the same geometry types
✅ both are reversible — WKT → WKB → WKT (without losing information)
✅ both support 2D, 3D (Z), M and ZM geometries
✅ both are CRS-independent (CRS info is in EWKT/EWKB)

docs.title: Differences — in depth
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Criterion           │ WKT                  │ WKB                  │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Format              │ ASCII string         │ bytes / hex string   │
│ Size (Point)        │ ~25 characters       │ 21 bytes             │
│ Size (Polygon 100p) │ ~2,500 characters    │ ~826 bytes           │
│ Compression         │ ≈1x (baseline)       │ ≈2-3x smaller        │
│ Parsing speed       │ slow (string parse)  │ fast (direct copy)   │
│ Readability         │ ✅ people can read it │ ❌ hex/bytes          │
│ Debug/explanation   │ ✅ ideal             │ ❌ hard               │
│ DB storage          │ TEXT column          │ BYTEA / geometry     │
│ Network transfer    │ in JSON/XML APIs     │ PostGIS native       │
│ Reading in SQL      │ ST_AsText()          │ ST_AsBinary()        │
│ Writing in SQL      │ ST_GeomFromText()    │ ST_GeomFromWKB()     │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

docs.title: Size comparison — a real example
docs.text:
# Point (44.8015, 41.6938)

WKT:  "POINT (44.8015 41.6938)"         → 23 characters = 23 bytes
WKB:  0101000000...                     → 21 bytes
      (header 5 + X 8 + Y 8 = 21)

# Polygon — 1000 points
WKT:  ≈ 22,000 bytes
WKB:  ≈  8,017 bytes   (≈ 2.7x smaller)

docs.title: 🌐 3D and M variants
docs.text: WKT/WKB support Z (elevation) and M (measure) coordinates:

docs.title: M — measure
docs.text:
POINT M (44.80 41.69 125.5)
--                    ↑ measure (e.g. pipeline km, a time value)

LINESTRING M (44.79 41.69 0, 44.82 41.70 5.2, 44.85 41.68 10.8)
--                          ↑ km chainage

docs.title: ZM — elevation + measure
docs.text:
POINT ZM (44.80 41.69 520.5 125.5)
--                    ↑Z    ↑M

LINESTRING ZM (44.79 41.69 400 0, 44.82 41.70 450 5.2)

💡 Use in Georgia: in pipeline GIS, M is the km chainage and Z is the elevation above sea level. Both can be stored in one geometry (ZM).

docs.title: 🐘 EWKT and EWKB — the PostGIS extension
docs.text: EWKT (Extended WKT) and EWKB (Extended WKB) are a PostGIS extension that adds SRID (CRS) information to the OGC standard.

docs.title: EWKB — with SRID (hex)
docs.text:
In EWKB the SRID is embedded in the WKB header (with a special flag):

01           → byte order (LE)
01000020     → Point type + SRID flag (0x20000000)
E6100000     → SRID = 4326 (little-endian)
...          → coordinates

docs.title: WKT vs EWKT
docs.text:
WKT:   POINT (44.8015 41.6938)
EWKT:  SRID=4326;POINT (44.8015 41.6938)
       ↑ the SRID is written directly

⚠️ OGC vs PostGIS: EWKT/EWKB are not an OGC standard — they are a PostGIS-specific extension. For exchange with other systems, use OGC WKT/WKB.

docs.title: Writing and reading WKT
docs.text:
-- create the table
CREATE TABLE pipeline_points (
    id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name    VARCHAR(100),
    geom    GEOMETRY(POINT, 32638)
);

-- insert from WKT — ST_GeomFromText()
INSERT INTO pipeline_points (name, geom)
VALUES (
    'Lake N1',
    ST_GeomFromText('POINT (490230.0 4741850.0)', 32638)
);

-- insert from EWKT — ST_GeomFromEWKT()
INSERT INTO pipeline_points (name, geom)
VALUES (
    'Lake N2',
    ST_GeomFromEWKT('SRID=32638;POINT (491000.0 4742000.0)')
);

-- read as WKT — ST_AsText()
SELECT name, ST_AsText(geom) AS wkt
FROM pipeline_points;
-- → "POINT(490230 4741850)"

-- read as EWKT — ST_AsEWKT()
SELECT name, ST_AsEWKT(geom) AS ewkt
FROM pipeline_points;
-- → "SRID=32638;POINT(490230 4741850)"

docs.title: Writing and reading WKB
docs.text:
-- read as WKB (hex) — ST_AsBinary() / ST_AsEWKB()
SELECT name,
       ST_AsBinary(geom)  AS wkb,    -- OGC WKB
       ST_AsEWKB(geom)    AS ewkb,   -- EWKB (with SRID)
       encode(ST_AsBinary(geom), 'hex') AS wkb_hex
FROM pipeline_points;

-- insert from WKB hex
INSERT INTO pipeline_points (name, geom)
VALUES (
    'Lake N3',
    ST_GeomFromWKB(decode('0101000020E6100000...', 'hex'))
);

docs.title: Useful PostGIS functions
docs.text:
-- type
SELECT ST_GeometryType(geom) FROM pipeline_points;  -- → "ST_Point"

-- SRID
SELECT ST_SRID(geom) FROM pipeline_points;           -- → 32638

-- validation
SELECT ST_IsValid(geom), ST_IsValidReason(geom) FROM pipeline_points;

-- WKT → GeoJSON
SELECT ST_AsGeoJSON(geom) FROM pipeline_points;

-- extract the coordinates
SELECT ST_X(geom), ST_Y(geom) FROM pipeline_points;  -- → 490230, 4741850

-- CRS transformation, as WKT
SELECT ST_AsText(
    ST_Transform(geom, 4326)
) FROM pipeline_points;
-- → "POINT(44.8015 41.6938)"

docs.title: WKT → QgsGeometry
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsGeometry, QgsWkbTypes

# create a geometry from WKT
geom_point = QgsGeometry.fromWkt("POINT (490230.0 4741850.0)")
geom_line  = QgsGeometry.fromWkt("LINESTRING (490230 4741850, 491000 4742000)")
geom_poly  = QgsGeometry.fromWkt(
    "POLYGON ((490000 4741000, 491000 4741000, 491000 4742000, 490000 4742000, 490000 4741000))"
)

# check validity
print(geom_point.isValid())         # → True
print(geom_point.type())            # → QgsWkbTypes.PointGeometry
print(QgsWkbTypes.displayString(geom_point.wkbType()))  # → "Point"

docs.title: QgsGeometry → WKT
docs.text:
# convert to WKT
wkt = geom_point.asWkt()
print(wkt)
# → "Point (490230 4741850)"

# with a given precision
wkt_precise = geom_point.asWkt(precision=6)
print(wkt_precise)
# → "Point (490230.000000 4741850.000000)"

docs.title: WKB in QgsGeometry
docs.text:
# QgsGeometry → WKB (bytes)
wkb_bytes = geom_point.asWkb()
print(type(wkb_bytes))   # → <class 'QByteArray'>
print(bytes(wkb_bytes).hex())
# → "0101000000000000004046174100000040..."

# WKB → QgsGeometry
from qgis.core import QgsGeometry

wkb_hex = "0101000000713D0A574040464..."
geom_from_wkb = QgsGeometry()
geom_from_wkb.fromWkb(bytes.fromhex(wkb_hex))

docs.title: A feature's geometry as WKT
docs.text:
layer = iface.activeLayer()

for feature in layer.getFeatures():
    geom = feature.geometry()

    # WKT
    print(f"ID {feature.id()}: {geom.asWkt()}")

    # type
    print(f"  type: {QgsWkbTypes.displayString(geom.wkbType())}")

    # validation
    if not geom.isValid():
        print(f"  ⚠️ broken geometry: {geom.lastError()}")
        fixed = geom.makeValid()
        print(f"  ✅ fixed: {fixed.asWkt()}")

docs.title: Using WKT for new features
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsFields, QgsField
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

# turn a list of WKT strings into features
wkt_list = [
    ("Pipeline KP 0",  "POINT ZM (490230 4741850 520 0)"),
    ("Pipeline KP 5",  "POINT ZM (491000 4742000 510 5)"),
    ("Pipeline KP 10", "POINT ZM (491500 4741700 505 10)"),
]

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('name', QVariant.String))
fields.append(QgsField('km',   QVariant.Double))

features = []
for name, wkt in wkt_list:
    feat = QgsFeature(fields)
    feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromWkt(wkt))
    feat['name'] = name
    features.append(feat)

print(f"✅ {len(features)} features prepared")

docs.title: Compared with GeoJSON
docs.text:
WKT:     POINT (44.80 41.69)
WKB:     0101000000...
GeoJSON: {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [44.80, 41.69]}
WKT WKB GeoJSON Readability ✅ ❌ ✅ Size Medium Small Large Web API 🔶 ❌ ✅ DB storage ✅ ✅ (native) 🔶 CRS ❌ (✅ in EWKT) ❌ (✅ in EWKB) ❌ (CRS84 default)

docs.title: Shapefile (.shp)
docs.text:
Shapefile → a binary format similar to WKB, but ESRI-specific.
In PostGIS: shp2pgsql → converts to WKB automatically.

docs.title: GML (Geography Markup Language)
docs.text:
<!-- GML — XML-based, an OGC standard -->
<gml:Point srsName="EPSG:4326">
    <gml:coordinates>44.80,41.69</gml:coordinates>
</gml:Point>

docs.title: The Python shapely library
docs.text:
from shapely import wkt, wkb
from shapely.geometry import Point, LineString, Polygon

# create from WKT
geom = wkt.loads("POINT (44.80 41.69)")

# convert to WKT
print(geom.wkt)           # → "POINT (44.8 41.69)"

# convert to WKB
wkb_bytes = wkb.dumps(geom)
print(wkb_bytes.hex())

# create from WKB
geom2 = wkb.loads(wkb_bytes)
print(geom2.wkt)

# operations based on WKT
poly = wkt.loads("POLYGON ((44.79 41.69, 44.82 41.69, 44.82 41.71, 44.79 41.71, 44.79 41.69))")
point_in = wkt.loads("POINT (44.80 41.70)")
point_out = wkt.loads("POINT (44.85 41.75)")

print(poly.contains(point_in))   # → True
print(poly.contains(point_out))  # → False

docs.title: SFA — Simple Features Access
docs.text:
WKT and WKB are defined in the OGC Simple Features Access (SFA) standard:

OGC 06-103r4 — OpenGIS Implementation Standard
"Geographic information — Simple feature access — Part 1: Common architecture"

ISO 19125-1:2004 — Geographic information — Simple feature access

docs.title: Evolution of the standard
docs.text:
1999 → OGC SFA 1.0 — the first version of WKT/WKB
2003 → OGC SFA 1.1 — multi-geometries
2006 → OGC SFA 1.2 — ISO 19125 adoption, Z/M support
2011 → OGC SFA 1.2.1 — the current standard

docs.title: PostGIS EWKT/EWKB — extensions
docs.text:
PostGIS introduced EWKT/EWKB:
  → embedding the SRID in the geometry
  → an alternative to ISO SQL/MM

ISO SQL/MM (ISO 13249-3):
  → geometry types in SQL
  → the standard for ST_ functions
  → PostGIS 1.5+ — full support

docs.title: WKT vs WKB — full comparison
docs.text: Criterion WKT WKB EWKT EWKB Format ASCII text binary/hex ASCII text binary/hex SRID ❌ ❌ ✅ ✅ Readability ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ Size Large Small Large Small Speed Slow Fast Slow Fast OGC standard ✅ ✅ ❌ (PostGIS) ❌ (PostGIS) PostGIS ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ PyQGIS ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌ Shapely ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌ GeoServer ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Debug ✅ ideal ❌ hard ✅ ❌ 3D (Z) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ M ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

docs.title: Where to use which
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Writing to PostGIS EWKT or EWKB Debugging a PostGIS query WKT (ST_AsText()) Creating geometry in PyQGIS WKT (fromWkt()) DB export / exchange WKT or GeoJSON Native DB storage WKB (automatic) Web API GeoJSON (WKT is less common) Pipeline GIS EWKT with ZM (SRID + Z + M) Logs/documentation WKT

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
WKT   → "POINT (44.80 41.69)"           ← readable, debug, API
WKB   → 0101000000...                   ← fast, DB native, compact
EWKT  → "SRID=4326;POINT (44.80 41.69)" ← PostGIS, with CRS
EWKB  → 0101000020E6100000...           ← PostGIS native storage
  • WKT: read by people → use it for debugging, in documentation, in APIs
  • WKB: read by computers → the native DB format, fast, compact
  • EWKT/EWKB: a PostGIS extension → SRID embedded, the standard in PostGIS
  • Both are OGC SFA standards and convertible into each other without losing information
  • Z and M: 3D and measure coordinates are built into the standard itself

👉 In PyQGIS → fromWkt() / asWkt() | In PostGIS → ST_GeomFromText() / ST_AsText()

docs.title: 📚 Resources used
docs.text:
• OGC Simple Features Access Standard
  • PostGIS — WKT/WKB Functions
  • PyQGIS — QgsGeometry
  • Shapely — WKT/WKB

docs.title: 🔹 Introduction
docs.text:
PyQGIS is the Python API of QGIS. It lets us write scripts and plugins for processing and visualizing GIS data. Using Python classes in PyQGIS gives us: - structured code - reusable functionality - a way to model complex GIS processes

👉 How to use OOP (object-oriented programming) in PyQGIS.

docs.title: 🔹 Why use classes in PyQGIS?
docs.text:
• ✅ Modularity – the code is split into small, manageable parts
  • ✅ Reuse – the same logic is used in different projects
  • ✅ Clarity – large QGIS scripts become easier to understand
  • ✅ Plugin development – QGIS plugins are mostly built on classes

docs.title: 🔹 Preparing the PyQGIS environment
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsProject, QgsVectorLayer, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY,
    QgsFeature, QgsField, QgsFields, QgsVectorFileWriter
)
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant
import os

👉 These libraries give us access to QGIS objects (layers, features, geometry).

docs.title: 🔹 Creating a class: a simple example
docs.text:
Let's create a class that works with points (Point). 

class MyPoint:
    def __init__(self, x, y, name=""):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.name = name

    def to_qgspoint(self):
        return QgsPointXY(self.x, self.y)

    def describe(self):
        return f"Point {self.name} ({self.x}, {self.y})"

Usage: 

tbilisi = MyPoint(44.8, 41.7, "Tbilisi")
print(tbilisi.describe())  
# result: Point Tbilisi (44.8, 41.7)

👉 Here the class provided attributes (x, y, name) and methods (to_qgspoint, describe).

docs.title: 🔹 Using a PyQGIS class to add a point to a layer
docs.text:
class PointLayerManager:
    def __init__(self, layer_name="MyPoints"):
        self.layer = QgsVectorLayer("Point?crs=EPSG:4326", layer_name, "memory")
        provider = self.layer.dataProvider()
        provider.addAttributes([QgsField("Name", QVariant.String)])
        self.layer.updateFields()
        QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(self.layer)

    def add_point(self, my_point: MyPoint):
        feat = QgsFeature()
        feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(my_point.to_qgspoint()))
        feat.setAttributes([my_point.name])
        self.layer.dataProvider().addFeature(feat)
        self.layer.updateExtents()

Usage: 

manager = PointLayerManager()
tbilisi = MyPoint(44.8, 41.7, "Tbilisi")
manager.add_point(tbilisi)

👉 Here the class created an in-memory layer and added features to it.

docs.title: 🔹 Inheritance in PyQGIS
docs.text:
We can create a general GeometryObject class and derive PointObject, LineObject, PolygonObject from it. 

class GeometryObject:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def describe(self):
        return f"Geometry: {self.name}"

class PointObject(GeometryObject):
    def __init__(self, x, y, name=""):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.point = QgsPointXY(x, y)

    def get_geometry(self):
        return QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(self.point)

class LineObject(GeometryObject):
    def __init__(self, points, name=""):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.points = [QgsPointXY(x, y) for x, y in points]

    def get_geometry(self):
        return QgsGeometry.fromPolylineXY(self.points)

👉 This approach makes it easy to add different types of objects.

docs.title: 🔹 Adding different kinds of objects to a layer
docs.text:
class LayerManager:
    def __init__(self, geom_type="Point", layer_name="MyLayer"):
        self.layer = QgsVectorLayer(f"{geom_type}?crs=EPSG:4326", layer_name, "memory")
        self.provider = self.layer.dataProvider()
        self.provider.addAttributes([QgsField("Name", QVariant.String)])
        self.layer.updateFields()
        QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(self.layer)

    def add_geometry(self, geom_object: GeometryObject):
        feat = QgsFeature()
        feat.setGeometry(geom_object.get_geometry())
        feat.setAttributes([geom_object.name])
        self.provider.addFeature(feat)
        self.layer.updateExtents()

Usage: 

point = PointObject(44.8, 41.7, "Tbilisi")
line = LineObject([(44.8, 41.7), (41.6, 41.6)], "Tbilisi-Batumi")

manager = LayerManager("Point", "Cities")
manager.add_geometry(point)

line_manager = LayerManager("LineString", "Roads")
line_manager.add_geometry(line)

👉 Now we have a general class that works with both points and lines.

docs.title: 🔹 PyQGIS classes in plugins
docs.text:
QGIS plugins mainly use: - a main class (e.g. MyPlugin) - GUI classes (forms with PyQt) - data classes (spatial objects)

👉 That is why knowing classes is essential for PyQGIS development.

docs.title: 🔹 Best practices for PyQGIS classes
docs.text:
• Use modularity (one class = one responsibility)
  • Class names should be descriptive (PointLayerManager, RoadLine)
  • Use inheritance to share common properties
  • Add docstrings and comments
  • Make testing easier with small classes

docs.title: 🔹 Conclusion
docs.text:
Python classes in PyQGIS: - keep the code organized - simplify working with layers, features and attributes - are essential for building plugins

👉 Start with simple classes (e.g. Point + Layer Manager) and build more complex structures step by step. This way you can build professional GIS tools in QGIS. 🚀

docs.title: 🌍 OOP examples with geographic objects and their use in PyQGIS
Introduction
docs.text: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm that helps us organize code and model it closely on the real world. In GIS (Geographic Information Systems) this is especially important, because geographic objects can naturally be described as classes and objects.

docs.title: 🎯 Core principles of OOP
docs.text:
• Class — a template that describes an object (e.g. "Point", "Polygon").
  • Object — a concrete instance of a class (e.g. Tbilisi = Point(41.7, 44.8)).
  • Attributes — the object's characteristics (e.g. coordinates, colour, name).
  • Methods — actions the object performs (e.g. "calculate the length", "draw on the map").
  • Inheritance — a structure where classes inherit from each other (e.g. Geometry → Point, Line, Polygon).
  • Polymorphism — different implementations of the same method for different classes.

docs.title: 📌 Example: a point as an object
docs.text:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y, name=""):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.name = name

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.name}: {self.x}, {self.y})"

    def distance_to(self, other):
        return ((self.x - other.x)**2 + (self.y - other.y)**2)**0.5

# objects
tbilisi = Point(44.8, 41.7, "Tbilisi")
batumi = Point(41.6, 41.65, "Batumi")

print(tbilisi)
print("Distance:", tbilisi.distance_to(batumi))

📍 Result: describing the objects and calculating the distance between them.

docs.title: 📌 Example: a line and its length
docs.text:
class Line:
    def __init__(self, points):
        self.points = points

    def length(self):
        length = 0
        for i in range(len(self.points)-1):
            length += self.points[i].distance_to(self.points[i+1])
        return length

# objects
p1 = Point(0, 0)
p2 = Point(3, 4)
p3 = Point(6, 8)

line = Line([p1, p2, p3])
print("Line length:", line.length())

📏 Result: line length = the sum of the distances between the points.

docs.title: 📌 Example: a polygon and its area
docs.text:
class Polygon:
    def __init__(self, points):
        self.points = points

    def area(self):
        # Shoelace formula
        n = len(self.points)
        area = 0
        for i in range(n):
            j = (i + 1) % n
            area += self.points[i].x * self.points[j].y
            area -= self.points[j].x * self.points[i].y
        return abs(area) / 2

# a triangle
triangle = Polygon([Point(0,0), Point(4,0), Point(4,3)])
print("Area:", triangle.area())

📐 Result: calculating the polygon's area.

docs.title: 🌐 Use in PyQGIS
docs.text: PyQGIS is the Python API for QGIS. Here the classes already exist: - QgsPointXY — a point - QgsGeometry — a geometry - QgsFeature — an object with attributes - QgsVectorLayer — a layer

docs.title: 📌 PyQGIS example: creating a point and adding it to the map
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject, QgsPointXY, QgsGeometry, QgsFeature, QgsVectorLayer

# create the layer
layer = QgsVectorLayer("Point?crs=EPSG:4326", "Cities", "memory")
prov = layer.dataProvider()

# add attributes
layer.startEditing()
prov.addAttributes([QgsField("Name", QVariant.String)])
layer.updateFields()

# create the object
feat = QgsFeature()
feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(44.8, 41.7)))
feat.setAttributes(["Tbilisi"])
prov.addFeatures([feat])
layer.commitChanges()

# add the layer to the project
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)

📍 Result: a point (Tbilisi) is added to the map.

docs.title: 📌 PyQGIS example: calculating a line's length
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

line = QgsGeometry.fromPolylineXY([
    QgsPointXY(0,0), QgsPointXY(3,4), QgsPointXY(6,8)
])

print("Line length:", line.length())

📏 Result: the length is calculated in the CRS units.

docs.title: 📌 PyQGIS example: calculating a polygon's area
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

polygon = QgsGeometry.fromPolygonXY([[
    QgsPointXY(0,0),
    QgsPointXY(4,0),
    QgsPointXY(4,3),
    QgsPointXY(0,0)
]])

print("Polygon area:", polygon.area())

📐 Result: calculating the polygon's area.

docs.title: 🚀 Best practices for OOP in GIS
docs.text:
1. Describe geographic objects with classes — this makes the code understandable and reusable.
  2. Use inheritance — create a parent Geometry class and children (Point, Line, Polygon).
  3. Connect Python classes to the PyQGIS API — as in the example, your classes can have a method that returns a QgsGeometry object.
  4. Use attributes in classes — GIS objects often have a name, category, colour.
  5. Documentation — for students it is very important to explain what each class and method does.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
OOP is a powerful approach in GIS projects. - Geographic objects can easily be described with classes. - PyQGIS already provides implementations of many classes. - Used correctly, it lets you write structured, understandable and reusable code.

➡️ Next step for students: try to create your own Geometry class that works with PyQGIS and has methods for calculating area, length and distance.

docs.title: 📚 Using the OGR library in PyQGIS
docs.text:
This document introduces the OGR library (Open Geospatial Consortium Simple Features Reading/Writing) in the context of PyQGIS. OGR is part of GDAL (Geospatial Data Abstraction Library) and provides reading, manipulation and writing of vector GIS data in many formats.

In PyQGIS, OGR is integrated through QgsVectorLayer and QgsVectorFileWriter, which makes automation possible in QGIS scripts.

👉 QGIS 3.28+ and the Python Console (Plugins > Python Console) are recommended.

docs.title: What is OGR?
docs.text:
• It supports 400+ vector formats (Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, KML and more).
  • In PyQGIS it is used to create and manage vector layers.

docs.title: Main classes:
docs.text:
• QgsVectorLayer – represents a vector layer.
  • QgsFeature – a single element of the layer (geometry + attributes).
  • QgsVectorFileWriter – writes to a file using OGR drivers.

docs.title: 🚀 Why use OGR in PyQGIS?
docs.text:
• Automation – loading, transforming and filtering data.
  • Conversion – converting from one format to another (e.g. Shapefile → GeoJSON).

docs.title: Prerequisites:
docs.text: from qgis.core import *

docs.title: 🧩 Core OGR concepts
docs.text:
• Geometry: Point, LineString, Polygon.
  • Attributes: table fields (e.g. ID, name).
  • CRS (Coordinate Reference System): EPSG codes (e.g. EPSG:4326 WGS84).

docs.title: 📂 OGR drivers in PyQGIS
docs.text:
Drivers define the data format. The most common:

Driver Format Example file extension ESRI Shapefile Shapefile .shp GeoJSON GeoJSON .geojson GPKG GeoPackage .gpkg CSV CSV (WKT) .csv KML KML .kml

👉 You must set driverName when writing a file.

docs.title: 📥 Loading a vector layer (reading)
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsProject

layer_path = "/path/to/your/data/airports.shp"
vlayer = QgsVectorLayer(layer_path, "Airports", "ogr")

if not vlayer.isValid():
    print("Error: the layer failed to load!")
else:
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(vlayer)
    print("Layer loaded successfully.")
  • ogr – specifies the OGR provider.
  • isValid() – checks that the layer is valid.

docs.title: 🔎 Inspecting the layer (iteration)
docs.text:
features = vlayer.getFeatures()

for feature in features:
    geom = feature.geometry()
    attrs = feature.attributes()
    print(f"ID: {feature.id()}")
    if geom.type() == 0:  # Point
        print(f"Coordinates: {geom.asPoint()}")
    print(f"Attributes: {attrs}")
    break
  • getFeatures() – returns an iterator over the features.
  • geometry().asPoint() – coordinates of a Point.

docs.title: 🎯 Filtering (spatial and attribute)
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsRectangle, QgsFeatureRequest

roi = QgsRectangle(450290, 400520, 450750, 400780)
request = QgsFeatureRequest().setFilterRect(roi)

request = QgsFeatureRequest().setFilterExpression("name = 'Tbilisi'")

for feature in vlayer.getFeatures(request):
    print(f"Matching feature: {feature['name']}")

docs.title: 💾 Writing vector data
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsProject

save_options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
save_options.driverName = "GPKG"
save_options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"

transform_context = QgsProject.instance().transformContext()

output_path = "/path/to/output/my_data.gpkg"
error = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
    vlayer, output_path, transform_context, save_options
)

if error[0] == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("Saved successfully!")
else:
    print(f"Error: {error}")
  • driverName – the format (e.g. "ESRI Shapefile").
  • writeAsVectorFormatV3 – the modern way to write.

docs.title: 🆕 Creating a new layer from scratch
docs.text:
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant
from qgis.core import QgsFields, QgsField, QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField("name", QVariant.String))

new_layer = QgsVectorLayer(
    "Point?crs=epsg:4326&field=ID:integer&field=name:string",
    "new_layer", "memory"
)
new_layer.dataProvider().addFeatures([])

feat = QgsFeature(new_layer.fields())
feat.setAttribute("ID", 1)
feat.setAttribute("name", "Tbilisi")
feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(44.7937, 41.7151)))
new_layer.dataProvider().addFeature(feat)

save_options.driverName = "ESRI Shapefile"
QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(new_layer, "/path/to/new.shp", transform_context, save_options)

docs.title: 📝 Practical tasks
docs.text:
1. Download the Natural Earth shapefiles, load them in PyQGIS and count the features: 

    print(f"Number of features: {vlayer.featureCount()}")

  2. Create a new Point layer with the coordinates of Tbilisi and save it as GeoJSON.

  3. Filter the layer by CRS and save it in a new format: 

    print(layer.crs().authid())

docs.title: ⚠ Errors and tips
docs.text:
• "Layer not valid" – check the file path and format.
  • Use the QGIS Python Console for testing.
  • For more examples: the QGIS PyQGIS Cookbook.

docs.text:

  • GDAL Vector Drivers

docs.title: What is QVariant?
docs.text:
QVariant is a universal container in the Qt Framework that can hold data of different types. It is a "generic container" object used to pass data between Qt components.

For example, a QVariant can hold: - integers (int) - decimal numbers (float, double) - strings (QString / Python str) - boolean values (bool) - dates and times (QDate, QTime, QDateTime) - other Qt types or user-defined objects.

This variety lets us work with different data types through one interface.

docs.title: Why is QVariant used in PyQGIS?
docs.text:
In PyQGIS, QVariant often appears in these scenarios:

  1. Storing attributes in vector layers The fields of QGIS vector layers make up the table columns, and each attribute is stored in a QVariant object.

  2. QgsField field types When we create a new layer, a field is described by a QgsField object, where the data type is given with QVariant.

  3. Greater flexibility The same API can work with different data types; PyQGIS uses QVariant as a kind of "backbone".

docs.title: 1. QVariant in attributes
docs.text:
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant
from qgis.core import QgsField

# create a field that stores integers
field_id = QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int)

# create a field that stores text
field_name = QgsField("Name", QVariant.String)

In this example: - QVariant.Int -> integer - QVariant.String -> text

docs.title: 2. QVariant with different types
docs.text:
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant

# store as an integer
val_int = QVariant(42)
print(val_int.toInt())

# store as a string
val_str = QVariant("Tbilisi")
print(val_str.toString())

# store as a decimal number
val_float = QVariant(3.14)
print(val_float.toDouble())

Note: in PyQGIS/PyQt, QVariant objects have methods (toInt(), toString(), toDouble()) that can convert the value to the required type.

docs.title: 3. QVariant in vector layers
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsField, QgsFields
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant

# create a new layer in memory
layer = QgsVectorLayer("Point?crs=epsg:4326", "Cities", "memory")

# add fields
pr = layer.dataProvider()
fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField("Name", QVariant.String))

pr.addAttributes(fields)
layer.updateFields()

Here the field types are defined with the QVariant class.

docs.title: QVariant types in Qt/PyQGIS
docs.text:
The most frequently used QVariant types are:

QVariant type Description QVariant.Int Integer QVariant.Double Decimal number QVariant.String Text QVariant.Bool Boolean value (True/False) QVariant.Date Date QVariant.Time Time QVariant.DateTime Date and time QVariant.LongLong Long integer QVariant.ByteArray Binary data

docs.title: Practical tasks for students
docs.text:
1. Create a new Point layer with the fields:
  2. ID (Int)
  3. Name (String)

  4. Population (Int)

  5. Add at least 3 records (for example, about Tbilisi, Kutaisi and Batumi).

  6. Save the layer in GeoPackage format. Check in the file that the field types are set correctly.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• QVariant is a universal container used in Qt and PyQGIS to store and pass data of different types.
  • It often appears in QgsField, in attribute management and in data conversion.
  • To use PyQGIS effectively, it is important to understand how QVariant works and how it converts to the required data type.

docs.title: QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem (short: QgsCRS) is the PyQGIS class that represents and manages coordinate reference systems (CRS). A CRS defines how a flat GIS map relates to the real surface of the Earth.

docs.title: 🔑 Main purpose
docs.text:
• storing and managing CRS information
  • supporting EPSG codes and PROJ strings
  • checking CRS validity
  • getting information about units, the ellipsoid and the projection
  • transforming coordinates from one CRS to another

docs.title: 📦 Import
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem,
    QgsCoordinateTransform,
    QgsProject
)

docs.title: By EPSG code (recommended)
docs.text:
# WGS 84 — geographic coordinates
crs_geo = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:4326")

# WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N — Georgia
crs_utm = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638")

print(crs_utm.isValid())      # → True
print(crs_utm.authid())       # → "EPSG:32638"
print(crs_utm.description())  # → "WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N"

docs.title: By PROJ string
docs.text:
crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem.fromProj(
    "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
)
print(crs.isValid())   # → True
print(crs.authid())    # → "EPSG:4326"

docs.title: In WKT (Well-Known Text) format
docs.text:
wkt = 'GEOGCS["WGS 84",DATUM["WGS_1984",SPHEROID["WGS 84",6378137,298.257]]]'

crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem()
crs.createFromWkt(wkt)

print(crs.isValid())   # → True

💡 Recommendation: always use an EPSG code; it is the most readable and standard. Use a PROJ string or WKT only in special cases.

docs.title: 📖 Main methods
docs.text: Method Purpose Example isValid() Is the CRS valid? True / False authid() Authority ID "EPSG:32638" description() Human-readable name "WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N" mapUnits() Unit of measure QgsUnitTypes.DistanceMeters toWkt() Convert to WKT full WKT string toProj() PROJ string "+proj=utm +zone=38..." ellipsoidAcronym() Ellipsoid name "WGS84" isGeographic() Is it geographic? (degrees) True for EPSG:4326 projectionAcronym() Projection name "utm", "longlat"

docs.title: 🔍 Printing CRS information
docs.text:
crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638")

if crs.isValid():
    print("✅ CRS is valid")
    print("   Auth ID:     ", crs.authid())
    print("   Name:        ", crs.description())
    print("   Ellipsoid:   ", crs.ellipsoidAcronym())
    print("   Projection:  ", crs.projectionAcronym())
    print("   Geographic?: ", crs.isGeographic())
    print("   WKT:         ", crs.toWkt()[:60], "...")
else:
    print("❌ CRS is invalid")

Output:

✅ CRS is valid
   Auth ID:      EPSG:32638
   Name:         WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N
   Ellipsoid:    WGS84
   Projection:   utm
   Geographic?:  False
   WKT:          PROJCRS["WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N",BASEGEOGCRS["WGS 84" ...

docs.title: 🔄 Transforming coordinates — QgsCoordinateTransform
docs.text:
Transforming a point from one CRS to another:

from qgis.core import (
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem,
    QgsCoordinateTransform,
    QgsPointXY,
    QgsProject
)

# source and target CRS
src_crs  = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638")  # UTM 38N
dest_crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:4326")   # WGS 84

# transform object
transform = QgsCoordinateTransform(
    src_crs,
    dest_crs,
    QgsProject.instance()
)

# a UTM coordinate (roughly Tbilisi)
point_utm = QgsPointXY(490230.0, 4741850.0)

# transform to WGS 84
point_geo = transform.transform(point_utm)

print(f"UTM:   X={point_utm.x():.1f},  Y={point_utm.y():.1f}")
print(f"WGS84: lon={point_geo.x():.6f}, lat={point_geo.y():.6f}")

Output:

UTM:   X=490230.0,  Y=4741850.0
WGS84: lon=44.796132, lat=42.835241

docs.title: 🗺️ Transforming a layer to another CRS
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsProject

layer = iface.activeLayer()

# target CRS
dest_crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:4326")

options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
options.driverName   = "ESRI Shapefile"
options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
options.ct = QgsCoordinateTransform(
    layer.crs(),
    dest_crs,
    QgsProject.instance()
)

output_path = r'C:\GIS\output_wgs84.shp'

error, _, _, _ = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
    layer,
    output_path,
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(),
    options
)

if error == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print(f"✅ Layer saved in WGS84: {output_path}")
else:
    print(f"❌ Error: {error}")

docs.title: 🌍 CRSs used in Georgia
docs.text:
EPSG Name Use EPSG:4326 WGS 84 GPS, geographic coordinates EPSG:32637 WGS 84 / UTM Zone 37N Western Georgia EPSG:32638 WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N Eastern Georgia EPSG:5342 ETRS89 / UTM Zone 38N European standard EPSG:28408 Pulkovo 1942 / GK Zone 8 Old Soviet maps

💡 Recommendation for Georgia: EPSG:32638 — WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N. Metric units, for correct area and length calculations.

docs.title: CRS mismatch
docs.text:
layer1 = QgsVectorLayer(r'C:\GIS\roads.shp',    'Roads',    'ogr')
layer2 = QgsVectorLayer(r'C:\GIS\buildings.shp', 'Buildings', 'ogr')

# check whether they match
if layer1.crs() != layer2.crs():
    print("⚠️ The CRSs do not match!")
    print(f"   Roads:     {layer1.crs().authid()}")
    print(f"   Buildings: {layer2.crs().authid()}")
    print("   Transform them to one CRS before spatial analysis")
else:
    print("✅ The CRSs match")

docs.title: Validating a CRS
docs.text:
crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:99999")  # a non-existent code

if not crs.isValid():
    print("❌ The CRS is invalid — check the EPSG code")

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem represents and manages a CRS in PyQGIS
  • An EPSG code is the most convenient way to define a CRS
  • isValid(): always check it after creating a CRS
  • QgsCoordinateTransform transforms coordinates from one CRS to another
  • CRS mismatch is the most common source of errors in spatial analysis
  • For Georgia → EPSG:32638 (UTM Zone 38N, meters)

👉 Before any spatial operation, check the CRS. This guarantees that area, length and location are calculated correctly.
