docs.text:
• QGIS Documentation — CRS
  • PyQGIS Developer Cookbook — CRS
  • EPSG Registry

docs.title: QgsExpressionContext in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsExpressionContext is the PyQGIS class that defines the context in which expressions run, i.e. it answers the question: "when this expression runs, which variables and values should be available?"

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
QgsExpressionContext contains a stack of scopes (QgsExpressionContextScope), where each scope defines a set of variables.

This class is used:

  • when running a QgsExpression: the context "tells" the expression which values to use
  • to access feature attributes in an expression
  • to access project, layer or feature variables
  • to pass custom variables to an expression

docs.title: 📦 Import
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsExpressionContext,
    QgsExpressionContextScope,
    QgsExpressionContextUtils,
    QgsExpression,
    QgsFeatureRequest
)

docs.title: 🧱 Structure of the context
docs.text:
QgsExpressionContext is a stack: scopes are placed on top of each other:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  QgsExpressionContext (stack)           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  scope 3 → custom variables             │  ← highest priority
│  scope 2 → feature attributes           │
│  scope 1 → layer variables              │
│  scope 0 → project variables            │  ← lowest priority
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

📌 If a variable with the same name is in several scopes, the topmost scope "wins".

docs.title: ▶️ Simple use — QgsExpressionContextUtils
docs.text:
QgsExpressionContextUtils gives us ready-made helper methods that create the standard scopes:

from qgis.core import QgsExpressionContext, QgsExpressionContextUtils, QgsProject

# project context
context = QgsExpressionContextUtils.projectScope(QgsProject.instance())

# layer context
layer = iface.activeLayer()
context = QgsExpressionContextUtils.layerScope(layer)

# global context (QGIS global variables)
context = QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalScope()

docs.title: 🔗 The full context — all scopes together
docs.text:
In practice all scopes are combined into one context:

from qgis.core import (
    QgsExpressionContext,
    QgsExpressionContextUtils,
    QgsProject
)

layer = iface.activeLayer()

context = QgsExpressionContext()
context.appendScopes(
    QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer)
)

# or by hand:
context.appendScope(QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalScope())
context.appendScope(QgsExpressionContextUtils.projectScope(QgsProject.instance()))
context.appendScope(QgsExpressionContextUtils.layerScope(layer))

📌 globalProjectLayerScopes() is a convenient shortcut that adds all standard scopes at once.

docs.title: ➕ Attaching a feature to the context
docs.text:
To access @feature or field names in an expression:

from qgis.core import QgsExpression, QgsExpressionContext, QgsExpressionContextUtils

layer = iface.activeLayer()

context = QgsExpressionContext()
context.appendScopes(
    QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer)
)

expr = QgsExpression('"area" * 2')  # a field named "area"

for feature in layer.getFeatures():
    context.setFeature(feature)     # ← attach the feature to the context
    result = expr.evaluate(context)
    print(f"Feature {feature.id()}: {result}")

docs.title: 🔧 Adding custom variables
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsExpressionContext,
    QgsExpressionContextScope,
    QgsExpressionContextUtils
)

# a new scope
custom_scope = QgsExpressionContextScope()

# add variables
custom_scope.setVariable('my_city',     'Tbilisi')
custom_scope.setVariable('my_factor',   1.5)
custom_scope.setVariable('project_year', 2025)

# add it to the context
context = QgsExpressionContext()
context.appendScope(custom_scope)

# use in an expression: @my_city, @my_factor
expr = QgsExpression("@my_factor * 100")
result = expr.evaluate(context)
print(result)  # → 150.0

📌 In an expression you refer to custom variables with the @ prefix: @my_city.

docs.title: 🔍 Looking up a variable in the context
docs.text:
# read a variable's value
value = context.variable('my_city')
print(value)  # → 'Tbilisi'

# all available variables
all_vars = context.variableNames()
print(all_vars)
# → ['my_city', 'my_factor', 'project_year', 'layer_name', ...]

docs.title: 📋 Practical example — filtering with an expression
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsExpression,
    QgsExpressionContext,
    QgsExpressionContextUtils,
    QgsFeatureRequest
)

layer = iface.activeLayer()

# context
context = QgsExpressionContext()
context.appendScopes(
    QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer)
)

# expression ('კახეთი' = Kakheti, as stored in the data)
expr = QgsExpression('"population" > 50000 AND "region" = \'კახეთი\'')

if expr.hasParserError():
    print("❌ Expression error:", expr.parserErrorString())
else:
    for feature in layer.getFeatures():
        context.setFeature(feature)
        if expr.evaluate(context):
            print(f"✅ {feature['name']} — {feature['population']}")

docs.title: 📋 Practical example — calculating a new field
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsExpression,
    QgsExpressionContext,
    QgsExpressionContextUtils
)

layer = iface.activeLayer()

context = QgsExpressionContext()
context.appendScopes(
    QgsExpressionContextUtils.globalProjectLayerScopes(layer)
)

# area in square meters → hectares
expr = QgsExpression('$area / 10000')

layer.startEditing()
for feature in layer.getFeatures():
    context.setFeature(feature)
    hectares = expr.evaluate(context)
    layer.changeAttributeValue(feature.id(), layer.fields().indexFromName('area_ha'), round(hectares, 4))

layer.commitChanges()
print("✅ Field updated")

docs.title: 🌐 Setting/reading project variables
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsExpressionContextUtils, QgsProject

project = QgsProject.instance()

# set a variable on the project
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setProjectVariable(project, 'company_name', 'GGTC')
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setProjectVariable(project, 'year',         2025)

# read it back
val = QgsExpressionContextUtils.projectScope(project).variable('company_name')
print(val)  # → 'GGTC'

# in a QGIS expression: @company_name, @year

docs.title: 🛠 Setting layer variables
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsExpressionContextUtils

layer = iface.activeLayer()

# attach a variable to the layer
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setLayerVariable(layer, 'layer_source', 'PostGIS')
QgsExpressionContextUtils.setLayerVariable(layer, 'update_date',  '2025-01-15')

# read it back
val = QgsExpressionContextUtils.layerScope(layer).variable('layer_source')
print(val)  # → 'PostGIS'

docs.title: ⚡ Error handling
docs.text:
expr = QgsExpression('"nonexistent_field" + 1')

# parser error (syntax)
if expr.hasParserError():
    print("❌ Parser error:", expr.parserErrorString())

# eval error (at run time)
result = expr.evaluate(context)
if expr.hasEvalError():
    print("❌ Eval error:", expr.evalErrorString())
else:
    print("✅ Result:", result)

docs.title: 📊 QgsExpressionContextUtils — methods summary
docs.text: Method Purpose globalScope() QGIS global variables projectScope(project) Project variables layerScope(layer) Layer variables featureBasedContext(feat, fields) Feature-based context globalProjectLayerScopes(layer) All three together (shortcut) setProjectVariable(project, name, value) Set a project variable setLayerVariable(layer, name, value) Set a layer variable

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsExpressionContext is a stack of scopes that "tells" an expression which variables to use
  • QgsExpressionContextScope is one set of variables
  • QgsExpressionContextUtils is a helper class for creating ready-made scopes
  • context.setFeature(feat) attaches a feature to the context for field access
  • context.variable('name') reads a variable
  • In an expression you refer to custom variables with the @ prefix

👉 Whenever you need not just a QgsExpression but its results, QgsExpressionContext is your essential tool.

docs.title: 🧩 PyQGIS — QgsFeature
docs.text: QgsFeature represents a single geographic object in a vector layer: it has a geometry (QgsGeometry) and attributes (values for the fields).

docs.title: 📚 When do we use QgsFeature?
docs.text:
• to add a new object to a layer (point/line/polygon)
  • to collect, read and change existing objects
  • to set/update attributes
  • to write the results of buffers/overlays/other analysis

docs.title: 🧠 Core concepts
docs.text:
• Feature (object) — a combination of geometry and attributes
  • FID/ID — a unique identifier within the layer (different from an "ID" in an attribute column)
  • Geometry — QgsGeometry (Point/LineString/Polygon/Multiparts…)
  • Attributes — a list of values that matches the layer's QgsFields() structure

docs.title: ✅ Quick example — creating a QgsFeature and setting attributes
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

feat = QgsFeature()                              # an empty object
geom = QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(44.8, 41.7))
feat.setGeometry(geom)                           # assign the geometry
feat.setAttributes([1, "Tbilisi", 1110000])     # assign the attributes (preferably in the layer's field order)

Note: the number of elements in the setAttributes() list must match the number of the layer's QgsFields() (or use setAttribute(index, value)).

docs.title: 🧪 Use with a layer — writing a new object
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject, QgsVectorLayer, QgsField, QgsFields, QgsWkbTypes, QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

# create a memory layer (Point, EPSG:4326)
vl = QgsVectorLayer("Point?crs=EPSG:4326", "Cities", "memory")
pr = vl.dataProvider()

# add fields
pr.addAttributes([QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int), QgsField("Name", QVariant.String), QgsField("Pop", QVariant.Int)])
vl.updateFields()

# create the object
f = QgsFeature(vl.fields())                      # pass the field structure
f.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(44.8, 41.7)))
f["ID"] = 1                                      # alternative: f.setAttribute("ID", 1)
f["Name"] = "Tbilisi"
f["Pop"] = 1110000

pr.addFeatures([f])                              # add it to the layer
vl.updateExtents()

QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(vl)

docs.title: 🔁 Reading and changing existing objects (edit mode)
docs.text:
# edit mode is needed to change attributes/geometry
vl.startEditing()

for f in vl.getFeatures():                       # iterate over all objects
    if f["Name"] == "Tbilisi":
        vl.changeAttributeValue(f.id(), vl.fields().indexOf("Pop"), 1200000)  # Pop = 1.2m

# change the geometry (e.g. a tiny shift)
for f in vl.getFeatures():
    g = f.geometry()
    if g and g.isMultipart() is False:
        p = g.asPoint()
        new_g = QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(p.x() + 0.001, p.y()))
        vl.changeGeometry(f.id(), new_g)

vl.commitChanges()                               # save the changes

TIP: use vl.rollBack() to undo the changes on error.

docs.title: 🧮 Useful methods
docs.text:
• QgsFeature(fields=None) — constructor; optionally with a field structure
  • setGeometry(QgsGeometry) / geometry()
  • setAttributes(list) / attributes()
  • setAttribute(index_or_name, value) / attribute(index_or_name)
  • id() — the layer's internal identifier (FID)
  • isValid() — whether the assigned geometry/attributes are consistent

docs.title: 🧷 Multipart geometry
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

# a Multipart Point from two points
mp = QgsGeometry.fromMultiPointXY([QgsPointXY(44.8, 41.7), QgsPointXY(41.6, 41.65)])
f = QgsFeature(vl.fields())
f.setGeometry(mp)
f.setAttributes([2, "Cities MP", None])
vl.dataProvider().addFeatures([f])
vl.updateExtents()

Use geometry().isMultipart() to find out whether an object is multipart.

docs.title: 🧰 Getting QgsFeatures from layers (selection / filter)
docs.text:
# 1) Feature iterator + expression filter
expr = '"Pop" > 1000000'                         # QGIS expression
for f in vl.getFeatures(expr):
    print(f["Name"], f["Pop"])

# 2) by identifying feature IDs
ids = [f.id() for f in vl.getFeatures() if f["Name"].startswith("T")]
for fid in ids:
    feat = next(vl.getFeatures(f"id = {fid}"))   # find a specific FID
    print("Selected:", feat["Name"])

docs.title: 🧱 Errors and common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Field mismatch — the length of the setAttributes() list does not match the number of QgsFields() → use setAttribute() individually.
  • Forgetting edit mode — changeAttributeValue / changeGeometry require startEditing() and commitChanges().
  • FID vs attribute ID — f.id() != f["ID"] (the first is an internal technical identifier).
  • CRS/units — geometry().area()/length() return results in the units of the layer's CRS.

docs.title: 🧭 Small exercises
docs.text: 1) Create a Point memory layer with the fields ID(Int), Name(String), Elev(Double) and add 5 points. 2) Find all points where Elev > 1200 and set High=True in a new field. 3) From an existing line layer, take each feature and write its length to the field Len_m (keep in mind the CRS must be in meters). 4) Create a Multipart Polygon with one feature made of two triangles and add it to the layer.

docs.title: 🔚 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsFeature is the basic building block of vector data.
  • You use it together with QgsGeometry and QgsFields/QgsField.
  • The correct editing cycle: startEditing() → changes → commitChanges() (or rollBack()).
  • Work with a clear attribute schema and an understanding of CRSs.

docs.title: 📝 PyQGIS: what is QgsFields() and what does it do?
▶️ What is QgsFields()?
docs.text:
QgsFields is a PyQGIS class that represents the collection of columns of an attribute table. When we create a new vector layer (e.g. a shapefile), we must define the columns of its table (ID, name, age, etc.). These columns are stored in a QgsFields() object. Fields are data structures that define the data stored in a layer or file. Each field has a name, a type (e.g. text, number) and other properties. layerfield = QgsFields() As a result of this code:

an empty QgsFields object is created. This object is used to add new attribute fields, or to hold a layer's existing fields.

docs.title: 📦 Main function
docs.text:
• Stores QgsField objects (i.e. the description of each column).
  • Lets you add, remove or look up columns.
  • Is used when writing data to a new layer.

docs.title: 🧱 Example – creating a new attribute table
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsFields, QgsField
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

# create an empty collection of columns
fields = QgsFields()

# add columns
fields.append(QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField("Name", QVariant.String))
fields.append(QgsField("Age", QVariant.Double))

# now the fields object holds 3 columns: ID, Name, Age
print(fields.count())   # prints 3

docs.title: 📊 How does it work?
docs.text:
• QgsField – describes one column (name + type).
  • QgsFields – is a group of columns.
  • When we pass QgsFields to QgsVectorFileWriter, it creates a new shapefile with the given columns.

docs.title: 🔎 Why is it important?
docs.text:
1. Defining the structure – without attribute columns we cannot store values.
  2. Managing data – in code we control what type of information is written (integer, text, decimal, etc.).
  3. Automation – when many shapefiles with the same structure must be created, QgsFields() simplifies the process.

docs.title: 🚀 Practical example: creating a layer with columns
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem, QgsWkbTypes, QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

# file path
fn = r"C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\new_points.shp"

# create the columns
fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField("Name", QVariant.String))

# create the layer
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(fn, "UTF-8", fields, QgsWkbTypes.Point,
                             QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638"), "ESRI Shapefile")

# add a point
feat = QgsFeature()
feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(356000, 4679000)))
feat.setAttributes([1, "Lake"])
writer.addFeature(feat)

del(writer)  # close the writer

iface.addVectorLayer(fn, "", "ogr")  # add it to QGIS

docs.title: 🎯 Conclusion
docs.text:
• QgsField – describes one column.
  • QgsFields – is the full list of columns (the structure of the attribute table).
  • If you want to create a new file in QGIS, QgsFields() is required.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: QgsGeometry is the main PyQGIS class for storing and processing geometry objects (points, lines, polygons and more). This class lets us create, transform, compare and combine geometric shapes.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Geometry Creation — creating points, lines and polygons.
  • Geometry Transformation — moving, buffering.
  • Geometry Analysis — checking overlaps, calculating distances.
  • Geometry Export — converting to other formats (WKT, WKB).

docs.title: 1. Geometry Creation
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsPointXY, QgsGeometry

# point geometry
point = QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56))

# line geometry
line = QgsGeometry.fromPolylineXY([
    QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56),
    QgsPointXY(357970.20, 4683360.10)
])

# polygon geometry
polygon = QgsGeometry.fromPolygonXY([[
    QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56),
    QgsPointXY(357970.20, 4683360.10),
    QgsPointXY(357960.10, 4683365.50),
    QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56)
]])

docs.title: 2. Geometry Transformation
docs.text:
# create a buffer (e.g. 50 meters)
buffer = point.buffer(50, 5)

# move the geometry
moved = point.translate(100, 200)

# simplify the geometry
simplified = line.simplify(10)

docs.title: 3. Geometry Analysis
docs.text:
# intersection of two geometries
intersects = point.intersects(buffer)

# distance between objects
dist = point.distance(line)

# geometry area (for a polygon)
area = polygon.area()

# geometry length / perimeter
length = line.length()

docs.title: 4. Geometry Export
docs.text:
# convert to WKT
print(point.asWkt())

# to JSON
print(polygon.asJson())

# binary form (WKB)
wkb = line.asWkb()

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• QgsGeometry works with every geometry type: Point, MultiPoint, LineString, MultiLineString, Polygon, MultiPolygon.
  • It is often used together with other classes: QgsFeature, QgsVectorLayer.
  • It relies on the GEOS library for geometric operations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: QgsGeometry is one of the most important PyQGIS classes. It gives us the tools to create, process and analyse spatial data. Students should practise using it in a variety of GIS operations.

docs.title: ℹ️ Overview
docs.text: QgsPointXY is a simple object that represents a point (with X,Y coordinates). It is used to create geometry objects (e.g. QgsGeometry) and in various geographic operations.

docs.title: 🛠️ Main constructors
docs.text:
# an empty point
pt = QgsPointXY()

# with X and Y values
pt = QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56)

# copy another QgsPointXY object
pt2 = QgsPointXY(pt)

docs.title: Accessing the coordinates
docs.text:
x = pt.x()   # returns the X value
y = pt.y()   # returns the Y value

docs.title: Changing the coordinates
docs.text:
pt.setX(358000.0)
pt.setY(4683400.0)

docs.title: Comparing points
docs.text:
pt1 = QgsPointXY(10, 20)
pt2 = QgsPointXY(10, 20)
pt3 = QgsPointXY(15, 25)

print(pt1 == pt2)  # True
print(pt1 == pt3)  # False

docs.title: 🧭 Use with QgsGeometry
docs.text:
QgsPointXY is often used to create a geometry: 

pt = QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56)
geom = QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(pt)

docs.title: 🌍 Practical example — creating a point layer
docs.text:
fn = r'C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/points.shp'

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('ID', QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField('Name', QVariant.String))

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(fn, 'UTF-8', fields, QgsWkbTypes.Point,
                             QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'), 'ESRI Shapefile')

# points
coords = [(357960, 4683350), (357970, 4683360), (357980, 4683370)]

for i, (x, y) in enumerate(coords):
    pt = QgsPointXY(x, y)
    geom = QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(pt)
    feat = QgsFeature()
    feat.setGeometry(geom)
    feat.setAttributes([i, f"point_{i}"])
    writer.addFeature(feat)

del(writer)

layer = iface.addVectorLayer(fn, '', 'ogr')

docs.title: 📖 When to use it
docs.text:
• For simple point objects (e.g. X,Y coordinates).
  • To create a geometry (QgsGeometry).
  • To store temporary points and for analysis.
  • To simplify algorithms where a full geometry object is not needed.

✅ QgsPointXY is one of the most frequently used PyQGIS classes when working with point data.

docs.title: QgsProject
docs.text:
QgsProject is one of the most important PyQGIS classes. It is used to manage QGIS project files (.qgz or .qgs). With this class you can:

  • open an existing project
  • create a new project
  • save the project
  • add/remove layers in the project
  • manage project properties (CRS, paths, entries)

docs.title: 1. QgsProject.instance()
docs.text:
QGIS has only one active project. You access it with the instance() method.

project = QgsProject.instance()

docs.title: 2. setFileName(path)
docs.text:
Sets the path of the project file.

project.setFileName("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/my_project.qgz")

docs.title: 3. read(path) – opening a project
docs.text:
Loads an existing .qgz or .qgs file.

project.read("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/existing_project.qgz")

docs.title: 4. write()
docs.text:
Saves the project to the file set with setFileName().

project.write()

or under a new name:

project.write("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/new_project.qgz")

docs.title: 5. Adding layers to the project
docs.text:
You can add both vector and raster layers.

from qgis.core import QgsVectorLayer, QgsRasterLayer

# add a vector layer
vlayer = QgsVectorLayer("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/roads.shp", "Roads", "ogr")
project.addMapLayer(vlayer)

# add a raster layer
rlayer = QgsRasterLayer("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/dem.tif", "DEM")
project.addMapLayer(rlayer)

docs.title: 6. removeMapLayer(layer)
docs.text:
Removes a layer from the project.

project.removeMapLayer(vlayer.id())

docs.title: 7. mapLayers()
docs.text:
Returns a dictionary of all layers in the project (layer_id: layer_object).

layers = project.mapLayers()
for layer_id, layer in layers.items():
    print(layer.name(), layer.type())

docs.title: 8. The project's CRS (Coordinate Reference System)
docs.text:
Sets the project's main CRS.

from qgis.core import QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem

crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:4326")  # WGS84
project.setCrs(crs)

docs.title: 📌 Full example
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsProject, QgsVectorLayer, QgsRasterLayer, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem

# get the project instance
project = QgsProject.instance()

# set the file name
project.setFileName("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/my_project.qgz")

# add a vector layer
roads = QgsVectorLayer("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/roads.shp", "Roads", "ogr")
project.addMapLayer(roads)

# add a raster layer
dem = QgsRasterLayer("C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/dem.tif", "DEM")
project.addMapLayer(dem)

# set the CRS
crs = QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638")  # UTM Zone 38N
project.setCrs(crs)

# save the project
project.write()

docs.title: 📖 Conclusion
docs.text: QgsProject lets us manage a whole QGIS project in code. For students this is one of the basic topics, because practically every PyQGIS script works with the project's layers.

docs.title: QgsRasterLayer in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsRasterLayer is the QGIS class used to load and manage raster data (e.g. GeoTIFF, JPEG, DEM, satellite images, etc.).

docs.title: 🔑 The main concept
docs.text:
A raster layer is made of a matrix of pixels. Each pixel has a value (e.g. elevation, temperature, image colour). In PyQGIS, QgsRasterLayer lets you:

  • load and display rasters in various formats (GeoTIFF, ASCII GRID, JPEG, PNG, etc.)
  • work with multiband data.
  • read pixel values.
  • apply styling (symbology).
  • run analysis with the Raster Processing Toolbox.

docs.title: 📂 Main attributes
docs.text:
• Datasource path – the file path (e.g. "C:/data/dem.tif")
  • Layer name – the layer's name in the QGIS project
  • Provider type – usually "gdal" (because GDAL is used to read raster files)

docs.title: 1. Loading a raster file
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsRasterLayer

path = r"C:\Users\Public\GIS\data\dem.tif"
layer_name = "Digital Elevation Model"

raster_layer = QgsRasterLayer(path, layer_name, "gdal")

if raster_layer.isValid():
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(raster_layer)
    print("Raster loaded successfully!")
else:
    print("Failed to load raster.")

docs.title: 2. Getting information about the raster layer
docs.text:
print("Layer name:", raster_layer.name())
print("Crs:", raster_layer.crs().authid())
print("Width:", raster_layer.width())
print("Height:", raster_layer.height())
print("Bands:", raster_layer.bandCount())

docs.title: 3. Information from a specific band
docs.text:
provider = raster_layer.dataProvider()

# calculate band statistics
stats = provider.bandStatistics(1)
print("Minimum:", stats.minimumValue)
print("Maximum:", stats.maximumValue)
print("Mean:", stats.mean)

docs.title: 4. Getting a pixel value at a coordinate
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsPointXY

point = QgsPointXY(356671, 4679923)
ident = raster_layer.dataProvider().identify(point, QgsRaster.IdentifyFormatValue)

if ident.isValid():
    print("Pixel value:", ident.results())

docs.title: 5. Changing the symbology (Singleband Gray)
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsSingleBandGrayRenderer

provider = raster_layer.dataProvider()
renderer = QgsSingleBandGrayRenderer(provider, 1)  # first band
raster_layer.setRenderer(renderer)
raster_layer.triggerRepaint()

docs.title: 6. Symbology with a colour palette (Pseudo color)
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsColorRampShader, QgsRasterShader, QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer
from qgis.PyQt.QtGui import QColor

provider = raster_layer.dataProvider()
fcn = QgsColorRampShader()
fcn.setColorRampType(QgsColorRampShader.Interpolated)

# min/max values
fcn.setColorRampItemList([
    QgsColorRampShader.ColorRampItem(0, QColor(0,0,255), 'Low'),
    QgsColorRampShader.ColorRampItem(1000, QColor(0,255,0), 'Medium'),
    QgsColorRampShader.ColorRampItem(2000, QColor(255,0,0), 'High')
])

shader = QgsRasterShader()
shader.setRasterShaderFunction(fcn)

renderer = QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer(provider, 1, shader)
raster_layer.setRenderer(renderer)
raster_layer.triggerRepaint()

docs.title: ⚙️ Areas of use
docs.text:
• DEM (Digital Elevation Model) → elevation analysis, slope, aspect
  • Satellite images → Landsat, Sentinel, MODIS
  • Orthophotos (orthoimagery) → cartography, topographic maps
  • Climate data → temperature, precipitation

docs.title: ℹ️ Notes
docs.text:
• In PyQGIS a raster always uses the GDAL provider.
  • Matching CRSs are required for correct overlay with other layers.
  • When working with large rasters, pyramids and tiling may be needed.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: QgsRasterLayer is the main PyQGIS tool for managing raster data.

docs.title: QgsVectorFileWriter in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsVectorFileWriter is the PyQGIS class used to create and write vector files — e.g. Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON and other formats.

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
QgsVectorFileWriter lets us:

  • create a new vector file from scratch
  • write QgsFeature objects to the file
  • choose the file format, CRS and encoding
  • export an existing layer to another format

docs.title: 📦 Import
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsVectorFileWriter,
    QgsFields,
    QgsField,
    QgsFeature,
    QgsGeometry,
    QgsPointXY,
    QgsWkbTypes,
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem,
    QgsProject
)
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

docs.title: ▶️ Basic syntax — the old style
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(
    path,          # file path
    encoding,      # encoding, e.g. 'UTF-8'
    fields,        # a QgsFields object
    geometryType,  # QgsWkbTypes.Point / LineString / Polygon
    crs,           # QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem
    driverName     # 'ESRI Shapefile', 'GPKG', 'GeoJSON', etc.
)

📌 This syntax still works in QGIS 3.x, but it is considered deprecated.

docs.title: 🛠 Simple example — Point Shapefile
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsFields, QgsField,
    QgsWkbTypes, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem
)
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

shapefile_path = r'C:\Users\Public\Documents\GIS\shapefile\saxli.shp'

# define the fields
fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('ID',    QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField('Name',  QVariant.String, len=100))
fields.append(QgsField('Area',  QVariant.Double, prec=2))

# create the writer
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(
    shapefile_path,
    'UTF-8',
    fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point,
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
    'ESRI Shapefile'
)

# ⚠️ del is required! Only then is the file closed
del writer

docs.title: ➕ Writing features
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsFeature, QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY

# after creating the writer — add features
feat = QgsFeature(fields)
feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(490230.0, 4741850.0)))
feat['ID']   = 1
feat['Name'] = 'House N1'
feat['Area'] = 120.5

if writer.addFeature(feat):
    print("✅ Feature written")
else:
    print("❌ Writing failed")

del writer

docs.title: 🚀 Modern syntax — create() (QGIS 3.22+)
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsProject

options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
options.driverName   = "ESRI Shapefile"
options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
options.actionOnExistingFile = QgsVectorFileWriter.CreateOrOverwriteFile

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(
    shapefile_path,
    fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point,
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(),
    options
)

if writer.hasError() != QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("❌ Error:", writer.errorMessage())
else:
    writer.addFeature(feat)
    del writer
    print("✅ File created")

📌 create() is the recommended approach since QGIS 3.22.

docs.title: 💾 Supported formats
docs.text: driverName Format Extension "ESRI Shapefile" Shapefile .shp "GPKG" GeoPackage .gpkg "GeoJSON" GeoJSON .geojson "KML" Keyhole Markup Language .kml "CSV" CSV (without geometry) .csv "MapInfo File" MapInfo TAB .tab "DXF" AutoCAD DXF .dxf

docs.title: 📤 Exporting a layer — writeAsVectorFormatV3
docs.text:
If you have an existing QgsVectorLayer and want to save it in another format:

layer = iface.activeLayer()  # or any QgsVectorLayer

options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()
options.driverName   = "GPKG"
options.fileEncoding = "UTF-8"

error, new_file, _, _ = QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3(
    layer,
    r'C:\GIS\output.gpkg',
    QgsProject.instance().transformContext(),
    options
)

if error == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("✅ Export succeeded:", new_file)
else:
    print("❌ Error:", error)

📌 With writeAsVectorFormatV3, del is not needed.

docs.title: 🛡️ Checking for errors
docs.text:
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(...)

# error code
error_code = writer.hasError()

if error_code == QgsVectorFileWriter.NoError:
    print("✅ Writer is ready")
elif error_code == QgsVectorFileWriter.ErrDriverNotFound:
    print("❌ Driver not found")
elif error_code == QgsVectorFileWriter.ErrCreateDataSource:
    print("❌ Failed to create the file")
elif error_code == QgsVectorFileWriter.ErrCreateLayer:
    print("❌ Failed to create the layer")
else:
    print("❌ Other error:", writer.errorMessage())

docs.title: ♻️ Cleanup — del writer and try / finally
docs.text:
QgsVectorFileWriter locks the file while it is alive. del writer calls the C++ destructor and closes the file.

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter.create(...)

try:
    for feat in features:
        writer.addFeature(feat)
    print(f"✅ {len(features)} features written")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"❌ Error: {e}")
finally:
    del writer  # guaranteed cleanup
    print("🔒 File closed")

Without del: the file may stay locked, the last data may not be written, and memory may leak in loops.

docs.title: 📋 SaveVectorOptions parameters
docs.text:
options = QgsVectorFileWriter.SaveVectorOptions()

options.driverName        = "ESRI Shapefile"   # format
options.fileEncoding      = "UTF-8"             # encoding
options.layerName         = "my_layer"          # layer name (in GPKG)
options.onlySelectedFeatures = False            # selected features only?
options.actionOnExistingFile = QgsVectorFileWriter.CreateOrOverwriteFile
# or: QgsVectorFileWriter.AppendToLayerNoNewFields
# or: QgsVectorFileWriter.AppendToLayerAddNewFields

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsVectorFileWriter creates vector files in PyQGIS
  • create() is the modern, recommended way (QGIS 3.22+)
  • writeAsVectorFormatV3() is for exporting an existing layer
  • del writer is always required for writers created with create()
  • try / finally guarantees cleanup in any scenario

👉 This class is the main tool for saving vector data in PyQGIS.

docs.title: QgsVectorLayer in QGIS
docs.text: QgsVectorLayer is one of the most important PyQGIS classes. It is used to load and manage vector data (e.g. Shapefile, GeoPackage, PostGIS).

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
QgsVectorLayer represents a vector layer (points, lines, polygons) that has: - geometry (spatial data) - attributes (tabular data)

This object lets us: - load an existing file - create a new layer - read/add/write features - manage the symbology and layer style

docs.title: ▶️ Creating a QgsVectorLayer
docs.text:
# connect to an existing vector file
fn = r"C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/shapefile/lake.shp"
layer = QgsVectorLayer(fn, "Lake Layer", "ogr")

if not layer.isValid():
    print("❌ Failed to load the layer")
else:
    print("✅ Layer loaded successfully")

📌 Here: - fn = the file path - "Lake Layer" = the name in QGIS - "ogr" = data provider (Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, etc.)

docs.title: 🛠 Layer types
docs.text: A QgsVectorLayer can be: - QgsWkbTypes.Point → points - QgsWkbTypes.LineString → lines - QgsWkbTypes.Polygon → polygons

docs.title: 📋 Accessing attributes
docs.text:
for feature in layer.getFeatures():
    geom = feature.geometry()
    attrs = feature.attributes()
    print("Geometry:", geom.asWkt())
    print("Attributes:", attrs)

docs.title: ➕ Adding a new feature
docs.text:
from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QVariant

pr = layer.dataProvider()

# new attribute fields
pr.addAttributes([QgsField("Name", QVariant.String),
                  QgsField("Value", QVariant.Double)])
layer.updateFields()

# create a new feature
feat = QgsFeature(layer.fields())
feat.setGeometry(QgsGeometry.fromPointXY(QgsPointXY(357965.61, 4683353.56)))
feat.setAttributes(["Lake1", 123.45])

pr.addFeature(feat)
layer.updateExtents()

docs.title: 💾 Creating a new vector file
docs.text:
from qgis.core import QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsFields, QgsField, QgsWkbTypes, QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem

fn = r"C:/Users/Public/Documents/GIS/shapefile/new_layer.shp"
fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField("ID", QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField("Name", QVariant.String))

writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(fn, "UTF-8", fields,
                             QgsWkbTypes.Point,
                             QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem("EPSG:32638"),
                             "ESRI Shapefile")

del writer

docs.title: 🔍 Filtering and queries
docs.text:
expr = QgsExpression("Value > 100")
it = layer.getFeatures(QgsFeatureRequest(expr))

for f in it:
    print(f["Name"], f["Value"])

docs.title: 🎨 Symbols and visualization
docs.text:
symbol = QgsSymbol.defaultSymbol(layer.geometryType())
symbol.setColor(QColor("blue"))
symbol.setSize(3)

layer.renderer().setSymbol(symbol)
layer.triggerRepaint()

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsVectorLayer is the main object for vector data in PyQGIS.
  • With it we can:
  • load a layer
  • add new features
  • manage attributes
  • write it to a file
  • change the symbols

👉 This class is one of the most used tools of the QGIS API for managing GIS data.

docs.title: QgsWkbTypes in PyQGIS
docs.text: QgsWkbTypes is the PyQGIS class that defines geometry types, i.e. it answers the question: "is this layer made of points, lines or polygons?"

docs.title: 🔑 The main idea
docs.text:
QgsWkbTypes contains constants (enumerations) that describe the geometry type according to the WKB (Well-Known Binary) format.

This class is used:

  • when creating a new layer or file (QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsMemoryLayer)
  • when checking a geometry type
  • when defining an object's geometry

docs.title: 📐 Main geometry types
docs.text: Constant Meaning Use QgsWkbTypes.Point Point House, station, other object QgsWkbTypes.LineString Line Road, river, pipeline QgsWkbTypes.Polygon Polygon Land parcel, lake, building QgsWkbTypes.MultiPoint Multiple points Many points in one feature QgsWkbTypes.MultiLineString Multiple lines Road network QgsWkbTypes.MultiPolygon Multiple polygons Islands, enclaves QgsWkbTypes.NoGeometry No geometry Attribute table only QgsWkbTypes.Unknown Unknown type Undefined

docs.title: ▶️ Use — when creating a layer
docs.text:
from qgis.core import (
    QgsVectorFileWriter,
    QgsFields,
    QgsField,
    QgsWkbTypes,
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem
)
from PyQt5.QtCore import QVariant

fields = QgsFields()
fields.append(QgsField('ID',   QVariant.Int))
fields.append(QgsField('Name', QVariant.String))

# create a Point layer
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(
    r'C:\GIS\points.shp',
    'UTF-8',
    fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.Point,                          # ← here
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
    'ESRI Shapefile'
)
del writer

📌 QgsWkbTypes.Point tells the writer that only points will be written to the file.

docs.title: 🔍 Checking the geometry type
docs.text:
layer = QgsVectorLayer(r'C:\GIS\roads.shp', 'Roads', 'ogr')

geom_type = layer.wkbType()
print(geom_type)  # → 2 (LineString)

# human-readable name
type_name = QgsWkbTypes.displayString(geom_type)
print(type_name)  # → "LineString"

docs.title: QgsWkbTypes.geometryType(wkb_type)
docs.text:
Converts a WKB type into a general category:

from qgis.core import QgsWkbTypes

wkb = QgsWkbTypes.MultiPolygon

# category
category = QgsWkbTypes.geometryType(wkb)
# → QgsWkbTypes.PolygonGeometry

# name
print(QgsWkbTypes.displayString(wkb))
# → "MultiPolygon"

Geometry categories:

Category WKB types PointGeometry Point, MultiPoint LineGeometry LineString, MultiLineString PolygonGeometry Polygon, MultiPolygon NullGeometry NoGeometry

docs.title: QgsWkbTypes.hasZ(wkb_type) and QgsWkbTypes.hasM(wkb_type)
docs.text:
Checks whether there is a Z (elevation) or M (measure) coordinate:

# PointZ — a 3D point
wkb_3d = QgsWkbTypes.PointZ

print(QgsWkbTypes.hasZ(wkb_3d))  # → True
print(QgsWkbTypes.hasM(wkb_3d))  # → False

docs.title: QgsWkbTypes.isSingleType() and QgsWkbTypes.isMultiType()
docs.text:
print(QgsWkbTypes.isSingleType(QgsWkbTypes.Point))        # → True
print(QgsWkbTypes.isMultiType(QgsWkbTypes.MultiPolygon))  # → True

docs.title: 🌐 Z and M types (3D and measure)
docs.text:
Type Description QgsWkbTypes.PointZ 3D point (X, Y, Z) QgsWkbTypes.PointM Measured point (X, Y, M) QgsWkbTypes.PointZM 3D + measure (X, Y, Z, M) QgsWkbTypes.LineStringZ 3D line QgsWkbTypes.PolygonZ 3D polygon 
# create a 3D Point layer
writer = QgsVectorFileWriter(
    r'C:\GIS\points_3d.shp',
    'UTF-8',
    fields,
    QgsWkbTypes.PointZ,                         # ← Z coordinate
    QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem('EPSG:32638'),
    'ESRI Shapefile'
)
del writer

docs.title: 📊 WKB numeric values
docs.text:
QgsWkbTypes constants are actually integers (the OGC WKB standard):

print(int(QgsWkbTypes.Point))        # → 1
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.LineString))   # → 2
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.Polygon))      # → 3
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.MultiPoint))   # → 4
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.PointZ))       # → 1001
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.PointM))       # → 2001
print(int(QgsWkbTypes.PointZM))      # → 3001

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• QgsWkbTypes defines the geometry type in PyQGIS
  • It is used in QgsVectorFileWriter, QgsMemoryLayer and other classes
  • It supports 2D, 3D (Z) and M types
  • displayString() returns the geometry name as a string
  • geometryType() converts to a general category

👉 Every time you create a new layer or check a geometry type, QgsWkbTypes is your first tool.

docs.title: What is iface?
docs.text: iface is a QgisInterface object that gives the Python console and QGIS plugins access to the QGIS graphical user interface (GUI). With it you can: - add/remove layers - control the map view - show messages to the user - interact with the project window

docs.title: Description
docs.text: iface.addVectorLayer() is used to add a vector layer to the QGIS interface.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: iface.addVectorLayer(path, layer_name, provider)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• path (str) – file path or data source URI
  • layer_name (str) – the name in the Layers Panel
  • provider (str) – data provider (e.g. "ogr", "postgres", "spatialite", "memory")

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: Returns a QgsVectorLayer object (or None if the layer failed to load).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Shapefile
iface.addVectorLayer("C:/data/roads.shp", "Roads", "ogr")

# GeoJSON
iface.addVectorLayer("C:/data/buildings.geojson", "Buildings", "ogr")

# PostGIS
uri = "dbname='gisdb' host=localhost port=5432 user='postgres' password='1234' table=\"public\".\"roads\" (geom)"
iface.addVectorLayer(uri, "Roads from PostGIS", "postgres")

docs.title: Alternative: QgsVectorLayer + QgsProject
docs.text:
layer = QgsVectorLayer("C:/data/roads.shp", "Roads", "ogr")
if layer.isValid():
    QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(layer)

docs.title: 1. Controlling the map view
docs.text:
• iface.mapCanvas() – returns the map canvas object
  • iface.zoomIn() – zoom in
  • iface.zoomOut() – zoom out
  • iface.zoomFull() – zoom to the full extent
  • iface.zoomToActiveLayer() – zoom to the active layer

docs.title: 2. Working with layers
docs.text:
• iface.activeLayer() – returns the currently active layer
  • iface.addRasterLayer(path, name) – add a raster layer
  • iface.legendInterface() (QGIS 2.x) – layer control (QGIS 3 uses QgsLayerTree)

docs.title: 3. Messages and dialogs
docs.text:
• iface.messageBar().pushMessage("Title", "Text") – show a message in the Message Bar
  • iface.messageBar().pushWarning("Warning", "Something went wrong")
  • iface.messageBar().pushSuccess("Success", "Operation completed")

docs.title: 4. GUI windows and panels
docs.text:
• iface.mainWindow() – returns the QGIS main window (a QMainWindow object)
  • iface.layerTreeView() – returns the layer tree view
  • iface.newProject() – creates a new empty project

docs.title: 5. Cursor position
docs.text:
• iface.mapCanvas().mouseLastXY() – the last cursor coordinates on the canvas
  • iface.mapCanvas().extent() – the current extent

docs.title: Where iface is used
docs.text:
• QGIS Python Console – for running scripts directly
  • QGIS Plugins – for reacting to the GUI and managing layers
  • Teaching examples – when introducing students to the QGIS API

docs.title: ✍️ Summary
docs.text:
• iface = QgisInterface, which connects Python with the QGIS interface.
  • iface.addVectorLayer() adds a vector layer to the GUI.
  • iface also covers map control, showing messages, layer control and access to the project window.

docs.title: 📂 Writing directory paths correctly in Python
docs.text: When writing file and directory paths in Python, it is important to tell the backslash (\) and the forward slash (/) apart correctly.

docs.title: ✅ Valid ways to write directory paths
docs.text:
Python has more than one way to write a path correctly:

  • a double backslash (\)
  • a forward slash (/)
  • the raw string syntax (r"...")

If you use / or \\, the r prefix is no longer required.

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
r"C:\Lessons\Georgia.gpkg\ambulances"
"C:/Lessons/Georgia.gpkg/ambulances"
"C:\\Lessons\\Georgia.gpkg\\ambulances"

All of these are correct and interchangeable.

docs.title: 🔹 Paths in code
docs.text:
In Python a single backslash () is used as the escape character. Because of this, in paths it is recommended to use a double backslash (\), a raw string (r"...") or a forward slash (/).

Examples:

r"C:\QGIS\PyQGIS\database.gpkg"
"C:/QGIS/PyQGIS/database.gpkg"
"C:\\QGIS\\PyQGIS\\database.gpkg"

docs.title: 🔑 The escape character in Python
docs.text: The escape character is the backslash ( \ ), which is used to output special characters.

docs.title: Quotes inside a string
docs.text:
Special characters
City = "My city is \"Chiatura!\""
print(City)
# output: My city is "Chiatura!"

docs.title: New line \n
docs.text:
New line
City = "My city is \nChiatura"
print(City)
# output:
# My city is
# Chiatura

docs.title: Tab \t
docs.text:
Tab character
City = "My city is \tChiatura"
print(City)
# output: My city is   Chiatura

docs.title: Backslash \\
docs.text:
If we need the backslash itself to appear, we write it twice:

Backslash
path = "C:\\QGIS\\PyQGIS\\database.gpkg"
print(path)
# output: C:\QGIS\PyQGIS\database.gpkg

docs.title: 🖼️ Path examples at a glance
docs.text:
Examples of Windows and Linux paths:

Windows:   C:\Users\Student\Documents\project\data.csv
Linux:     /home/student/project/data.csv
Raw string: r"C:\Users\Student\Documents\project\data.csv"

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
• ** → the escape character (for special characters).
  • \ → a real backslash in a path.
  • / → can be used on Windows too.
  • r"..." → raw string, removes the need for escape characters.

👉 All of this is essential in Python for writing correct paths and keeping text accurate.

docs.title: ESRI Shapefile — technical specification
docs.text: Source: ESRI White Paper — July 1998 This page: a structured summary for the documentation

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Why Shapefile?
  2. Technical description
  3. File structure
  4. Naming conventions
  5. Numeric types
  6. Organization of the main file (.shp)
  7. Byte order
  8. File header
  9. Record header
  10. Record contents: geometry types
  11. Null Shape
  12. Point
  13. MultiPoint
  14. PolyLine
  15. Polygon
  16. Measured types (M)
  17. Three-dimensional types (Z)
  18. MultiPatch
  19. Organization of the index file (.shx)
  20. Organization of the dBASE file (.dbf)
  21. Glossary

docs.title: Why Shapefile?
docs.text: A shapefile stores non-topological geometry and attribute information for spatial features. The geometry of each feature is stored as a set of vector coordinates.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Fast drawing: there is no processing overhead for a topological data structure
  • Simple editing: data is easy to change
  • Flexibility: overlapping and non-contiguous features are supported
  • Compactness: it usually needs less disk space
  • Accessibility: easy to read and write

Shapefiles support point, line and area features. Area features are represented as closed-loop, double-digitized polygons. Attributes are kept in a dBASE format file, where each attribute record has a one-to-one relationship with the associated shape record.

docs.title: Ways to create a shapefile
docs.text: Method Description Export Convert any data source using ARC/INFO, ArcView GIS, SDE or BusinessMAP Digitizing Draw directly with ArcView GIS tools Programming Use Avenue, MapObjects, AML or SML scripts Direct writing Write your own program following the specification

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
An ESRI shapefile consists of three files:

counties.shp   ← main file (geometry)
counties.shx   ← index file (offsets)
counties.dbf   ← dBASE table (attributes)
File Extension Contents Main file .shp Geometry — vector coordinates Index file .shx Offsets of the records in the main file dBASE table .dbf Attribute data

The main file is a direct-access, variable-record-length file in which each record describes a shape with a list of its vertices. The index file: each record contains the offset of the corresponding main-file record from the beginning of the file. The dBASE table contains the attributes, one record per feature.

⚠️ The attribute records in the dBASE file must be in the same order as the shape records in the main file.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
All file names follow the 8.3 format:

  • the prefix is the same for all three files
  • the prefix starts with an alphanumeric character (a–Z, 0–9)
  • followed by 0 to 7 characters (a–Z, 0–9, _, -)
  • on case-sensitive systems the file names are lowercase

docs.title: Numeric types
docs.text:
A shapefile uses two main numeric types:

Type Definition Size Integer Signed 32-bit integer 4 bytes Double Signed 64-bit IEEE double-precision floating point 8 bytes

"No data" value: any floating-point number smaller than –10³⁸ is treated as "no data". A shapefile does not store +∞, –∞ or NaN values.

docs.title: Byte order
docs.text:
A shapefile uses two byte orders:

Type Order Used for Big Endian (Motorola / Sun) Left to right File management fields (length, offsets) Little Endian (Intel / PC) Right to left Data fields (coordinates, shape type)

docs.title: File header
docs.text:
The main file header is 100 bytes. Positions are from the start of the file:

Byte Field Value Type Order 0 File Code 9994 Integer Big 4–20 Unused 0 Integer Big 24 File Length File length (in 16-bit words) Integer Big 28 Version 1000 Integer Little 32 Shape Type Shape type Integer Little 36 Bounding Box Xmin Double Little 44 Bounding Box Ymin Double Little 52 Bounding Box Xmax Double Little 60 Bounding Box Ymax Double Little 68* Bounding Box Zmin Double Little 76* Bounding Box Zmax Double Little 84* Bounding Box Mmin Double Little 92* Bounding Box Mmax Double Little

* 0.0 if the type is not Measured or Z

File Length = the total length of the file in 16-bit words (including the 50 words of the header).

docs.title: Shape types
docs.text:
Code Type 0 Null Shape 1 Point 3 PolyLine 5 Polygon 8 MultiPoint 11 PointZ 13 PolyLineZ 15 PolygonZ 18 MultiPointZ 21 PointM 23 PolyLineM 25 PolygonM 28 MultiPointM 31 MultiPatch

✏️ Currently all shapes in a file must be of the same type. Mixed types may be allowed in the future.

docs.title: Record header
docs.text:
Each record header is 8 bytes (fixed):

Byte Field Value Type Order 0 Record Number Record number (starts at 1) Integer Big 4 Content Length Content length (in 16-bit words) Integer Big

docs.title: Null Shape
docs.text:
A null shape has no geometric data. It is used as a placeholder when creating a file.

Byte Field Value Type 0 Shape Type 0 Integer

docs.title: Point
docs.text:
A point consists of a pair of double-precision X, Y coordinates.

Point {
    Double X  // X coordinate
    Double Y  // Y coordinate
}
Byte Field Type 0 Shape Type (1) Integer 4 X Double 12 Y Double

docs.title: MultiPoint
docs.text:
Represents a set of points.

MultiPoint {
    Double[4] Box        // Bounding Box (Xmin, Ymin, Xmax, Ymax)
    Integer   NumPoints  // number of points
    Point[NumPoints] Points  // the points
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (8) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumPoints Integer 1 40 Points Point NumPoints

docs.title: PolyLine
docs.text:
A polyline is an ordered set of vertices consisting of one or more parts. A part is a connected sequence of two or more vertices. Parts may or may not be connected to one another.

PolyLine {
    Double[4]        Box        // Bounding Box
    Integer          NumParts   // number of parts
    Integer          NumPoints  // total number of vertices
    Integer[NumParts] Parts     // index of the first vertex of each part
    Point[NumPoints] Points     // vertices of all parts
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (3) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumParts Integer 1 40 NumPoints Integer 1 44 Parts Integer NumParts X* Points Point NumPoints

* X = 44 + 4 × NumParts

Field definitions: - Box: the bounding box in the order Xmin, Ymin, Xmax, Ymax - Parts: an array (length = NumParts) holding, for each part, the index of its first vertex in the Points array (0-based) - Points: the vertices of all parts in sequence; there is no delimiter between parts

docs.title: Polygon
docs.text:
A polygon consists of one or more rings. A ring is a closed, non-self-intersecting loop of four or more vertices. A polygon may have several outer rings.

Polygon {
    Double[4]         Box        // Bounding Box
    Integer           NumParts   // number of rings
    Integer           NumPoints  // total number of vertices
    Integer[NumParts] Parts      // index of the first vertex of each ring
    Point[NumPoints]  Points     // vertices of all rings
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (5) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumParts Integer 1 40 NumPoints Integer 1 44 Parts Integer NumParts X* Points Point NumPoints

* X = 44 + 4 × NumParts

docs.title: ⚠️ Important rules for polygons
docs.text:
1. Rings are closed: the first and last vertex must be the same point.
  2. Vertex order:
  3. outer (solid) rings: vertices in clockwise order
  4. hole rings: vertices in counterclockwise order
  5. A "clean" polygon:
  6. must not self-intersect
  7. segments of different rings must not cross (touching only at vertices is allowed)
  8. The order of the rings in the Points array does not matter

Example (NumParts=2, NumPoints=10 — a polygon with a hole): 

Parts:  [0, 5]
Points: [v1, v2, v3, v4, v1,  v5, v8, v7, v6, v5]
         ← outer ring →       ← hole (CCW) →

docs.title: Measured types (M)
docs.text: M-type shapes have an extra measure coordinate (M). A "no data" value may be given for M.

docs.title: PointM
docs.text:
PointM {
    Double X  // X coordinate
    Double Y  // Y coordinate
    Double M  // measure
}
Byte Field Type 0 Shape Type (21) Integer 4 X Double 12 Y Double 20 M Double

docs.title: MultiPointM
docs.text:
MultiPointM {
    Double[4]        Box       // Bounding Box
    Integer          NumPoints // number of points
    Point[NumPoints] Points    // the points
    Double[2]        M Range   // Mmin, Mmax
    Double[NumPoints] M Array  // M values
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (28) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumPoints Integer 1 40 Points Point NumPoints X* Mmin Double 1 X+8* Mmax Double 1 X+16* Marray Double NumPoints

* X = 40 + 16 × NumPoints · (* optional)

docs.title: PolyLineM
docs.text:
PolyLineM {
    Double[4]         Box
    Integer           NumParts
    Integer           NumPoints
    Integer[NumParts] Parts
    Point[NumPoints]  Points
    Double[2]         M Range   // Mmin, Mmax
    Double[NumPoints] M Array
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (23) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumParts Integer 1 40 NumPoints Integer 1 44 Parts Integer NumParts X Points Point NumPoints Y* Mmin Double 1 Y+8* Mmax Double 1 Y+16* Marray Double NumPoints

X = 44 + 4×NumParts · Y = X + 16×NumPoints · (* optional)

docs.title: PolygonM
docs.text: The structure is identical to PolyLineM (Shape Type = 25). The rules are the same as for Polygon: - rings are closed - the order of the rings in Points does not matter

docs.title: Three-dimensional types (Z)
docs.text: Z-type shapes have a Z coordinate and an optional M measure.

docs.title: PointZ
docs.text:
PointZ {
    Double X
    Double Y
    Double Z
    Double M  // measure
}
Byte Field Type 0 Shape Type (11) Integer 4 X Double 12 Y Double 20 Z Double 28 M Double

docs.title: MultiPointZ
docs.text:
MultiPointZ {
    Double[4]         Box
    Integer           NumPoints
    Point[NumPoints]  Points
    Double[2]         Z Range    // Zmin, Zmax
    Double[NumPoints] Z Array
    Double[2]         M Range    // Mmin, Mmax  (optional)
    Double[NumPoints] M Array    // (optional)
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (18) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumPoints Integer 1 40 Points Point NumPoints X Zmin Double 1 X+8 Zmax Double 1 X+16 Zarray Double NumPoints Y* Mmin Double 1 Y+8* Mmax Double 1 Y+16* Marray Double NumPoints

X = 40 + 16×NumPoints · Y = X + 16 + 8×NumPoints

docs.title: PolyLineZ
docs.text:
PolyLineZ {
    Double[4]         Box
    Integer           NumParts
    Integer           NumPoints
    Integer[NumParts] Parts
    Point[NumPoints]  Points
    Double[2]         Z Range
    Double[NumPoints] Z Array
    Double[2]         M Range    // optional
    Double[NumPoints] M Array    // optional
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (13) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumParts Integer 1 40 NumPoints Integer 1 44 Parts Integer NumParts X Points Point NumPoints Y Zmin Double 1 Y+8 Zmax Double 1 Y+16 Zarray Double NumPoints Z* Mmin Double 1 Z+8* Mmax Double 1 Z+16* Marray Double NumPoints

X = 44 + 4×NumParts · Y = X + 16×NumPoints · Z = Y + 16 + 8×NumPoints

docs.title: PolygonZ
docs.text: The structure is identical to PolyLineZ (Shape Type = 15). The rules are the same as for Polygon: - rings are closed - Z values are stored end to end, with no delimiter between parts

docs.title: MultiPatch
docs.text: A MultiPatch consists of a number of surface patches. Each patch describes a surface. The patch type determines how the order of the vertices is interpreted.

docs.title: Part types
docs.text:
Code Type Description 0 Triangle Strip A chain of triangles — each new vertex forms a new triangle with the two previous vertices 1 Triangle Fan A fan of triangles — each new vertex forms a triangle with the previous vertex and the first vertex 2 Outer Ring The outer ring of a polygon 3 Inner Ring A hole ring of a polygon 4 First Ring The first ring of a polygon (type unspecified) 5 Ring A ring of a polygon (type unspecified) 
MultiPatch {
    Double[4]         Box
    Integer           NumParts
    Integer           NumPoints
    Integer[NumParts] Parts
    Integer[NumParts] PartTypes   // ← not present in PolyLine!
    Point[NumPoints]  Points
    Double[2]         Z Range
    Double[NumPoints] Z Array
    Double[2]         M Range     // optional
    Double[NumPoints] M Array     // optional
}
Byte Field Type Count 0 Shape Type (31) Integer 1 4 Box Double 4 36 NumParts Integer 1 40 NumPoints Integer 1 44 Parts Integer NumParts W PartTypes Integer NumParts X Points Point NumPoints Y Zmin Double 1 Y+8 Zmax Double 1 Y+16 Zarray Double NumPoints Z* Mmin Double 1 Z+8* Mmax Double 1 Z+16* Marray Double NumPoints

W = 44 + 4×NumParts · X = W + 4×NumParts · Y = X + 16×NumPoints · Z = Y + 16 + 8×NumPoints

docs.title: ⚠️ Important rules for MultiPatch
docs.text:
• Ring-type parts must be closed (first = last vertex)
  • The order of rings matters: an Inner Ring must follow its Outer Ring
  • A sequence of rings describing one surface patch must start with a First Ring
  • Parts may share boundaries, but they must not intersect each other

docs.title: Organization of the index file (.shx)
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────┐
│     File header     │  (100 bytes — identical to the main file)
├─────────────────────┤
│       Record        │  (8 bytes, fixed)
├─────────────────────┤
│       Record        │
├─────────────────────┤
│         ...         │
└─────────────────────┘

The header is a full copy of the main file header (100 bytes). The difference: File Length is the total length of the index file in 16-bit words (50 words of header + 4 × number of records).

docs.title: Index record
docs.text:
The I-th record stores the offset and content length of the I-th record of the main file:

Byte Field Type Order 0 Offset Integer Big 4 Content Length Integer Big
  • Offset: the number of 16-bit words from the start of the file to the first byte of the record header
  • The offset of the first record = 50 (100-byte header ÷ 2)
  • Content Length in the index record is identical to the value stored in the main file's record header

docs.title: Organization of the dBASE file (.dbf)
docs.text: The .dbf file contains the attributes, or attribute keys that can be joined to other tables. It is the standard DBF format used by many Windows and DOS applications.

docs.title: Mandatory requirements
docs.text:
1. File name: the same prefix as the .shp and .shx files (extension: .dbf)
  2. Number of records: one record per shape
  3. Record order: the same order as the shapes in the main file
  4. Year value in the dBASE header: the number of years since 1900

💡 Any combination of fields can be in the table; there are no restrictions on field names or types.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition big endian A byte order where the "most significant" byte is on the left (first). UNIX systems: Sun, HP, IBM little endian A byte order where the "least significant" byte is on the left (first). PC/Windows systems Bounding Box A rectangle that exactly encloses a shape. Defined by: Xmin, Ymin, Xmax, Ymax coverage An ARC/INFO unit of vector data; stores geographic features with a topological structure feature A representation of a geographic object — geometry + a set of attributes index file The shapefile's index file — gives direct access to the main file's records MultiPoint A cluster of points linked to one attribute record NumPoints The total number of X,Y vertices in a shape PolyLine An ordered set of X,Y vertices representing a line or boundary ring A closed sequence of X,Y vertices (first = last vertex); a closed PolyLine or Polygon shapefile ArcView GIS data format that represents geographic features (point, line, area) theme A user-defined set of geographic features in ArcView GIS topology Spatial relationships between adjacent or connected features. A shapefile does not store topology vector A data structure for geographic features based on Cartesian (X,Y) coordinates vertex One pair of X,Y coordinates that makes up a line

docs.title: Quizzes
docs.text:
JavaScript is required for the quiz.

Language

The quiz starts in Georgian. Press KA → EN to switch to English; the choice is remembered.

How do I add a new subject?

  1. Create docs/Quiz/data/<subject>.js (see gis.js as an example).
  2. Add the file name to the data-subjects attribute on this page (and on the Georgian index.md).
